docs.title: 2. Actions, Routing, Responses
docs.text: This chapter examines the path a request takes, from the browser to the action that processes it, and the response that action returns. Views will not be covered until Chapter 4: here, actions return text or JSON directly.

docs.title: 2.1. Example 01: The Structure of a Laravel Application
docs.text:
The first example is the smallest possible [Laravel] application. A project created by [composer create-project laravel/laravel] contains about fifty files and folders (see introduction); here, we’ll keep only those that the application cannot do without:

01-structure/
├── bootstrap/
│   ├── cache/
│   └── app.php
├── public/
│   └── index.php
├── routes/
│   └── web.php
├── storage/
├── .env
├── artisan
└── composer.json
  • [public/index.php]: the application’s entry point. All requests for HTTP, regardless of their URL, are handled by this file. The [public] folder is the only folder that the web server serves: it also contains static files (style sheets, images, scripts), and only those;
  • [bootstrap/app.php]: the application’s build and configuration. The [bootstrap/cache] folder receives files that [Laravel] calculates itself to start up faster;
  • [routes/web.php]: the routing table, which associates each URL with the action that processes it;
  • [storage]: the files that the application writes during operation: the error log ([storage/logs]), sessions, the cache, and compiled views ([storage/framework]);
  • [.env]: the application configuration, in the form of [NOM=valeur] pairs;
  • [artisan]: the command-line tool for [Laravel];
  • [composer.json]: the project description for [Composer].

docs.title: 2.1.1. The entry point: public/index.php
docs.text:
<?php
// public/index.php: the entry point for TOUTES requests HTTP

use Illuminate\Http\Request;

// the Composer class loader (shared in the examples/vendor folder)
require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php';

// the application, built by bootstrap/app.php, processes the current request
$app = require_once __DIR__.'/../bootstrap/app.php';
$app->handleRequest(Request::capture());
  • Line 1: A [PHP] file begins with the [<?php] tag. Everything that follows is [PHP] code; a file containing only code does not close this tag;
  • line 2: a comment, from [//] to the end of the line ([/* ... */] delimits a multi-line comment);
  • line 4: the statement [use] imports a class name. The full name of a class [PHP] includes its namespace (*namespace*), the equivalent of packages in [Java]: [Illuminate\Http\Request] is the class [Request] in the namespace [Illuminate\Http]. After [use], the file can simply be named [Request]. [Illuminate] is the code name for the components of [Laravel];
  • Line 7: [require] executes another file, [PHP]. [__DIR__] is the directory of the current file (here, [public]); the operator [.] concatenates two strings. The file [vendor/autoload.php], written by [Composer], installs the class loader: the first time a class is used, it finds and loads the file that defines it. Thanks to this, we never have to write a [require] file for classes. The [vendor] folder is the same as the [exemples] folder, shared by all the examples (see introduction): hence the two [..] files;
  • Line 10: A file executed by [require] can return a value using the instruction [return]: [bootstrap/app.php] returns the application—an object of class [Illuminate\Foundation\Application]—stored in the variable [$app]. In [PHP], variable names always begin with [$]. [require_once] would do nothing if the file had already been executed;
  • line 11: [Request::capture()] calls the static method [capture] of the class [Request] (the operator [::] refers to a member of a class, while the operator [->] refers to a member of an object). It creates a [Request] object from the HTTP request received by [PHP]. [$app->handleRequest(...)] has the application process this request and sends the response to the browser.

This file is the same for all examples, and—with the exception of two [..] files—is the same as that of a standard [Laravel] project. It highlights a unique feature of [PHP], which explains a lot about [Laravel]: the application is rebuilt with every request. The web server executes [public/index.php] from start to finish for each request it receives: it loads the classes, builds the application, processes the request, sends the response, and then forgets everything. No objects survive from one request to the next. In the chapter on data scopes, we will see the consequences of this behavior, which is the opposite of that of [Java], [C#], or [Python], whose applications remain in memory between requests.

docs.title: 2.1.2. The application structure: bootstrap/app.php
docs.text:
<?php
// bootstrap/app.php: application build and configuration

use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;

// The classes in the CET example (App namespace) are located in the app/ folder
(require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php')->addPsr4('App\\', __DIR__.'/../app/');

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
     // The application routes are defined in the routes/web.php file
    ->withRouting(web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php')
     // Middleware and exception handling: default settings
    ->withMiddleware()
    ->withExceptions()
    ->create();
  • Line 7: The class loader for [Composer] knows the classes in the libraries located in the [vendor] folder. It must also know the application’s classes, which are conventionally stored in its [app] folder, under the [App] namespace. In a standard project, [Composer] obtains this information from the project’s [composer.json] file. Our examples share a single folder named [vendor], but each has its own folder named [app]: each example therefore declares it to the loader itself, via its [addPsr4] method (the [PSR-4] standard maps namespaces to folders: the [App\Http\Controllers\PremierController] class is in the [app/Http/Controllers/PremierController.php] file). A [require] returns the value of the executed file; [vendor/autoload.php] returns the loader (it installs it only once, even if executed twice). In a string enclosed in single quotes, [\\] refers to a single character, [\]. This example does not yet have a [app] file: the line is there for the following ones;
  • line 9: the application’s construction. [Application::configure(...)] returns a builder object (*builder*), each method of which configures an aspect of the application and returns the builder itself, allowing calls to be chained; [create()] finally builds the application. The parameter [basePath: dirname(__DIR__)] is a named parameter: the value is associated with the parameter [basePath] by its name, not by its position. [dirname(__DIR__)] is the parent folder of [bootstrap]—that is, the folder in the example: it is from this folder that [Laravel] locates all the others ([routes], [storage]...);
  • Line 11: The application routes are those in the [routes/web.php] file. The name [web] is significant: these routes receive middleware from the [web] group (sessions, encrypted cookies, anti-CSRF protection, etc.), which are suitable for an application that generates HTML pages. We’ll encounter them throughout the chapters;
  • lines 13–14: the middleware and exception handling, with their default settings. We’ll expand on these in the following examples.

docs.title: 2.1.3. The routing table: routes/web.php
docs.text:
<?php
// routes/web.php: the smallest possible Laravel application, with a single route

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

// An action: the function called for the request GET /
Route::get('/', function () {
     // the value returned by the function EST the response sent to the browser
    return 'Bonjour de la part de Laravel !';
});
  • line 4: importing the [Route] class. This is a facade for [Laravel]: a class whose static methods ([Route::get]) forward the call to an application object, in this case the router. Facades are one of the hallmarks of [Laravel]: they provide quick access to the application’s services without having to obtain the object that provides them;
  • Lines 7–10: [Route::get] declares a route: requests for [GET /] will be handled by the function specified as the second parameter. This is routing. This function has no name: it is an anonymous function—a value like any other—that can be passed as a parameter. The function associated with a route is an action. There are also [Route::post], [Route::put], [Route::delete]...;
  • line 9: the action returns a string. The value returned by an action is the response sent to the browser: [Laravel] places it in the body of the response HTTP. A string enclosed in single quotes (['...']) is written as-is; when enclosed in double quotes (["..."]), the variables it contains are replaced with their values (e.g., 02).

docs.title: 2.1.4. Configuration: .env
docs.text:
# .env: the application configuration, specific to each installation
APP_NAME="Exemple 01"
# local: the development environment
APP_ENV=local
# the application’s secret key, created by: php artisan key:generate
APP_KEY=base64:g8MwuoKVJMhijOpvCTna/El25lmlLhjXCmmfqz3e3G8=
# true: detailed error pages, for development (JAMAIS in production)
APP_DEBUG=true
# Sessions and cache are stored in files under the `storage` folder
SESSION_DRIVER=file
CACHE_STORE=file

The file [.env] contains settings specific to a given installation of the application: the same application, installed on a developer’s machine and on a production server, will not have the same [.env]. Furthermore, this file must not be published with the source code (it contains secrets). Lines beginning with [#] are comments.

  • Line 2: the application name. [Laravel] uses this, for example, to name the session cookie ([exemple01_session], below);
  • line 4: the environment: [local] for development, [production] on a server;
  • line 6: the application’s secret key: 32 random bytes, encoded in base 64. [Laravel] uses it to encrypt cookies and sign certain data (we’ll come back to this). It is created by the command [php artisan key:generate], which writes it to the file [.env]; each example has its own. Without it, the application refuses to start (“No application encryption key has been specified”);
  • line 8: debug mode: an unhandled exception displays a detailed page (see Example 03). This mode is intended for development, and development only: the error page reveals the application’s source code and configuration;
  • Lines 10–11: Sessions and the cache (see the chapter on scopes) are stored in files within the [storage] folder. By default, [Laravel] stores them in a database, which we do not yet have.

Anything that [Laravel] cannot find in [.env] retains its default value. These default values are defined by the framework’s configuration files ([vendor/laravel/framework/config/*.php]); a standard project has a copy of these in its [config] folder, which can be modified. Our examples do without them: a few lines of [.env] are sufficient.

docs.title: 2.1.5. The artisan tool and the composer.json file
docs.text:
The [artisan] file is a [PHP] script that builds the application, just like [public/index.php], but to execute a command rather than process a request:

#!/usr/bin/env php
<?php
// artisan: Laravel’s command-line tool (php artisan serve, php artisan route:list...)

use Symfony\Component\Console\Input\ArgvInput;

// Composer’s class loader: the `vendor` folder is the same as the one in the examples folder,
// shared by all examples
require __DIR__.'/../vendor/autoload.php';

// The application, built by bootstrap/app.php, executes the requested command
$app = require_once __DIR__.'/bootstrap/app.php';
exit($app->handleCommand(new ArgvInput));
  • Line 1: In [Linux] and [macOS], this line allows the file to be executed directly ([./artisan]); for [Windows], you always enter [php artisan];
  • Line 13: [ArgvInput] represents the command-line parameters ([serve], [route:list]...); [handleCommand] executes the command and returns its exit code.

[php artisan list] displays the list of available commands: about a hundred, of which we will use a few. Finally, the file [composer.json] describes the example:

{
    "name": "exemples/01-structure",
    "description": "Exemple 01 : la structure d'une application Laravel",
    "autoload": {
        "psr-4": {
            "App\\": "app/"
        }
    }
}

This is a JSON document. [Laravel] reads the application’s class namespace ([App\], located in the [app/] folder) from this file, which it needs, for example, to distinguish the application’s code from the framework’s code in its error pages. The [composer.json] file for a standard project also contains the list of its libraries; for the examples, this list is in the [exemples/composer.json] file (see introduction).

docs.title: 2.1.6. Execution
docs.text:
In a terminal window open to the [01-structure] folder, type [php artisan serve]. [Laravel] displays:

   INFO  Server running on [http://127.0.0.1:8000].

  Press Ctrl+C to stop the server

The command [serve] launches the development server integrated into [PHP] ([php -S]), which is configured to forward all requests to [public/index.php] (except for requests for files located in the [public] folder, which it sends as-is). It listens on port 8000 at the address [127.0.0.1], which is the address of the machine itself ([localhost]): it accepts only requests from this machine, which is suitable for development ([--host=0.0.0.0] would open it to other machines on the network; [--port=8001] would change the port). It is stopped by [Ctrl-C]. This server is intended for development: in production, it will be a web server such as [Apache] or [Nginx], paired with [PHP-FPM] (see case study). It is not necessary to restart it after a code change: since [PHP] re-reads the files with every request, the change takes effect on the next request. Only a change to the file [.env] requires a restart, which the command [serve] performs automatically.

Let’s request URL and [http://localhost:8000/] using a browser:

then with [curl]. The [-i] option also displays the HTTP headers from the response:

curl -i http://localhost:8000/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Host: localhost:8000
Connection: close
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.4.21
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Cache-Control: no-cache, private
Date: Sat, 26 Sep 2026 15:49:59 GMT
Set-Cookie: XSRF-TOKEN=eyJpdiI6InZTa2ViTjhuTS9NL1J5aEZh...; expires=Sat, 26 Sep 2026 17:49:59 GMT; Max-Age=7200; path=/; samesite=lax
Set-Cookie: exemple01_session=eyJpdiI6IlZFY3NlN056Z3NQZmFG...; expires=Sat, 26 Sep 2026 17:49:59 GMT; Max-Age=7200; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax

Bonjour de la part de Laravel !

The first line of the response is the protocol version, the status code (200), and its label ([OK]). Next come the headers: the requested host, [Connection: close] (the development server closes the connection after each response), the version, [PHP], the content type, a cache directive, the date, and two cookies. An empty line separates the headers from the body of the response. In the rest of this document, we will no longer reproduce the headers for [Host], [Connection], [X-Powered-By], [Cache-Control], and [Date]—which do not vary—nor the cookies, except when they are the subject of the example.

The header [Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8] indicates that the response is HTML, whose characters are encoded in UTF-8. This is the default encoding ([Laravel]) for any string returned by an action: the browser therefore interprets the string as HTML (here, without a tag, it is displayed as-is). Example 03 will show how to specify a different encoding type.

The two cookies may come as a surprise: the application did not request either of them. They are set by two middleware components from the [web] group (see [bootstrap/app.php]): [exemple01_session] identifies the user’s session, and [XSRF-TOKEN] contains the anti-CSRF token. Their values are encrypted with the key [APP_KEY]. We’ll examine them in Examples 20 and 21.

For each request, the server console displays a log entry: the date, the requested path, and the processing time.

  2026-09-26 17:49:51 / ............................................ ~ 0.09ms

docs.title: 2.2. Example 02: Routing
docs.text:
Routing associates a URL and a method HTTP (GET, POST...) with an action. Writing all the actions in [routes/web.php] as anonymous functions would quickly become unreadable; instead, they are organized into classes—the controllers. Example 02 has two of them:

02-routage/
├── app/
│   └── Http/
│       └── Controllers/
│           ├── AccueilController.php
│           └── PremierController.php
├── bootstrap/
│   └── app.php
├── routes/
│   └── web.php
└── ...

The files [artisan], [public/index.php], [composer.json], and [.env], as well as the folders [bootstrap/cache] and [storage], are the same as those in Example 01: we will not mention them again (only the example name and the secret key change). Each controller is a class in the [App\Http\Controllers] namespace, located in the [app/Http/Controllers] folder: this is the convention for [Laravel], and the standard [PSR-4] maps the two together (Example 01).

docs.title: 2.2.1. The AccueilController controller
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/AccueilController.php: the home page

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

class AccueilController
{
     // GET /: a page (HTML) that contains links to other actions.
     // A string returned by an action is sent with the text/html MIME type
    public function index(): string
    {
        return <<<'HTML'
            <h2>Exemple 02 - le routage</h2>
            <ul>
              <li><a href="/premier">/premier</a></li>
              <li><a href="/premier/action01">/premier/action01</a></li>
              <li><a href="/premier/produits/17">/premier/produits/17</a></li>
              <li><a href="/premier/produits/17/avis/3">/premier/produits/17/avis/3</a></li>
              <li><a href="/premier/fichiers/images/logo.png">/premier/fichiers/images/logo.png</a></li>
              <li><a href="/premier/produits/abc">/premier/produits/abc</a></li>
              <li><a href="/inconnue">/inconnue</a></li>
            </ul>
            HTML;
    }
}
  • line 4: the class namespace. Its full name is therefore [App\Http\Controllers\AccueilController];
  • line 6: the class. By convention, a class name is written with a capital letter at the beginning of each word ([AccueilController]), while a method or variable name starts with a lowercase letter ([action01Post]). A controller named [Laravel] does not need to inherit from any class;
  • line 10: the action [index], a public method of the class (the router can only call public methods). [: string] declares the type of the returned value: a string. Types are optional in [PHP], but when they are specified, [PHP] checks them at runtime;
  • lines 12–23: a multi-line string. The syntax [<<<'HTML'] ... [HTML] (*nowdoc*) delimits text that is written as-is, between two lines containing the same word, in this case [HTML]; the indentation of the closing line is removed from all lines. The action returns HTML, sent with the type [text/html] (see Example 01).

The action [index] thus returns a page HTML that contains links to the actions of the other controller:

docs.title: 2.2.2. The controller PremierController
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/PremierController.php: the actions for URL /first/...

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

class PremierController
{
     // GET /first
    public function index(): string
    {
        return 'Action [index] du contrôleur [PremierController]';
    }

     // GET /first/action01
    public function action01(): string
    {
        return 'Action [action01] du contrôleur [PremierController], requête GET';
    }

     // POST /first/action01
    public function action01Post(): string
    {
        return 'Action [action01Post] du contrôleur [PremierController], requête POST';
    }

     // GET /first/products/17: the route parameter {id} is passed to the
     // action parameter $id; the int type converts it to an integer
    public function produit(int $id): string
    {
        return "Produit n° $id";
    }

     // GET /first/products/17/reviews/3: two route parameters
    public function avis(int $id, int $numero): string
    {
        return "Avis n° $numero du produit n° $id";
    }

     // GET /first/files/images/logo.png
    public function fichier(string $chemin): string
    {
        return "Fichier demandé : $chemin";
    }
}
  • lines 9–11: the same [index] method as in the other controller: there is no conflict, as each controller is a different class;
  • lines 21–23: the action for the request [POST /premier/action01]. The name of an action can be anything; it is the routing table that associates it with a URL and a method HTTP;
  • lines 28–30: The action’s parameter [$id] receives the value of the route parameter [{id}] (see [routes/web.php]): for URL and [/premier/produits/17], it is 17. The [int] parameter type instructs [PHP] to convert the value (a string, extracted from URL) into an integer. This is data binding, which will be discussed in detail in the next chapter. In the string enclosed in quotes ["Produit n° $id"], the variable [$id] is replaced by its value: this is interpolation;
  • lines 34–36: two route parameters, passed to two parameters of the action. [Laravel] associates them by name: the order of the action’s parameters does not matter;
  • lines 40–42: a route parameter that contains [/].

docs.title: 2.2.3. The routing table: routes/web.php
docs.text:
<?php
// routes/web.php: the routing table from Example 02

use App\Http\Controllers\AccueilController;
use App\Http\Controllers\PremierController;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

// GET / : the action [index] of the class AccueilController
Route::get('/', [AccueilController::class, 'index']);

// a GROUPE route: the /first prefix and the controller are common to all
Route::prefix('premier')->controller(PremierController::class)->group(function () {
     // GET /first: the group’s ‘/’ route refers to the prefix itself
    Route::get('/', 'index');
     // GET /first/action01
    Route::get('action01', 'action01');
     // POST /first/action01: same path, different method HTTP, different action
    Route::post('action01', 'action01Post');
     // GET /first/products/17: {id} is a route parameter; whereNumber
     // accepts only numbers
    Route::get('produits/{id}', 'produit')->whereNumber('id');
     // GET /first/products/17/reviews/3: two route parameters
    Route::get('produits/{id}/avis/{numero}', 'avis')->whereNumber(['id', 'numero']);
     // GET /first/files/... : the expression .* accepts any ending
     // for the path, including slashes
    Route::get('fichiers/{chemin}', 'fichier')->where('chemin', '.*');
});
  • Lines 4–5: Importing the two controllers;
  • Line 9: The action is no longer an anonymous function, but an array with two elements: the controller class and the method name. [AccueilController::class] is the full name of the class, as a string (['App\Http\Controllers\AccueilController']). For each request [GET /], [Laravel] creates a [AccueilController] object and calls its method [index];
  • line 12: a route group: the routes declared in the function passed to [group] share the group’s settings. [prefix('premier')] prepends [/premier] to their paths; [controller(PremierController::class)] assigns them their controller, and each route then simply needs to name its method. The URL for an action is the concatenation of the group prefix and the path of its route;
  • line 14: the route ['/'] refers to the prefix itself: [GET /premier];
  • Lines 16–18: The same path, HTTP, corresponds to two methods: [GET] and [POST], which are handled by two different actions. There is also [Route::match(['get', 'post'], ...)], for an action that handles multiple methods, and [Route::any], for all of them;
  • Line 21: [{id}] is a route parameter: this segment of URL can take multiple values. By default, a parameter accepts any text without a slash; [whereNumber('id')] restricts the parameter to contain only digits: otherwise, the route does not match. There are also [whereAlpha] (letters), [whereUuid], [whereIn('id', [...])] (a list of values), and [where], which accepts a regular expression;
  • line 23: two route parameters, both of which are constrained ([whereNumber] accepts an array of names). In [PHP], [[a, b]] is an array (*array*);
  • line 26: the constraint [where('chemin', '.*')] is a regular expression: [.] denotes any character, and [*] denotes its repetition. The parameter therefore accepts any ending of URL, including [/].

docs.title: 2.2.4. The configuration: bootstrap/app.php
docs.text:
<?php
// bootstrap/app.php: the application in Example 02

use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Middleware;

(require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php')->addPsr4('App\\', __DIR__.'/../app/');

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php')
    ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
         // CSRF protection (Example 21) would reject requests POST
         // sent by curl: we exclude it for URL /first/...
        $middleware->preventRequestForgery(except: ['premier/*']);
    })
    ->withExceptions()
    ->create();
  • Lines 11–15: The [withMiddleware] method this time receives a function, which [Laravel] calls by passing it the [$middleware] object that describes the application’s middleware. [: void] indicates that the function returns nothing. We use it to bypass the anti-CSRF protection of URL and [/premier/...]: This protection, which we will examine in Example 21, rejects any POST request that does not originate from an application form—including those we will send using [curl]. The parameter named [except] specifies the list of paths to exclude, where [*] stands for any sequence of characters. Without this line, the request POST from [curl] would receive a 419 error response (*Page Expired*).

docs.title: 2.2.5. Execution
docs.text:
Here are the responses to a few requests:

curl -i http://localhost:8000/first

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

Action [index] du contrôleur [PremierController]

curl -i http://localhost:8000/first/products/17/reviews/3

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

Avis n° 3 du produit n° 17

curl -i http://localhost:8000/first/files/images/logo.png

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

Fichier demandé : images/logo.png

To send a POST request, use the [-X POST] option of [curl]:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8000/first/action01

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

Action [action01Post] du contrôleur [PremierController], requête POST

A HTTP method for which no action handles this path results in a 405 error ([Method Not Allowed]). The [allow] header lists the accepted methods; [Laravel] adds [HEAD] (the same request as GET, without the response body), which it handles itself for any route GET:

curl -i -X PUT http://localhost:8000/first/action01

HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
allow: GET, HEAD, POST
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
...
    <title>Exemple 02</title>
...

In debug mode, the response body is the detailed error page for [Laravel], which we’ll see in Example 03: It explains that the PUT method is not supported for this route (“The PUT method is not supported for route premier/action01.” Supported methods: GET, HEAD, POST.”).

Finally, a URL that no route handles results in a 404 error. This is also the case for an identifier that is not a number: the constraint [whereNumber] prevents the route from matching [/premier/produits/abc].

curl -i http://localhost:8000/first/products/abc

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
    <head>
...
        <title>Not Found</title>
...

The response is an error page for [Laravel], in English. In a browser:

Chapter 7 will show how to replace it with a page specific to the application. Note also that [Laravel] does not distinguish between [/premier] and [/premier/]: the trailing slash is ignored by the router, and both URL entries lead to the same action.

The command [php artisan route:list], run in the example directory, lists all the routes in the application:

php artisan route:list

  GET|HEAD  / ............................................................ AccueilController@index
  GET|HEAD  premier ...................................................... PremierController@index
  GET|HEAD  premier/action01 .......................................... PremierController@action01
  POST      premier/action01 ...................................... PremierController@action01Post
  GET|HEAD  premier/fichiers/{chemin} .................................. PremierController@fichier
  GET|HEAD  premier/produits/{id} ...................................... PremierController@produit
  GET|HEAD  premier/produits/{id}/avis/{numero} ........................... PremierController@avis
  GET|HEAD  storage/{path} storage.local › .../vendor/laravel/framework/...
  PUT       storage/{path} storage.local.upload › .../vendor/laravel/framework/...

                                                                                Showing [9] routes

Each line lists the HTTP methods, the path, and the action ([Contrôleur@méthode]). The last two routes, named [storage.local] and [storage.local.upload], are created by [Laravel] itself: they serve the files that the application stores in its [storage/app] folder, provided they are accompanied by a signature (a signed URL, which only the application knows how to generate). We will not use them.

docs.title: 2.3. Example 03: Responses to an Action
docs.text:
What an action returns determines the HTTP response. Example 03 reviews the main cases:

03-reponses/
├── app/
│   ├── Http/
│   │   ├── Controllers/
│   │   │   └── ReponsesController.php
│   │   └── Middleware/
│   │       └── JsonLisible.php
│   └── Models/
│       └── Personne.php
├── bootstrap/
│   └── app.php
├── routes/
│   └── web.php
└── ...

The routing table maps each URL and [/reponses/xxx] to the controller action [xxx]:

<?php
// routes/web.php: Routes from Example 03

use App\Http\Controllers\ReponsesController;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

// Route::controller(...)->group(...): all routes in the group are processed
// by the same controller; only the action name is provided
Route::prefix('reponses')->controller(ReponsesController::class)->group(function () {
    Route::get('texte', 'texte');
    Route::get('html', 'html');
    Route::get('json', 'json');
    Route::get('tableau', 'tableau');
    Route::get('liste', 'liste');
    Route::get('collection', 'collection');
    Route::get('cree', 'cree');
    Route::get('vide', 'vide');
    Route::get('introuvable', 'introuvable');
    Route::get('abandon', 'abandon');
    Route::get('erreur', 'erreur');
});

The controller [ReponsesController]:

<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/ReponsesController.php: the different responses of an action

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Models\Personne;
use Illuminate\Http\JsonResponse;
use Illuminate\Http\Response;
use Illuminate\Support\Collection;
use RuntimeException;

class ReponsesController
{
     // a string, marked as plain text: the browser displays it as-is.
     // response(): the complete response, constructed by the action itself
    public function texte(): Response
    {
        return response('<h1>Action [texte]</h1>')
            ->header('Content-Type', 'text/plain; charset=utf-8');
    }

     // a single string: Laravel sends it with the text/html type; the browser interprets it
    public function html(): string
    {
        return '<h1>Action [html]</h1>';
    }

     // an object: `response()->json` serializes it to `JSON`, with the type `[application/json]`
    public function json(): JsonResponse
    {
        return response()->json(new Personne('Martin', 'Jean', 42));
    }

     // an associative array rendered as-is: Laravel serializes it itself as JSON
    public function tableau(): array
    {
        return ['nom' => 'Martin', 'prenom' => 'Jean', 'age' => 42];
    }

     // an indexed array: serialized as an array JSON
    public function liste(): array
    {
        return ['Mme', 'Melle', 'Mr'];
    }

     // a Laravel collection: this is also serialized as JSON
    public function collection(): Collection
    {
        return collect([3, 1, 2])->sort()->values()->map(fn (int $n) => $n * 10);
    }

     // status code 201 (Created) instead of 200 (OK)
    public function cree(): JsonResponse
    {
        return response()->json(['message' => 'ressource créée'], 201);
    }

     // no response: status code 204 (No Content) means “nothing to display”
    public function vide(): Response
    {
        return response()->noContent();
    }

     // an “expected” error: a JSON response with status code 404
    public function introuvable(): JsonResponse
    {
        return response()->json(['message' => "Cette ressource n'existe pas"], 404);
    }

     // the same, due to an abort: a HTTP exception, which Laravel converts into a 404 response
    public function abandon(): never
    {
        abort(404, "Cette ressource n'existe pas non plus");
    }

     // an "unexpected" error: an unhandled exception produces a 500 response
    public function erreur(): never
    {
        throw new RuntimeException('Une erreur imprévue');
    }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Lines 16–19: The function [response] constructs a complete response, HTTP, which is a [Illuminate\Http\Response] object whose first parameter is the body. [Laravel] provides many functions of this type, available everywhere, which it calls “helpers”: [response], [redirect], [abort], [view], [collect]... The [header] method sets a response header—in this case, its type: [text/plain] (plain text). The browser will not interpret the tags. [header] returns the response itself: the calls follow one after another;
  • lines 23–25: the same string, rendered on its own: [Laravel] sends it with the type [text/html], and the browser interprets it;
  • Lines 29–31: [response()], called without any parameters, returns a response factory, whose method [json] converts its parameter to JSON and generates a response of type [application/json] (a [JsonResponse] object). The conversion is performed by the [json_encode] function of [PHP]: an object becomes a JSON object whose fields are the public properties of the object. The [Personne] class is described below;
  • lines 35–37: even simpler: an action that returns an array produces a JSON response, without calling [response()->json]. The array [PHP] is a general-purpose structure: [['nom' => 'Martin', ...]] is an associative array, where each element has a key (here, ['nom']); it becomes a JSON object. An ordinary object, on the other hand, cannot be rendered on its own: [Laravel] would attempt to convert it to a string, and the operation would fail (“Object of class App\Models\Personne could not be converted to string”); it must go through [response()->json];
  • lines 41–43: an array with implicit keys (0, 1, 2) is a list; it becomes an array JSON;
  • lines 47–49: the function [collect] creates a [Laravel] collection—an object that wraps an array and provides about a hundred methods to transform it—which are then chained together: [sort] sorts the elements, [values] renumbers the keys starting from 0, and [map] applies a function to each element. [fn (int $n) => $n * 10] is an arrow function: an anonymous function reduced to an expression, whose value it returns. A collection returned by an action also becomes an array, JSON. We’ll revisit collections in the context of databases in Chapter 9;
  • lines 53–55: the second parameter of [json] is the status code: 201 ([Created]) replaces 200. A third, optional parameter would provide headers: [['X-Exemple' => '03']];
  • lines 59–61: the code 204 ([No Content]) means “nothing to display”: the response has no body;
  • lines 65–67: an “expected” error: a 404 response ([Not Found]), with a body (JSON) chosen by the action. The text is enclosed in quotation marks because it contains an apostrophe;
  • lines 71–73: the same error, generated by the function [abort]. [abort] returns nothing: it throws an exception ([NotFoundHttpException], for code 404), which terminates the action; [Laravel] converts it into an error response. The type [never] indicates that the method never terminates normally. This is the most common way to terminate an action due to an error, even deep within a function called by the action;
  • lines 77–79: an “unexpected” error—an exception that no one handles—produces a 500 response ([Internal Server Error]). The statement [throw] throws an exception; [RuntimeException] is an exception class from the standard library of [PHP], imported by a [use] (line 10) like any other class. The action is not named [exception], as in the other versions of the course: for [Laravel], an action named ['exception'] would refer to the class [Exception] from [PHP] (class names are case-insensitive), and the route would be rejected.

The class [Personne]:

<?php
// app/Models/Personne.php: a person

namespace App\Models;

// a class whose properties are declared in the constructor (promotion);
// readonly: properties cannot change after construction
readonly class Personne
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $nom,
        public string $prenom,
        public int $age,
    ) {
    }
}
  • Line 8: [readonly] makes all properties of the class non-modifiable after they are initialized: a [Personne] object is immutable;
  • Lines 10–14: [__construct] is the class constructor, called by [new Personne('Martin', 'Jean', 42)]. Its parameters, preceded by [public], are promoted: each declares a property of the same name, initialized by the parameter. This syntax avoids having to declare the properties and then assign them one by one in the body of the constructor (which is empty here). The properties are public: [json_encode] can access them.

That leaves the file [bootstrap/app.php]:

<?php
// bootstrap/app.php: the application from Example 03

use App\Http\Middleware\JsonLisible;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Middleware;

(require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php')->addPsr4('App\\', __DIR__.'/../app/');

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php')
    ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
         // all responses JSON pass through the middleware JsonLisible:
         // Accents preserved, indented formatting
        $middleware->append(JsonLisible::class);
    })
    ->withExceptions()
    ->create();
  • line 15: a middleware component is added to the application: the [JsonLisible] class, shown below.
<?php
// app/Http/Middleware/JsonLisible.php: a human-readable JSON

namespace App\Http\Middleware;

use Closure;
use Illuminate\Http\JsonResponse;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

class JsonLisible
{
     // a MIDDLEWARE: a class whose `handle` method is called for each
     // request; $next($request) has the action process the request and returns the response
    public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next): Response
    {
        $reponse = $next($request);
        if ($reponse instanceof JsonResponse) {
             // "created" instead of "created", "/" instead of "\/", and an
             // indented, multi-line output
            $reponse->setEncodingOptions(JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE | JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES
                | JSON_PRETTY_PRINT);
        }
        return $reponse;
    }
}

By default, [Laravel] produces a compact, single-line JSON, in which non-ASCII characters are written as escape sequences: [créée] becomes [créée], which is valid JSON, but not very readable. For the examples in this course, we want a readable JSON. A middleware is a class whose method [handle]*** is called for every request, *wrapped around the action: [$next($request)] passes the request to the rest of the application (the other middlewares, then the action), and returns the response (line 17). The middleware can then modify it: if it is a JSON response (the [instanceof] operator checks an object’s class), it changes its encoding options: non-ASCII characters and slashes are written as-is, and the output is indented (line 21). The [|] operator combines the three options, which are constants of [PHP]. The chapter on the request lifecycle will examine middleware in detail; examples 05 through 12 reuse this one.

In a browser, the difference between [text/plain] and [text/html] is visible:

Here are the responses from the other actions:

curl -i http://localhost:8000/responses/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "nom": "Martin",
    "prenom": "Jean",
    "age": 42
}

The object was converted to object JSON, with one field per public property. The [/reponses/tableau] action produces exactly the same response.

curl -i http://localhost:8000/reponses/liste
curl http://localhost:8000/answers/collection

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

[
    "Mme",
    "Melle",
    "Mr"
]
[
    10,
    20,
    30
]

curl -i http://localhost:8000/responses/create

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "message": "ressource créée"
}

curl -i http://localhost:8000/responses/empty

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

curl -i http://localhost:8000/responses/not-found

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "message": "Cette ressource n'existe pas"
}

curl -i http://localhost:8000/answers/abandoned

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
...
        <title>Not Found</title>
...

The response from [abort] is the standard 404 error page for [Laravel], as shown in Example 02. Our message does not appear there: the standard page displays only the code and its label. However, it does appear when the client requests a JSON response, via the [Accept: application/json] header (option [-H] of [curl]): [Laravel] then adapts its error responses, which become JSON documents:

curl -i -H "Accept: application/json" http://localhost:8000/answers/abandoned

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "message": "Cette ressource n'existe pas non plus",
    "exception": "Symfony\\Component\\HttpKernel\\Exception\\NotFoundHttpException",
    "file": ".../vendor/laravel/framework/src/Illuminate/Foundation/Application.php",
    "line": 1444,
    "trace": [
        ...
    ]
}

In debug mode, the JSON document also contains the name of the exception, the file and line where it was thrown, and the call stack (the list of functions that were executing at the time of the error). Without debug mode, it contains only the message. Chapter 7 will show how to display the message on a custom error page.

That leaves the unhandled exception. In debug mode, the browser displays the error page for [Laravel]: the exception type and message, the file and line where it was thrown, and then the call stack—from most recent to oldest—with the relevant line of code for each:

The first entry in the stack is our action, [erreur], on line 79 of the file [ReponsesController.php]. Further down, the page displays the request (its headers and parameters) and the application (routes and settings): this is why debug mode should never be enabled on a server accessible to others. The “Copy as Markdown” button copies the error description, ready to be pasted into a question on IA. The error is also written to the application log, the file [storage/logs/laravel.log] (we’re only showing the beginning here):

[2026-09-26 15:51:36] local.ERROR: Une erreur imprévue {"exception":"[object] (RuntimeException(code: 0): Une erreur imprévue at .../exemples/03-reponses/app/Http/Controllers/ReponsesController.php:79)
[stacktrace]
#0 .../vendor/laravel/framework/src/Illuminate/Routing/ControllerDispatcher.php(46): App\\Http\\Controllers\\ReponsesController->error()
...

Without debug mode ([APP_DEBUG=false] in [.env]), the same request produces a brief error page, “500 | Server Error,” which reveals nothing about the code; the error is described only in the log. Chapter 7 will show how to display an application-specific error page.

docs.title: 2.4. Example 04: Redirects
docs.text:
A redirect is a response that instructs the browser to fetch another URL: a 3xx code and the [Location] header, which contains the new address. The browser immediately sends a second request to that address. The controller [RedirectionsController]:

<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/RedirectionsController.php: redirects

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use Illuminate\Http\RedirectResponse;

class RedirectionsController
{
     // permanent redirect (301): the page has permanently moved to a new address
    public function ancienne(): RedirectResponse
    {
        return redirect('/nouvelle', 301);
    }

    public function nouvelle(): string
    {
        return 'Vous êtes sur la page [nouvelle]';
    }

     // Temporary redirect (302, the default code), to a calculated address
     // by piecing together text segments
    public function aller(string $destination): RedirectResponse
    {
        return redirect('/page/'.$destination);
    }

     // route() generates the address of a ROUTE, identified by its name:
     // the parameter [nom] is correctly encoded for a URL
    public function versRoute(string $destination): RedirectResponse
    {
        return redirect()->route('page', ['nom' => $destination]);
    }

    public function page(string $nom): string
    {
        return "Vous êtes sur la page [$nom]";
    }

     // redirect to another site
    public function documentation(): RedirectResponse
    {
        return redirect()->away('https://laravel.com/docs');
    }
}
  • lines 11–13: the function [redirect] generates a redirect response (a [RedirectResponse] object) to the specified address. Code 301 ([Moved Permanently]) means that the page has permanently changed its address: the browser (and search engines) can remember the new one;
  • lines 23–25: without a second parameter, [redirect] generates a temporary redirect with a 302 status code ([Found]). The URL is constructed by concatenating text fragments (the [.] operator), which poses a problem, as we will see;
  • lines 30–32: When called without a parameter, [redirect()] returns an object whose [route] method creates a redirect to a route, identified by its name (['page']), rather than by its path. The associative array provides the route parameters (here, [nom]), correctly encoded for a URL. If the path of the route [page] is ever changed, the redirects to it will update automatically;
  • lines 41–43: a redirect to another site. The [away] method takes the address as is.

It is assigned a route name in the routing table:

<?php
// routes/web.php: the routes from Example 04

use App\Http\Controllers\RedirectionsController;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::controller(RedirectionsController::class)->group(function () {
    Route::get('ancienne', 'ancienne');
    Route::get('nouvelle', 'nouvelle');
    Route::get('aller/{destination}', 'aller');
    Route::get('vers-route/{destination}', 'versRoute');
     // name: the route’s NOM, which is used to generate its URL (route function)
    Route::get('page/{nom}', 'page')->name('page');
    Route::get('documentation', 'documentation');
});
  • line 7: a group of routes without a prefix, which share only their controller (example 02);
  • line 13: the [name] method assigns a name to the route. The [route] function, available everywhere, generates the URL for a named route: [route('page', ['nom' => 'a?b'])] yields [http://localhost:8000/page/a%3Fb].

The results, using [curl] (which, without options, does not follow redirects):

curl -i http://localhost:8000/old

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: http://localhost:8000/new
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
    <head>
        <meta charset="UTF-8" />
        <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0;url='http://localhost:8000/nouvelle'" />

        <title>Redirecting to http://localhost:8000/new</title>
    </head>
    <body>
        Redirecting to <a href="http://localhost:8000/nouvelle">http://localhost:8000/new</a>.
    </body>
</html>

[Laravel] converted the address [/nouvelle] into an absolute address (including the protocol, host, and port), calculated from the received request. The response also includes a short body, HTML, for a client that does not follow redirects. The option [-L] from [curl] follows the redirect, just as a browser would:

curl -L http://localhost:8000/old

Vous êtes sur la page [nouvelle]

Now let’s compare the two calculated redirects, with a destination that contains a question mark, encoded as [%3F] in URL (an uncoded [?] would start the parameters of the URL):

curl -i http://localhost:8000/go/a%3Fb
curl -i http://localhost:8000/toward-route/a%3Fb

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: http://localhost:8000/page/a?b
...
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: http://localhost:8000/page/a%3Fb
...

[Laravel] decoded the route parameter before processing it: [$destination] equals [a?b]. The first action inserts it back into the address as-is: [/page/a?b], which the browser interprets as the path [/page/a] followed by the parameter [b]. The second action follows the named route, whose parameter is encoded again: [/page/a%3Fb]. Following the redirects:

curl -L http://localhost:8000/go/a%3Fb
curl -L http://localhost:8000/to-route/a%3Fb

Vous êtes sur la page [a]
Vous êtes sur la page [a?b]

Only the second one leads to the correct page. Hence the rule: an address containing a variable value is constructed using [route], never by concatenating strings. In the browser, only the final page is visible; the address bar displays the new URL:

Two other redirect codes exist: 303 ([See Other]) and 307 ([Temporary Redirect]), which are obtained via [redirect($url, 303)]. After a POST request, codes 302 and 303 cause the browser to send a GET request to the new address, whereas 307 (and 308, the permanent version) cause it to repeat the POST request. Example 20 will use redirection following a POST.

docs.title: 2.5. Example 05: The Request and Response Objects
docs.text:
Until now, actions only received route parameters and returned a value that [Laravel] converted into a response. An action can also access the current request and construct the response itself. The [HttpController] controller:

<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/HttpController.php: the request and response objects

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Http\Response;
use RuntimeException;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\StreamedResponse;

class HttpController
{
     // The request: method, path, parameters, headers...
     // Laravel INJECTE: the Request object for the current request in the typed parameter $request
    public function requete(Request $request): array
    {
        return [
            'methode' => $request->method(),
            'chemin' => $request->path(),
            'url' => $request->fullUrl(),
            'parametres' => $request->getQueryString(),
            'navigateur' => $request->userAgent(),
            'ip' => $request->ip(),
        ];
    }

     // the response: response() constructs the response object; a header is added to it
    public function entete(): Response
    {
        return response('Réponse avec un entête ajouté')
            ->header('X-Exemple', '05-requete-reponse');
    }

     // the "hand-built" response: body, status code, headers
    public function reponse(): Response
    {
        return new Response('Réponse construite par [new Response(...)]', 200,
            ['Content-Type' => 'text/plain; charset=utf-8']);
    }

     // a response sent as PAR MORCEAUX: the code and headers are sent with the
     // first chunk, and cannot be changed afterward
    public function flux(): StreamedResponse
    {
        return response()->stream(function () {
            echo 'Début de la réponse... ';
             // the chunk is sent immediately to the browser
            flush();
            sleep(1);
             // too late to report an error: the 200 status code has already been sent
            throw new RuntimeException('erreur au milieu de la réponse');
        }, 200, ['Content-Type' => 'text/plain; charset=utf-8']);
    }
}
  • line 15: the action has a parameter of type [Request]. This parameter does not come from URL: [Laravel] detects its type and provides it with the [Request] object from the current request. This is dependency injection, which the following example illustrates in detail: an action declares, through the type of its parameters, the objects it needs, and [Laravel] provides them. The order of the parameters does not matter: an action can receive both the request and route parameters;
  • lines 17–24: some methods of the request: its HTTP method, its path (without the leading slash), its full URL, its raw parameters (the part of the URL that follows the [?]), the [User-Agent] header (the browser; [$request->header('User-Agent')] is the shorter version), and the client’s IP address. The class [Illuminate\Http\Request] inherits from the class [Request], which in turn inherits from [Symfony], another framework, [PHP], on whose components [Laravel] is built. The parameters, one by one, will be discussed in the next chapter. The rendered type, [array], produces a response JSON (Example 03);
  • lines 28–31: the response generated by [response] receives a header [X-Exemple] (by convention, application-specific headers often begin with [X-]);
  • lines 35–38: the response built “by hand” by the operator [new]: the body, the status code, and the headers;
  • lines 43–52: a response sent in chunks (*streaming*). [response()->stream] receives a function, which itself writes the response body, via [echo] (the instruction from [PHP] that writes to the response) ; [flush()] immediately sends what has been written to the browser. The response’s length is not known in advance: the server sends the status code and headers, then each chunk as soon as it is generated. This is useful for a very long response that is generated bit by bit. But once the first chunk has been sent, the status code can no longer change: here, the function throws an exception after the first chunk. This is the mistake to avoid: a response that has already begun cannot become an error response.

The routing table and [bootstrap/app.php] contain nothing new ([bootstrap/app.php] adds the [JsonLisible] middleware from Example 03). The responses:

curl -i "http://localhost:8000/http/requete?nom=martin&age=42"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "methode": "GET",
    "chemin": "http/requete",
    "url": "http://localhost:8000/http/requete?age=42&nom=martin",
    "parametres": "age=42&nom=martin",
    "navigateur": "curl/8.5.0",
    "ip": "127.0.0.1"
}

The quotation marks around "URL" prevent the terminal from interpreting the character "[&]." Note that the parameters have been sorted alphabetically: [getQueryString] and [fullUrl] produce a normalized form of the parameter string, which allows for comparing two URL values (this is useful, for example, for a cache). In a browser, the header [User-Agent] is the browser’s header.

curl -i http://localhost:8000/http/header

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-Exemple: 05-requete-reponse
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

Réponse avec un entête ajouté

curl -i http://localhost:8000/http/response

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

Réponse construite par [new Response(...)]

curl -i http://localhost:8000/http/feed

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

Début de la réponse...

After one second, the response stops: [curl] received a 200 status code and a truncated body, with no way to know that an error occurred. Only the application log indicates this, through two errors: our exception, followed by the failure of [Laravel], which attempted to send an error page after the headers had already been sent:

[2026-09-26 15:52:11] local.ERROR: erreur au milieu de la réponse {"exception":"[object] (RuntimeException(code: 0): erreur au milieu de la réponse at .../HttpController.php:51)
...
[2026-09-26 15:52:11] local.ERROR: Uncaught ErrorException: Cannot modify header information - headers already sent in .../vendor/symfony/http-foundation/Response.php:328

docs.title: 2.6. Example 06: Shared Services and Dependency Injection
docs.text:
An action should not contain the application logic itself; it delegates it to services—objects that know how to perform a specific task (read products, calculate a shopping cart, etc.). Multiple actions often use the same service. [Laravel], like [Spring] or [ASP.NET Core], has a service container: an object that creates services and automatically provides them to those that need them. This is dependency injection, which we already encountered in Example 05 for the object [Request]. Example 06 organizes its code by domain (products, customers) rather than by type (controllers, models):

06-services/
├── app/
│   ├── Clients/
│   │   └── ClientsController.php
│   ├── Http/
│   │   └── Middleware/
│   │       └── JsonLisible.php
│   └── Produits/
│       ├── Produit.php
│       ├── ProduitsController.php
│       ├── ProduitsService.php
│       └── ProduitsServiceMemoire.php
├── bootstrap/
│   └── app.php
├── routes/
│   └── web.php
└── ...

There is no requirement to place controllers in [app/Http/Controllers]: [Laravel] locates a class by its full name, using the [PSR-4] standard (the class [App\Produits\ProduitsController] is in the file [app/Produits/ProduitsController.php]).

docs.title: 2.6.1. The product
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Products/Produit.php: a product

namespace App\Produits;

use Brick\Math\BigDecimal;

// readonly: the object is immutable (its properties are set by the constructor)
readonly class Produit
{
    public function __construct(
        public int $id,
        public string $nom,
         // BigDecimal: an exact decimal number (no binary rounding)
        public BigDecimal $prix,
    ) {
    }
}
  • line 9: an immutable class (see example 03). An immutable object can be safely shared among multiple parts of the code;
  • lines 12–15: the properties, promoted by the constructor, along with their types. The price is a [BigDecimal], an exact decimal number, provided by the [brick/math] library (installed with [Laravel], which uses it itself). [PHP] does not have a decimal type: a floating-point number, of type [float], is represented in binary and cannot exactly represent 0.1 or 3.2 (in binary, these numbers have an infinite number of digits): a price total in [float] might result in 5.500000000000001.

docs.title: 2.6.2. The service contract: ProduitsService.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Products/ProduitsService.php: the service's CONTRAT—what it can do, without specifying how

namespace App\Produits;

interface ProduitsService
{
     /** @return list<Product> */
    public function findAll(): array;

     // ?Product: a product, or null if it does not exist
    public function findById(int $id): ?Produit;
}
  • Line 6: the service contract: what it can do, without specifying how. In [PHP], as in [Java] or [C#], a contract is defined by an interface: a list of methods without bodies, all of which must be implemented by a class that implements the interface;
  • line 8: a documentation comment ([/** ... */]). The type [array] does not specify what the array contains; the annotation [@return list<Produit>]—which [PHP] ignores—specifies this for the code editor: a list of products;
  • line 11: [?Produit]: a product, or [null] if it does not exist.

docs.title: 2.6.3. The implementation: ProduitsServiceMemoire.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Products/ProduitsServiceMemoire.php: a IMPLÉMENTATION from the contract, with data in memory

namespace App\Produits;

use Brick\Math\BigDecimal;

class ProduitsServiceMemoire implements ProduitsService
{
     /** @var list<Product> */
    private array $produits;

    public function __construct()
    {
        $this->produits = [
            new Produit(1, 'stylo', BigDecimal::of('1.5')),
            new Produit(2, 'cahier', BigDecimal::of('3.2')),
            new Produit(3, 'gomme', BigDecimal::of('0.8')),
        ];
    }

    public function findAll(): array
    {
         // An array PHP is copied when it is passed: the caller receives a copy
        return $this->produits;
    }

    public function findById(int $id): ?Produit
    {
         // array_find: the first element for which the function returns true, or null
        return array_find($this->produits, fn (Produit $p) => $p->id === $id);
    }
}
  • line 8: the class implements the contract and defines its two methods;
  • line 11: a private property: only the class’s code can use it;
  • Lines 13–19: The constructor stores the products in the property designated by [$this->produits] ([$this] is the current object). [BigDecimal::of('1.5')] constructs a decimal from a string: constructed from [float] 1.5, it would inherit its inaccuracies;
  • lines 22–25: the method returns the array of products. In [PHP], an array is a value that is copied when passed: the caller receives a copy, which it can modify without affecting the service’s data (the [Produit] objects, on the other hand, are not copied, but they are immutable);
  • lines 28–30: The function [array_find] ([PHP] 8.4) returns the first element of an array for which the given function returns [true], or [null] if there are none. [===] represents strict equality: same value and same type.

docs.title: 2.6.4. The product validator: ProduitsController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Products/ProduitsController.php: the actions of /products

namespace App\Produits;

use Illuminate\Http\JsonResponse;

class ProduitsController
{
     // the service is INJECTÉ provided by Laravel in the constructor: the controller
     // knows only the contract (the interface), not its implementation
    public function __construct(private ProduitsService $service)
    {
    }

    public function liste(): array
    {
        return $this->service->findAll();
    }

    public function unProduit(int $id): JsonResponse
    {
        $produit = $this->service->findById($id);
        if ($produit === null) {
            return response()->json(['message' => "Produit n° $id introuvable"], 404);
        }
        return response()->json($produit);
    }
}
  • Lines 12–14: The controller needs the service; it declares it as a parameter of its constructor. When [Laravel] creates the controller (to process a request), it examines the types of the constructor’s parameters, requests an object of each type from the container, and passes them to the constructor: this is constructor injection. The parameter, prefixed with [private], is promoted to a private property (see Example 03): the actions use it via [$this->service]. The controller knows only the service contract (the interface), not its implementation: it is unaware that the products are in memory;
  • lines 16–18: the action delegates the work to the service. The returned array of products becomes a JSON array (Example 03): each [Produit] becomes a JSON object (its properties are public);
  • lines 21–27: An unknown product returns a 404 response, with a message in JSON. A standalone [Produit] object must pass through [response()->json] (example 03).

docs.title: 2.6.5. The client controller: ClientsController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Clients/ClientsController.php: a second controller, which uses the MÊME service

namespace App\Clients;

use App\Produits\Produit;
use App\Produits\ProduitsService;
use Brick\Math\BigDecimal;

class ClientsController
{
     // This time, the service is injected into the action’s parameters
    public function panier(ProduitsService $service): array
    {
        $produits = $service->findAll();
         // the sum of the prices: we add up the BigDecimal values, starting from zero
        $total = array_reduce($produits,
            fn (BigDecimal $somme, Produit $p) => $somme->plus($p->prix), BigDecimal::zero());
        return ['client' => 'Jean Martin', 'articles' => count($produits), 'total' => $total];
    }
}
  • Line 13: This controller uses the same service as the product controller. This time, it receives it as a parameter of the action: [Laravel] also injects the action parameters, as in the request from Example 05. Injection via the constructor is suitable for services required by all actions; injection via the action is suitable for those required by a single action;
  • Lines 17–18: [array_reduce] reduces an array to a single value: the function receives the accumulated value ([$somme]) and the current element, and returns the new accumulated value; the third parameter is the starting value, a zero [BigDecimal]. [plus] adds two decimals and returns a new decimal (a [BigDecimal] is immutable);
  • line 19: [count] returns the number of elements in an array.

docs.title: 2.6.6. The service declaration: bootstrap/app.php
docs.text:
<?php
// bootstrap/app.php: the application from Example 06

use App\Http\Middleware\JsonLisible;
use App\Produits\ProduitsService;
use App\Produits\ProduitsServiceMemoire;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Middleware;

(require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php')->addPsr4('App\\', __DIR__.'/../app/');

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php')
    ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
        $middleware->append(JsonLisible::class);
    })
    ->withExceptions()
     // the SERVICE: when a class requests a ProduitsService, the Laravel container
     // Laravel provides it with a ProduitsServiceMemoire, created only once (singleton)
    ->withSingletons([
        ProduitsService::class => ProduitsServiceMemoire::class,
    ])
    ->create();
  • lines 20–22: it is here, and only here, that the service implementation is chosen. The array associates a requested type (the interface) with the class that provides it. When a class requests a [ProduitsService], the container creates a [ProduitsServiceMemoire]; [withSingletons] indicates that it is created only once: anyone who subsequently requests a [ProduitsService] will receive the same object. This is a singleton. To switch to an implementation that reads from a database, you would simply need to change this line: the controllers, which only know the contract, would remain unchanged. That is the whole point of dependency injection: every part of the application depends on contracts, and a single location decides on the implementations.

A concrete class (which is not an interface) does not even need to be declared: the container knows how to create it on its own, by injecting the parameters into its constructor. This is how it creates controllers. An interface, on the other hand, must be associated with an implementation; otherwise, the container fails (“Target [App\Produits\ProduitsService] is not instantiable”). This association can also be declared on the interface itself, using an attribute (an annotation, in [PHP]): [#[Bind(ProduitsServiceMemoire::class)]] above [interface ProduitsService], and [#[Singleton]] above the implementation class. We will keep the declaration in [bootstrap/app.php], which brings together all the application’s choices in a single location; the case study will group them into a service provider, the class that [Laravel] provides for this purpose.

Finally, a word about the lifetime of this singleton. As we saw in Example 01: in [PHP], the application is rebuilt with each request. The singleton is therefore unique to a single request: all classes that request it during the processing of a request receive the same object, but the next request will receive a new one. For a service that only reads static data, like this one, this makes no difference. For a service whose data changes (the task list in Example 20), this data must be stored somewhere other than in the object: in a file, a database, or the cache of [Laravel]. On the other hand, a [PHP] service cannot be used by two requests at the same time: each request has its own. The precautions required for services shared by multiple simultaneous requests in [Java], [C#], or [Python] (locks, in particular) are unnecessary here.

The routing table:

<?php
// routes/web.php: routes from Example 06

use App\Clients\ClientsController;
use App\Produits\ProduitsController;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::get('produits', [ProduitsController::class, 'liste']);
Route::get('produits/{id}', [ProduitsController::class, 'unProduit'])->whereNumber('id');
Route::get('clients/panier', [ClientsController::class, 'panier']);

docs.title: 2.6.7. Execution
docs.text:
curl -i http://localhost:8000/products

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

[
    {
        "id": 1,
        "nom": "stylo",
        "prix": "1.5"
    },
    {
        "id": 2,
        "nom": "cahier",
        "prix": "3.2"
    },
    {
        "id": 3,
        "nom": "gomme",
        "prix": "0.8"
    }
]

The prices have become strings (["1.5"]): JSON has only one number type, which most programs read as a floating-point number; a [BigDecimal] is therefore converted to a string, so as not to lose any precision (the [BigDecimal] class implements the [JsonSerializable] interface from [PHP], which allows it to choose its form JSON).

curl -i http://localhost:8000/products/9

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "message": "Produit n° 9 introuvable"
}

curl -i http://localhost:8000/customers/cart

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "client": "Jean Martin",
    "articles": 3,
    "total": "5.5"
}

docs.title: 13.1. Installing PHP
docs.text:
The examples and case study require [PHP] 8.4 or a later version, with the extensions [intl] (number formatting, Example 16), [pdo_mysql] (access to [MySQL], Example 28 and case study), [mbstring], and [openssl]. They have been tested with version 8.4.

Under [Windows], the simplest option is [Laragon] (laragon.org), which installs [PHP], [Composer], a [MySQL] server, and the [HeidiSQL] administration tool. If the provided version of [PHP] is older than 8.4, download a more recent version from windows.php.net/download (the *Thread Safe* version, [.zip] archive), which you should extract into the [bin\php] folder of [Laragon]; the PHP / [Laragon] version allows you to select it. The PHP / Extensions menu activates an extension with a single click ([intl], [pdo_mysql]). The [Laragon] terminal (Terminal button) supports the commands [php], [composer], and [mysql].

Without [Laragon], extract the archive from [PHP] into a folder ([C:\php]), add this folder to the environment variable [Path], then create the configuration file [php.ini] by copying [php.ini-development], and remove the semicolon that comments out the lines for the required extensions:

extension=intl
extension=mbstring
extension=openssl
extension=pdo_mysql

Under [macOS], the package manager [Homebrew] installs [PHP] and its standard extensions: [brew install php]. For [Linux] ([Ubuntu]), the version provided by the distribution is often older; the [ppa:ondrej/php] repository provides the latest versions:

sudo add-apt-repository ppa:ondrej/php
sudo apt install php8.4-cli php8.4-intl php8.4-mbstring php8.4-mysql php8.4-xml php8.4-curl php8.4-zip

Verify the installation in a new console:

php -v
php -m

The first command should display a version number equal to or greater than 8.4 (for example, [PHP 8.4.12]); the second lists the loaded extensions, including [intl] and [pdo_mysql]. The command [php --ini] indicates which file, [php.ini], is being used.

docs.title: 13.2. Compose
docs.text:
[Composer] is the library manager for [PHP] (getcomposer.org). It is provided by [Laragon]; for [Windows], without [Laragon], its installer ([Composer-Setup.exe]) is used; for [macOS], use [brew install composer]; for [Linux], follow the instructions on the getcomposer.org/download page. Verify the installation:

composer -V

Useful commands in a project folder (the one containing [composer.json]):

composer install            # Install the project libraries (vendor folder)
composer show               # the installed libraries
composer update             # upgrade to the latest versions supported by composer.json
composer dump-autoload      # Rebuild the class loader (after adding a class folder)

[Composer] downloads the libraries from the [Packagist] (packagist.org) repository: an Internet connection is required during installation. If you are behind a corporate proxy, specify the proxy using the environment variables [HTTP_PROXY] and [HTTPS_PROXY]. The [vendor] folder is not copied from one machine to another (it may contain absolute paths and is large); it is recreated using [composer install]. This is why it is not included in the course materials. The [exemples] folder has its own [vendor] folder, shared by all 28 examples; the case study has its own.

docs.title: 13.3. Installing Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
[Visual Studio Code] is downloaded from code.visualstudio.com. Add two extensions (View menu / Extensions):

  • PHP Intelephense: code completion, code navigation (including the code from [Laravel], in the [vendor] folder), and error reporting;
  • Laravel (the official extension): syntax highlighting for [Blade] views, and autocompletion for route names, view names, configuration keys, and translation keys.

The PHP Debug extension allows you to step through the code using the [Xdebug] debugger (an extension of [PHP], which must be installed separately: xdebug.org).

Open the [exemples] folder or the case study folder (File menu / Open Folder). The built-in terminal (Terminal menu / New Terminal) allows you to launch applications without leaving the editor.

docs.title: 13.4. Installing MySQL with Laragon
docs.text:
[Laragon] installs a ready-to-use [MySQL] server under [Windows], along with the [HeidiSQL] administration tool. After installation:

  • the "Start All" button launches the [MySQL] server on port 3306;
  • the user [root] has no password: these are the values from the [.env] files in Example 28 and the case study ([DB_USERNAME=root], [DB_PASSWORD=]) ;
  • The Database button opens [HeidiSQL], where the File menu / Run a File menu item (SQL) runs the scripts [dbpersonnes.sql] (Example 28) and [dbrdvmedecins2.sql] (case study).

In [Linux] or [macOS], install [MySQL] or [MariaDB] using the system’s package manager, and run the scripts using the command-line client [mysql]. The [pdo_mysql] driver works with both without any configuration. Under [Linux], the [root] account for [MariaDB] is often configured to log in only via the system account [root] ([sudo mysql]): a user is then created for the applications, and this user is specified in their [.env] file:

sudo mysql -e "CREATE USER 'cours'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'cours'; GRANT ALL ON *.* TO 'cours'@'localhost';"

docs.title: 13.5. Installing curl
docs.text: [curl] comes bundled with [Windows] 10 and 11, [macOS], and most [Linux] distributions. In [PowerShell], you must type [curl.exe], not [curl]: In older versions of [PowerShell], [curl] is an alias for another command ([Invoke-WebRequest]), which has different options. In the command prompt for [Windows] ([cmd]), the quotation marks for a string JSON are written as [\"] (example 11), and a URL that contains [&] must be enclosed in double quotes.

docs.title: 8. Authentication and Authorization
docs.text:
Two distinct questions arise for each request:

  • Who is the user? This is authentication: the user has identified themselves with a username and password, and every subsequent request must prove that it comes from them;
  • Do they have permission to access this page? This is authorization: in the case study, only a user with the role ADMIN manages doctors and clients.

Proof of identity must accompany every request. [Laravel] typically stores the logged-in user’s ID in their session (see the chapter on scopes), which is the simplest solution for a web application. The case study, in all its versions ([ASP.NET Core MVC], [Spring MVC], [NestJS], [Flask]), instead uses a token (JWT (*JSON Web Token*)), which we will use here: after login, the server generates a token containing the user’s identity and signs it with a secret key. The token is stored in a cookie; the browser sends it back with every request; the server verifies the signature. The user can read their token but cannot modify it: any modification invalidates the signature. The format is standardized (RFC 7519), understood by all programming languages, and the token includes its expiration date. Most importantly, the server doesn’t need to store anything: any server that knows the key can verify the token.

[Laravel] has a complete authentication system, the components of which we will use as-is:

  • authentication is handled by a *guard*: an object that, for each request, identifies the authenticated user. [Laravel] provides a guard that reads the session; we’ll write our own, which reads the token, in just a few lines. The rest of the application sees only the guard: [auth()->user()], [#[CurrentUser]], and [@auth] in the views;
  • page protection is handled by route middleware (previous chapter): [auth] requires an authenticated user, [can:admin] requires authorization;
  • authorizations are described by Gates (e.g., 26);
  • Passwords are hashed by the [Hash] facade (using the *bcrypt* algorithm), and attempt limits are enforced by the [RateLimiter] facade (Example 27).

Token generation and verification are handled by the [firebase/php-jwt] library, the most widely used in [PHP], installed by the [composer.json] file from the examples.

docs.title: 8.1. Example 25: Login, Token, Protected Page
docs.text:
25-jwt/
├── app/
│   ├── Auth/
│   │   ├── AuthService.php
│   │   ├── Utilisateur.php
│   │   └── UtilisateursService.php
│   └── Http/

│       │   └── login.blade.php
│       ├── layout.blade.php
│       └── profil/
│           └── profil.blade.php
├── routes/
