docs.title: 8.1.1. Configuration: .env, config/jwt.php, and config/auth.php
docs.text:
The token is signed with a secret key, which must not be hard-coded. It’s time to truly separate the configuration from the code. The settings specific to an installation are in the file [.env] (Example 01), which now includes two new lines:

# the key that signs the tokens JWT (at least 32 characters), and their lifetime
JWT_SECRET=une-cle-secrete-d-au-moins-32-caracteres-pour-l-exemple-25
JWT_DUREE_MINUTES=60

The standard requires, for the algorithm used (HMAC-SHA256), a key of at least 256 bits, or 32 bytes; the library rejects a shorter key. The code, however, does not read the [.env] file: it reads the application configuration—a set of [PHP] files stored in the [config] folder—each of which returns an array. We create the [config/jwt.php] file:

<?php
// config/jwt.php: the configuration of the JWT tokens, read by config('jwt.secret')...
// env(NOM, default): the NOM variable from the environment or the .env file
return [
     // the key that signs tokens (at least 32 characters): never in the code
    'secret' => env('JWT_SECRET'),
     // the token's lifetime, in minutes
    'duree' => (int) env('JWT_DUREE_MINUTES', 60),
     // the name of the cookie that carries the token
    'cookie' => 'jeton',
];
  • Line 6: The [env] function reads a variable from the process environment or, failing that, from the [.env] file; its second parameter is a default value. An environment variable takes precedence over the file: in production, the secret key is provided by the environment, and the file [.env] does not contain one;
  • line 8: Environment variables are strings: [(int)] converts the duration to an integer.

The code reads these values using the [config] function: [config('jwt.secret')] refers to the [secret] key in the [jwt.php] file. [env] is only called in configuration files: in production, the command [php artisan config:cache] combines the entire configuration into a single file to speed up the process, and [.env] is no longer read. The [config/auth.php] file configures authentication:

<?php
// config/auth.php: authentication. This file COMPLÈTE contains the configuration
// Laravel’s default (vendor/laravel/framework/config/auth.php)
return [
     // the default "guard" used: the one that reads the token JWT
    'defaults' => [
        'guard' => 'jwt',
    ],
    'guards' => [
         // a driver guard [jwt], defined in bootstrap/app.php (Auth::viaRequest)
        'jwt' => [
            'driver' => 'jwt',
        ],
    ],
];

[Laravel] has its own authentication configuration (the [vendor/laravel/framework/config/auth.php] file; see Example 01); the application’s configuration supplements it: the keys it provides replace those of the framework, while the others retain their values. We declare a guard named [jwt], with driver [jwt] (line 12), and set it as the default guard (line 7). The driver [jwt] does not exist in [Laravel]: we define it in [bootstrap/app.php].

Under [Linux] or [macOS], we would launch the application with a different key as follows:

JWT_SECRET="une-autre-cle-d-au-moins-trente-deux-caracteres" php artisan serve

and under [Windows] (PowerShell):

$env:JWT_SECRET="une-autre-cle-d-au-moins-trente-deux-caracteres"
php artisan serve

<?php
// app/Auth/Utilisateur.php: a user. Authenticatable: the interface that
// Laravel expects authenticated users

namespace App\Auth;

use Illuminate\Contracts\Auth\Authenticatable;

readonly class Utilisateur implements Authenticatable
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $login,
        public string $nom,
        public string $role,
         // the password (empty for a user read from a token)
        public string $hachageMotDePasse = '',
         // the contents of the token that authenticated the user
        public array $claims = [],
    ) {
    }

     // The user's ID: their login
    public function getAuthIdentifierName(): string
    {
        return 'login';
    }

    public function getAuthIdentifier(): string
    {
        return $this->login;
    }

    public function getAuthPasswordName(): string
    {
        return 'hachageMotDePasse';
    }

    public function getAuthPassword(): string
    {
        return $this->hachageMotDePasse;
    }

     // the "remember me" session token: not needed here
    public function getRememberToken(): ?string
    {
        return null;
    }

    public function setRememberToken($valeur): void
    {
    }

    public function getRememberTokenName(): string
    {
        return '';
    }
}
  • Line 9: a user. [Laravel] expects authenticated users to implement the [Authenticatable] interface: its methods provide it with the user’s ID, their hashed password, and the “remember me” session token, which is unnecessary here. In a typical application, the [Eloquent] model for the user table (next chapter) implements this;
  • lines 12–18: the login, name, role, password hash, and the contents of the token that authenticated the user (empty for a user retrieved from the user list). A server never stores a password, even if it’s encrypted: if the database were stolen, the passwords would be too (and many people use the same password everywhere). It stores the result of a hash function, a one-way function: you can calculate the hash of a password, but you cannot recover a password from its hash. To verify an entered password, you calculate its hash and compare it to the one on file.
<?php
// app/Auth/UtilisateursService.php: users, in memory (Example 28 and
// the case study will store them in a database)

namespace App\Auth;

class UtilisateursService
{
     // we do not store JAMAIS a password, only its bcrypt hash, calculated
     // once and for all using: php -r "echo password_hash('marie', PASSWORD_BCRYPT);"
    private const UTILISATEURS = [
        'marie' => ['Marie Pélissier', 'USER', '$2y$10$2DnOgGBiVcyc07su9rj2E.EvOoyPFzHN/h9PLKDuoW5P7UGtclW6W'],
        'admin' => ['Administrateur', 'ADMIN', '$2y$10$m5o9euCi0EdgoZkLVw.UsO58RxJcqhMBfVrlLMCIOh2LyGSjuN29K'],
    ];

    public function chercher(string $login): ?Utilisateur
    {
        if (! isset(self::UTILISATEURS[$login])) {
            return null;
        }
        [$nom, $role, $hachage] = self::UTILISATEURS[$login];
        return new Utilisateur($login, $nom, $role, $hachage);
    }
}
  • Lines 11–14: Two test users, hard-coded into the program (Example 28 and the case study will populate a database with them): for each login, the name, role, and password hash. The hash is generated using the bcrypt algorithm, which is designed for passwords. It has two distinctive features. It is intentionally slow, with an adjustable level of slowness (the cost, here set to 10: 2^10 computational cycles, resulting in the hash [$10$]): a few tens of milliseconds, imperceptible to a user, but which make it very costly for a hacker to try billions of passwords. It is salted: a randomly generated salt is mixed with the password before hashing and stored within the hash itself (the 22 characters following [$10$]); thus, two users with the same password will have different hashes. The hashes were calculated once and for all by the function [password_hash] from [PHP] (line 10): calculating them with every request would be an unnecessary waste of time, since the application is rebuilt with every request. [bcrypt] considers only the first 72 bytes of a password: the case study takes this into account;
  • Lines 16–23: the user of a login, or [null]. [isset] checks for the existence of a key; the assignment [[$nom, $role, $hachage] = ...] deallocates an array: each variable receives the corresponding element.

docs.title: 8.1.3. The authentication service: app/Auth/AuthService.php
docs.text:
<?php
//app/Auth/AuthService.php: password verification and tokens

namespace App\Auth;

use Firebase\JWT\JWT;
use Firebase\JWT\Key;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Hash;
use Throwable;

class AuthService
{
    public function __construct(private UtilisateursService $utilisateurs)
    {
    }

     // the user, or null if the login is unknown or the password is incorrect.
     // Hash::check hashes the entered password with the stored hash salt,
     // then compares the two results
    public function valider(?string $login, ?string $motDePasse): ?Utilisateur
    {
        if (! $login || $motDePasse === null) {
            return null;
        }
        $utilisateur = $this->utilisateurs->chercher($login);
        if ($utilisateur === null || ! Hash::check($motDePasse, $utilisateur->hachageMotDePasse)) {
            return null;
        }
        return $utilisateur;
    }

     // the user’s token (JWT), signed with the secret key (HMAC-SHA256)
    public function creerJeton(Utilisateur $utilisateur): string
    {
        $maintenant = time();
         // the token’s content: the “claims” (statements about the user)
        $claims = [
            'sub' => $utilisateur->login,
            'nom' => $utilisateur->nom,
            'role' => $utilisateur->role,
            'iat' => $maintenant,
            'exp' => $maintenant + config('jwt.duree') * 60,
        ];
        return JWT::encode($claims, config('jwt.secret'), 'HS256');
    }

     // the user described by a token whose signature and expiration date
     // are valid; null otherwise (token is forged, expired, or unreadable)
    public function verifier(string $jeton): ?Utilisateur
    {
        try {
             // decode returns an object; (array) converts it to an associative array
            $claims = (array) JWT::decode($jeton, new Key(config('jwt.secret'), 'HS256'));
        } catch (Throwable) {
            return null;
        }
        return new Utilisateur($claims['sub'], $claims['nom'], $claims['role'], claims: $claims);
    }
}
  • lines 20–30: verification of a username and password. [Hash::check] hashes the entered password using the stored hash salt and compares the two hashes. An unknown username and an incorrect password yield the same result, [null];
  • lines 33–45: generating the token. Its content is an array of claims about the user. Some have standardized names: [sub] (*subject*), the user’s identifier; [iat] (*issued at*), the creation date; [exp] (*expiration*), the expiration date. Dates are expressed in seconds elapsed since January 1, 1970 (the function [time()] of [PHP]). The other fields are optional: here, the name and role. [JWT::encode] generates the token and signs it using the [HS256] algorithm (HMAC-SHA256, a signature using a shared secret key);
  • Lines 49–58: token verification. [JWT::decode] verifies the signature and expiration date, then returns the assertions (an object, converted to an array by [(array)]). Any anomaly (forged, expired, or malformed token) raises an exception; [catch (Throwable)] catches them all ([Throwable] is the interface for all exceptions and errors from [PHP]; the variable name is optional when not used). The [Key] object associates the key with an algorithm: a token that specifies a different algorithm (or none at all, [none]) would be rejected. The valid token becomes a [Utilisateur], without a hash, along with its assertions (parameter named [claims]).

docs.title: 8.1.4. The guard: bootstrap/app.php
docs.text:
<?php
// bootstrap/app.php: the application from Example 25

use App\Auth\AuthService;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Middleware;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Auth;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Cookie;

(require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php')->addPsr4('App\\', __DIR__.'/../app/');

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(
        web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php',
         // the route used by Bootstrap (see Example 15)
        then: fn () => require __DIR__.'/../../commun/bootstrap.php')
    ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
         // The token is already signed: the cookie carrying it is not encrypted
        $middleware->encryptCookies(except: ['jeton']);
         // An anonymous visitor requesting a protected page: redirected to /login
        $middleware->redirectGuestsTo('/login');
    })
    ->withExceptions()
    ->booted(function () {
         // the on-call handler [jwt] (see config/auth.php): a function that receives the
         // request, and returns the authenticated user, or null for an anonymous visitor
        Auth::viaRequest('jwt', function (Request $request) {
            $jeton = $request->cookie(config('jwt.cookie'));
            if ($jeton === null) {
                return null;
            }
            $utilisateur = app(AuthService::class)->verifier($jeton);
            if ($utilisateur === null) {
                 // a cookie that exists but is invalid (expired or forged token): it is deleted
                Cookie::queue(Cookie::forget(config('jwt.cookie')));
            }
            return $utilisateur;
        });
    })
    ->create();
  • line 20: the token is already signed; the cookie carrying it is not encrypted (example 22), which allows it to be examined;
  • line 22: the [auth] middleware will redirect anonymous visitors to the login page;
  • lines 28–39: [Auth::viaRequest] defines a guard driver using a simple function: it receives the request and returns the authenticated user, or [null] for an anonymous visitor. It is called only if the application needs the user, and, once it has found one, [Laravel] retains it for the entire request (for an anonymous visitor, it is called with every request) (the middleware [auth], [auth()->user()]...). It does not reject anything: it determines who the user is. This is authentication. [app(AuthService::class)] requests an object from the container (see Example 06): the function [app] grants access to the container everywhere;
  • Lines 34–39: If the browser sent a cookie but its token is invalid (expired or tampered with), we take this opportunity to delete it. [Cookie::forget] creates an empty cookie that has already expired; [Cookie::queue] queues it: the [AddQueuedCookiesToResponse] middleware in the [web] group will add it to the response, whatever that response may be.

docs.title: 8.1.5. The controllers
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/AuthController.php: login and logout

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Auth\AuthService;
use Illuminate\Http\RedirectResponse;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class AuthController
{
    public function __construct(private AuthService $auth)
    {
    }

    public function accueil(): RedirectResponse
    {
        return redirect('/profil');
    }

    public function formulaire(): View
    {
        return view('auth.login');
    }

    public function connexion(Request $request): View|RedirectResponse
    {
        $login = $request->input('login');
        $utilisateur = $this->auth->valider($login, $request->input('motDePasse'));
        if ($utilisateur === null) {
             // a deliberately vague message: it does not specify whether it is the username or the password
            return view('auth.login', ['login' => $login,
                'erreur' => 'Login ou mot de passe incorrect.']);
        }
         // the token, in a cookie: the page’s JavaScript cannot read it
         // (httpOnly); it does not accompany POST requests coming from other sites
         // (sameSite); it disappears when the token expires (duration in minutes)
        return redirect('/profil')->withCookie(cookie(config('jwt.cookie'),
            $this->auth->creerJeton($utilisateur), config('jwt.duree'),
            httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax'));
    }

     // logout: POST only (a simple link placed on another site does not
     //(cannot log the user out without their knowledge); the cookie is deleted
    public function deconnexion(): RedirectResponse
    {
        return redirect('/login')->withoutCookie(config('jwt.cookie'));
    }
}
  • lines 30–34: the login. If the login fails, the form is redisplayed with the entered username and a deliberately vague message: saying “unknown username” would reveal to a hacker which usernames exist;
  • lines 39–41: if successful, the token is stored in a cookie, and the user is redirected to the protected page (schema PRG). The cookie is [httpOnly]: the page’s [JavaScript] cannot read it, which protects the token against script injection (XSS); it is [sameSite: 'lax']: the browser does not send it with a POST request originating from another site, which protects the application against CSRF attacks (example 18); its lifetime (in minutes) is the same as the token’s. In production, for HTTPS, we would add [secure: true]: the cookie would never be sent over an unencrypted connection;
  • Lines 46–49: Logging out deletes the cookie ([withoutCookie]). This is a POST action: a simple link to [/logout], placed on another site or within an image, cannot log the user out without their knowledge. Note a limitation of tokens: the token itself remains valid until it expires. Someone who has made a copy of it could still use it. That is why their lifetime is limited.
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/ProfilController.php: a page reserved for authenticated users

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Auth\Utilisateur;
use Illuminate\Container\Attributes\CurrentUser;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class ProfilController
{
     // #[CurrentUser]: the container provides the authenticated user from the request,
     // the one found by the guard (see bootstrap/app.php)
    public function afficher(#[CurrentUser] User $utilisateur): View
    {
        return view('profil.profil', ['utilisateur' => $utilisateur]);
    }
}
  • Line 14: The attribute [#[CurrentUser]] requests the authenticated user from the container—the one found by the guard (see Example 12 for parameter attributes). The action is protected by the [auth] middleware (see the routing table): it is guaranteed to receive a user. It could also be obtained via [auth()->user()] or [$request->user()].

The routing table:

<?php
// routes/web.php: the routes from Example 25

use App\Http\Controllers\AuthController;
use App\Http\Controllers\ProfilController;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::get('/', [AuthController::class, 'accueil']);
Route::get('login', [AuthController::class, 'formulaire']);
Route::post('login', [AuthController::class, 'connexion']);
Route::post('logout', [AuthController::class, 'deconnexion']);

// the middleware [auth]: the route is accessible only to an authenticated user
Route::get('profil', [ProfilController::class, 'afficher'])->middleware('auth');
  • Line 14: The [auth] middleware protects the profile page. For an anonymous visitor, it throws a [AuthenticationException] exception, which [Laravel] converts into a redirect to the login page ([redirectGuestsTo]). [auth] is an alias—a short name that [Laravel] associates with the middleware [Illuminate\Auth\Middleware\Authenticate]. A group of routes can be protected all at once: [Route::middleware('auth')->group(...)].

docs.title: 8.1.7. Execution
docs.text:
Let’s request the protected page [/profil] without being logged in:

curl -i http://localhost:8000/profile

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: http://localhost:8000/login
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
...

An incorrect password:

Login successful. With [curl], you must first request the form to obtain the anti-CSRF token and the session cookie (example 18), then submit the form while retaining the received cookie:

curl -c jeton.txt -b jeton.txt http://localhost:8000/login
curl -i -c jeton.txt -b jeton.txt -d "_token=...&login=marie&motDePasse=marie" http://localhost:8000/login

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: http://localhost:8000/profile
Set-Cookie: jeton=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJtYXJpZSIsIm5vbSI6Ik1hcmllIFBcdTAwZTlsaXNzaWVyIiwicm9sZSI6IlVTRVIiLCJpYXQiOjE3OTA0Mzk2ODIsImV4cCI6MTc5MDQ0MzI4Mn0.IwcQODDFKxG7s01RZ4ezDAJgL4WS_xfq5Hwe7BiJiyI; expires=Sat, 26 Sep 2026 17:21:22 GMT; Max-Age=3600; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
...

The token consists of three parts, separated by periods, each encoded in Base64: the header, the content, and the signature. The first two parts can be decoded without any key:

{"typ":"JWT","alg":"HS256"}
{"sub":"marie","nom":"Marie Pélissier","role":"USER","iat":1790439682,"exp":1790443282}

The expiration time is one hour (3,600 seconds) after creation. In the browser, the profile page displays this same content:

A malicious user modifies their token: they replace the role [USER]*** in the content with [ADMIN]***, re-encode this part in Base64, and keep the original signature. The server recalculates the signature of the modified content, which no longer matches:

curl -i -b "jeton=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.<contenu modifié>.IwcQODDFKxG7s01RZ4ezDAJgL4WS_xfq5Hwe7BiJiyI" http://localhost:8000/profile

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: http://localhost:8000/login
Set-Cookie: jeton=deleted; expires=Fri, 26 Sep 2025 16:21:28 GMT; Max-Age=0; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
...

The forged token is rejected and deleted (the value [deleted] and the expired date instruct the browser to delete the cookie). To generate a valid signature, one would need to know the secret key—hence the importance of keeping it secret and choosing a long, random key.

docs.title: 8.2. Example 26: Roles
docs.text: Example 26 adds an administration page, restricted to the role ADMIN. Only new or modified files are displayed.

docs.title: 8.2.1. An authorization: bootstrap/app.php
docs.text:
<?php
// bootstrap/app.php: the application from Example 26

use App\Auth\AuthService;
use App\Auth\Utilisateur;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Middleware;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Auth;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Cookie;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Gate;

(require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php')->addPsr4('App\\', __DIR__.'/../app/');

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(
        web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php',
         // the route serving Bootstrap (see Example 15)
        then: fn () => require __DIR__.'/../../commun/bootstrap.php')
    ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
         // The token is already signed: the cookie carrying it is not encrypted
        $middleware->encryptCookies(except: ['jeton']);
         // An anonymous visitor requesting a protected page: redirected to /login
        $middleware->redirectGuestsTo('/login');
    })
    ->withExceptions()
    ->booted(function () {
         // the on-call handler [jwt] (see config/auth.php): a function that receives the
         // request, and returns the authenticated user, or null for an anonymous visitor
        Auth::viaRequest('jwt', function (Request $request) {
            $jeton = $request->cookie(config('jwt.cookie'));
            if ($jeton === null) {
                return null;
            }
            $utilisateur = app(AuthService::class)->verifier($jeton);
            if ($utilisateur === null) {
                 // a cookie that exists but is invalid (expired or forged token): it is deleted
                Cookie::queue(Cookie::forget(config('jwt.cookie')));
            }
            return $utilisateur;
        });
         // a AUTORISATION named [admin]: the function receives the
         // authenticated, and indicates whether the user has the requested permission
        Gate::define('admin', fn (Utilisateur $utilisateur) => $utilisateur->role === 'ADMIN');
    })
    ->create();
  • Line 44: The [Gate] facade (a “gate”) defines an authorization named [admin]. The function receives the authenticated user (and, optionally, other parameters: the object to be accessed, for example), and returns [true] if the user has the requested permission. A permission can be verified in several ways: [Gate::allows('admin')] or [Gate::authorize('admin')] (which throws an exception, 403) in the code, [@can('admin')] in the views, and the [can:admin] middleware on the routes. For a larger number of rules, [Laravel] suggests grouping them by template class into policies (*policies*).

docs.title: 8.2.2. The routing table and the controller
docs.text:
<?php
// routes/web.php: the routes from Example 26

use App\Http\Controllers\AdminController;
use App\Http\Controllers\AuthController;
use App\Http\Controllers\ProfilController;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::get('/', [AuthController::class, 'accueil']);
Route::get('login', [AuthController::class, 'formulaire']);
Route::post('login', [AuthController::class, 'connexion']);
Route::post('logout', [AuthController::class, 'deconnexion']);

// the middleware [auth]: the route is accessible only to an authenticated user
Route::get('profil', [ProfilController::class, 'afficher'])->middleware('auth');

// two middleware components: [auth] (an authenticated user), then [can:admin] (which has
// the authorization [admin]; see bootstrap/app.php)
Route::get('admin', [AdminController::class, 'afficher'])->middleware(['auth', 'can:admin']);
  • line 19: two middleware components, executed in order: [auth] verifies that a user is authenticated (otherwise, redirects to the login page), then [can:admin] verifies that the user has permission [admin] (otherwise, a 403 error, *Forbidden*). The text following [:] is the middleware parameter, which [Laravel] passes to it after [$next]. The difference between the two denial responses is significant: for a user who is authenticated but does not have the requested role, logging in would serve no purpose, since they are already authenticated.
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/AdminController.php: a page restricted to the ADMIN role

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Auth\Utilisateur;
use Illuminate\Container\Attributes\CurrentUser;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class AdminController
{
    public function afficher(#[CurrentUser] User $utilisateur): View
    {
        return view('admin.admin', ['nom' => $utilisateur->nom]);
    }
}

The controller performs no checks: that is the responsibility of the middleware. [Laravel] also allows you to specify middleware directly on the action itself, using attributes: [#[Middleware('auth')]], [#[Authorize('admin')]].

The 403 error page: [Laravel] searches for a view [errors/<code>.blade.php] when a HTTP error occurs, and displays it in place of its standard page (see previous chapter). There is nothing to declare. The profile page provides a link to the administration page:

@extends('layout')

@section('contenu')
  <h1 class="h3">Bonjour {{ $utilisateur->nom }}</h1>
  <p>Votre rôle : <b>{{ $utilisateur->role === 'ADMIN' ? 'administrateur' : 'utilisateur' }}</b>.</p>
  {{-- @can : le bloc n'est affiché que si l'utilisateur a l'autorisation [admin] --}}
  @can('admin')
    <p><a href="/admin">L'espace d'administration</a></p>
  @else
    <p><a href="/admin">L'espace d'administration</a> (qui vous est interdit)</p>
  @endcan
  <p>Le contenu de votre jeton :</p>
  <table class="table table-sm w-auto">
    @foreach ($utilisateur->claims as $cle => $valeur)
      <tr><td><code>{{ $cle }}</code></td><td>{{ $valeur }}</td></tr>
    @endforeach
  </table>
  {{-- la déconnexion : un formulaire POST réduit à son bouton --}}
  <form method="post" action="/logout">
    @csrf
    <button class="btn btn-outline-secondary" type="submit">Se déconnecter</button>
  </form>
@endsection
  • Lines 7–11: The [@can] directive displays its block only if the user has permission; [@else] handles the opposite case. This prevents a link from being displayed that would lead to an error; however, this is merely a convenience measure: the real protection comes from the routing logic.

docs.text:
Marie, with the role USER, follows the link to the administration page:

The administrator, on the other hand, has access to it:

With [curl]: a user with role USER (the [jeton.txt] file from Example 25), followed by an anonymous visitor:

curl -i -b jeton.txt http://localhost:8000/admin
curl -i http://localhost:8000/admin

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
...
        <div class="alert alert-danger">
    <h1 class="h4">Erreur 403</h1>
    <p class="mb-0">Accès refusé : cette page est réservée aux administrateurs.</p>
  </div>
...
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: http://localhost:8000/login
...

Protecting routes one by one has a flaw: if one is overlooked, the page becomes accessible to everyone. The case study will reverse this logic: all routes are protected by default by a group, and only a few routes (the login page, the registration page) are excluded.

docs.title: 8.3. Example 27: CAPTCHA and Attempt Limits
docs.text:
A login form is a target: a program can try thousands of passwords per minute (brute-force attack). Two protections complement each other:

  • a CAPTCHA (*Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart*): an image containing a distorted code that is easy for a human to read but difficult for a program;
  • an attempt limit: after three failed attempts, the client’s address IP is blocked for one minute.

Example 27 builds on Example 25 and adds these two security measures.

docs.title: 8.3.1. The CAPTCHA image: app/Auth/DessinCaptcha.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Auth/DessinCaptcha.php: a CAPTCHA image, SVG (text XML)
// hand-drawn

namespace App\Auth;

class DessinCaptcha
{
    public const LARGEUR = 150;

    public const HAUTEUR = 50;

     // The "font": each character is a list of strokes, each stroke a
     // sequence of x, y points in a 4 x 6 grid (y down).
     // Characters that are too easily confused with one another: excluded (0 O, 1 I L).
    private const POLICE = [
        'A' => [[0, 6, 2, 0, 4, 6], [0.8, 3.8, 3.2, 3.8]],
        'B' => [[0, 0, 0, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5, 4, 4, 3, 3, 0, 3], [0, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 3, 3]],
        'C' => [[4, 1, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 5, 1, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5]],
        'D' => [[0, 0, 0, 6, 2.5, 6, 4, 4.5, 4, 1.5, 2.5, 0, 0, 0]],
        'E' => [[4, 0, 0, 0, 0, 6, 4, 6], [0, 3, 3, 3]],
        'F' => [[4, 0, 0, 0, 0, 6], [0, 3, 3, 3]],
        'G' => [[4, 1, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 5, 1, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5, 4, 3.5, 2.5, 3.5]],
        'H' => [[0, 0, 0, 6], [4, 0, 4, 6], [0, 3, 4, 3]],
        'J' => [[4, 0, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5]],
        'K' => [[0, 0, 0, 6], [4, 0, 0, 3.5], [1.3, 2.6, 4, 6]],
        'M' => [[0, 6, 0, 0, 2, 3.5, 4, 0, 4, 6]],
        'N' => [[0, 6, 0, 0, 4, 6, 4, 0]],
        'P' => [[0, 6, 0, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 3, 3, 0, 3]],
        'Q' => [[1, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5, 0, 1, 1, 0], [2.5, 4.5, 4, 6.3]],
        'R' => [[0, 6, 0, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 3, 3, 0, 3], [2, 3, 4, 6]],
        'S' => [[4, 1, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5]],
        'T' => [[0, 0, 4, 0], [2, 0, 2, 6]],
        'U' => [[0, 0, 0, 5, 1, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5, 4, 0]],
        'V' => [[0, 0, 2, 6, 4, 0]],
        'W' => [[0, 0, 1, 6, 2, 2.5, 3, 6, 4, 0]],
        'X' => [[0, 0, 4, 6], [4, 0, 0, 6]],
        'Y' => [[0, 0, 2, 3, 4, 0], [2, 3, 2, 6]],
        'Z' => [[0, 0, 4, 0, 0, 6, 4, 6]],
        '2' => [[0, 1, 1, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 0, 6, 4, 6]],
        '3' => [[0, 1, 1, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 3, 3, 1.5, 3], [3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5]],
        '4' => [[3, 6, 3, 0, 0, 4, 4, 4]],
        '5' => [[4, 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5]],
        '6' => [[4, 1, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 5, 1, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5, 4, 4, 3, 3, 0, 3]],
        '7' => [[0, 0, 4, 0, 1.5, 6]],
        '8' => [[1, 3, 0, 2, 0, 1, 1, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 3, 3, 1, 3, 0, 4, 0, 5, 1, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5,
            4, 4, 3, 3]],
        '9' => [[4, 3, 1, 3, 0, 2, 0, 1, 1, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5]],
    ];

     // a few dark colors, clearly legible against the light background
    private const COULEURS = ['#1f4e79', '#7b2d26', '#2e6b30', '#5b2c83', '#8a5a00', '#23395d', '#9c2a5b'];

     // random text. random_int is a "cryptographic" generator,
     // unpredictable (unlike rand or mt_rand, whose sequence could be guessed)
    public static function texteAleatoire(int $longueur): string
    {
        $alphabet = array_keys(self::POLICE);
        $texte = '';
        for ($i = 0; $i < $longueur; $i++) {
            $texte .= $alphabet[random_int(0, count($alphabet) - 1)];
        }
        return $texte;
    }

     // a random decimal number between $minimum and $maximum
    private static function hasard(float $minimum, float $maximum): float
    {
        return $minimum + ($maximum - $minimum) * random_int(0, PHP_INT_MAX) / PHP_INT_MAX;
    }

    private static function couleur(): string
    {
        return self::COULEURS[random_int(0, count(self::COULEURS) - 1)];
    }

    public static function svg(string $texte): string
    {
        $l = self::LARGEUR;
        $h = self::HAUTEUR;
        $morceaux = ["<svg xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/2000/svg\" width=\"$l\" height=\"$h\" viewBox=\"0 0 $l $h\">",
             '<rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#f5f7fa"/>'];

         // the characters: each enlarged, tilted, and offset, and each dot
         // slightly shifted at random
        $pas = ($l - 20) / strlen($texte);
        foreach (str_split($texte) as $i => $caractere) {
            $echelle = self::hasard(4.6, 5.6);    // one grid unit in pixels
            $angle = self::hasard(-0.35, 0.35);   // rotation, in radians (approximately ±20°)
            $cx = 10 + $pas * ($i + 0.5) + self::hasard(-3, 3);    // center of the character
            $cy = $h / 2 + self::hasard(-4, 4);
            foreach (self::POLICE[$caractere] as $trait) {
                $d = [];
                for ($k = 0; $k < count($trait); $k += 2) {
                     // grid point, centered at (2, 3), distorted, rotated, positioned
                    $x = ($trait[$k] - 2 + self::hasard(-0.2, 0.2)) * $echelle;
                    $y = ($trait[$k + 1] - 3 + self::hasard(-0.2, 0.2)) * $echelle;
                    $px = $cx + $x * cos($angle) - $y * sin($angle);
                    $py = $cy + $x * sin($angle) + $y * cos($angle);
                    $d[] = sprintf('%s%.1f %.1f', $k === 0 ? 'M' : 'L', $px, $py);
                }
                $morceaux[] = sprintf('<path d="%s" fill="none" stroke="%s" stroke-width="%.1f" '
                    .'stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"/>',
                    implode(' ', $d), self::couleur(), self::hasard(2.2, 3));
            }
        }

         // 3 scrambling lines: curves that cross the image
        for ($n = 0; $n < 3; $n++) {
            $morceaux[] = sprintf('<path d="M%.1f %.1f C%.1f %.1f %.1f %.1f %.1f %.1f" fill="none" '
                .'stroke="%s" stroke-width="1.3"/>',
                self::hasard(0, 20), self::hasard(5, 45), self::hasard(30, 60), self::hasard(0, 50),
                self::hasard(90, 120), self::hasard(0, 50), self::hasard(130, 150), self::hasard(5, 45),
                self::couleur());
        }
        $morceaux[] = '</svg>';
        return implode('', $morceaux);
    }
}

The image is in SVG format (*Scalable Vector Graphics*): a vector graphic described in XML—that is, text—which the server generates without a graphics library and which the browser displays directly on the page.

  • Lines 16–49: a minimalist “font”: each character is a list of strokes, and each stroke is a list of coordinates [x, y] in a 4 × 6 grid. Characters that are easily confused ([0] and [O], [1], [I], and [L]) are excluded;
  • Lines 56–64: a random text string, selected from the characters in the font ([array_keys], the keys in the table). The functions [rand] and [mt_rand] from [PHP] produce predictable number sequences (anyone who knows a few values can guess the next ones): they are suitable for simulations, not for security. [random_int] is a cryptographic generator; it is unpredictable;
  • lines 67–70: a random floating-point number, generated from a random integer ([PHP_INT_MAX] is the largest integer in [PHP]);
  • lines 77–118: the drawing. Each character is randomly scaled, rotated, and moved, and each of its points is slightly offset; each line becomes an element [<path>] of SVG ([M]: displacement, [L]: line). Three curves ([C]: Bézier curve) cross the image to interfere with recognition programs. The [sprintf] function formats a string: [%s] inserts a string into it, and [%.1f] inserts a number with one decimal place. [str_split] splits a string into characters.

docs.title: 8.3.2. The CAPTCHA service: app/Auth/CaptchaService.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Auth/CaptchaService.php: pending CAPTCHAs, stored by the server,
// in the cache (see example 20)

namespace App\Auth;

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Cache;
use Illuminate\Support\Str;

class CaptchaService
{
     // the lifespan of a CAPTCHA, in seconds
    private const DUREE_VIE = 600;

    public function generer(): Captcha
    {
        $texte = DessinCaptcha::texteAleatoire(5);
         //: a random identifier that is impossible to guess
        $id = Str::random(24);
         // the expected answer, stored in the cache for 10 minutes: the cache will forget it
         // on its own afterward
        Cache::put("captcha:$id", $texte, self::DUREE_VIE);
        return new Captcha($id, DessinCaptcha::svg($texte));
    }

     // the CAPTCHA is CONSOMMÉ in all cases: an image is used only once
    public function verifier(?string $id, ?string $saisie): bool
    {
         // pull: reads the value ET and removes it from the cache (returns null if it doesn’t exist or has expired)
        $attendu = $id ? Cache::pull("captcha:$id") : null;
        if ($attendu === null || $saisie === null) {
            return false;
        }
        return strcasecmp($attendu, trim($saisie)) === 0;
    }
}
  • Lines 15–24: a new CAPTCHA: random text, a random identifier that is impossible to guess ([Str::random] also uses a cryptographic generator), and the image. For each identifier, the server stores the expected response in the cache (example 20) for ten minutes: [Cache::put(clé, valeur, secondes)]. After this time, the cache automatically discards it. The page receives only the identifier and the image: the answer never leaves the server. The class [Captcha] combines the identifier and the image;
  • lines 27–35: the verification. [Cache::pull] reads the value and removes it from the cache: the CAPTCHA is consumed in all cases, whether successful or not. Without this, a program could try all possible answers on the same image. The comparison ignores case ([strcasecmp] returns 0 for two equal strings, regardless of uppercase or lowercase letters) and spaces around the input ([trim]).

docs.title: 8.3.3. The controller: app/Http/Controllers/AuthController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/AuthController.php: login (with CAPTCHA and attempt limit) and logout

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Auth\AuthService;
use App\Auth\CaptchaService;
use Illuminate\Http\RedirectResponse;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\RateLimiter;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class AuthController
{
     // Maximum of 3 failed attempts within 60 seconds
    private const MAX_ECHECS = 3;

    private const DUREE_BLOCAGE = 60;

    public function __construct(private AuthService $auth, private CaptchaService $captchas)
    {
    }

    public function accueil(): RedirectResponse
    {
        return redirect('/profil');
    }

    public function formulaire(): View
    {
        return $this->pageLogin();
    }

    public function connexion(Request $request): View|RedirectResponse
    {
        $login = $request->input('login');
         // The key for the failure counter: the client's address IP
        $cle = 'login:'.$request->ip();

         // 1. A blocked address isn’t even listened to
        if (RateLimiter::tooManyAttempts($cle, self::MAX_ECHECS)) {
            $secondes = RateLimiter::availableIn($cle);
            return $this->pageLogin($login, "Trop de tentatives : réessayez dans $secondes s.");
        }
         // 2. Captcha first (low-cost), password (bcrypt, high-cost) next
        if (! $this->captchas->verifier($request->input('captchaId'), $request->input('captcha'))) {
            RateLimiter::hit($cle, self::DUREE_BLOCAGE);
            return $this->pageLogin($login, "Le code de l'image est incorrect.");
        }
        $utilisateur = $this->auth->valider($login, $request->input('motDePasse'));
        if ($utilisateur === null) {
            RateLimiter::hit($cle, self::DUREE_BLOCAGE);
            return $this->pageLogin($login, 'Login ou mot de passe incorrect.');
        }
        RateLimiter::clear($cle);
        return redirect('/profil')->withCookie(cookie(config('jwt.cookie'),
            $this->auth->creerJeton($utilisateur), config('jwt.duree'),
            httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax'));
    }

    public function deconnexion(): RedirectResponse
    {
        return redirect('/login')->withoutCookie(config('jwt.cookie'));
    }

     // Each time the form is displayed, it generates a NOUVEAU CAPTCHA
    private function pageLogin(?string $login = null, ?string $erreur = null): View
    {
        return view('auth.login', ['login' => $login, 'erreur' => $erreur,
            'captcha' => $this->captchas->generer()]);
    }
}
  • line 38: The limit is handled by the [RateLimiter] facade of [Laravel], which counts “attempts” under a key in the cache. The key here is the client’s address IP;
  • lines 41–44: A blocked address is not even listened to. [tooManyAttempts(clé, 3)] is true if the key has reached 3 attempts; [availableIn] returns the number of seconds remaining before the block ends;
  • lines 46–54: The CAPTCHA is verified before the password; verifying it costs almost nothing, whereas [bcrypt] is intentionally slow. A program that enters the wrong CAPTCHA would therefore not trigger [bcrypt]. Each failure—whether for the CAPTCHA or the password—is counted: [RateLimiter::hit(clé, 60)] adds one attempt and sets the counter’s lifetime to 60 seconds. On the third failure, the address is therefore blocked until the end of those 60 seconds, counted from the first failure;
  • line 55: a successful login clears the failed attempts;
  • lines 67–71: Each time the form is displayed, a new CAPTCHA is generated, even after a failed attempt.

[Laravel] also provides a middleware component, [throttle], which limits the number of requests for a route ([->middleware('throttle:5,1')]: 5 requests per minute); we chose to count only the failed attempts, so as not to inconvenience a user who is logging in normally.

docs.title: 11.1. The Problem
docs.text:
The RdvMedecins application manages appointments for a medical practice. Each doctor has time slots (from 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. in 20-minute increments, for example); an appointment consists of a day, a time slot, and a client (a patient). This is the exact port, in [Laravel], of the [Flask] application from the previous lesson (which was itself ported from versions [Spring MVC] and [ASP.NET Core MVC]): same database, same business rules, same pages, same URLs, same text. The HTML pages are generated by the server using [Blade] views; database access is handled by [Eloquent].

Three user roles share the application:

ADMINthe administrator ([admin])view schedules, make and cancel appointments for any patient; manage (list, add, edit, delete) doctors and clientsDOCTORDoctorsView schedules, make appointments, and cancel appointments for any patientUSERclients (patients)view schedules without seeing other patients’ names; book an appointment for themselves; cancel their appointment; manage their account; create an account

Key management rules:

  • No appointments in the past;
  • A time slot is reserved only once a day;
  • a patient has only one upcoming appointment at a time;
  • two doctors (or two clients) cannot have the same first and last names, and a login belongs to only one account;
  • A doctor with appointments cannot be deleted; A client is deleted along with their appointments;
  • the login page is protected against bots (CAPTCHA, limited attempts), and creating a client account requires first solving the CAPTCHA on that page.

docs.title: 11.2.1. The login page
docs.text:
The page features two buttons: Log In and Create a Customer Account. Both require you to enter the characters shown in the image. The buttons FR / EN change the language:

An error (in this case, an incorrectly entered CAPTCHA) is displayed at the bottom of the page on a light pink background:

docs.title: 11.2.2. The calendar, as seen by the administrator and doctors
docs.text:
Once logged in, the administrator is taken to the calendar page. They select a doctor and a day:

Each time slot is either available (Book button) or occupied (patient’s name, Cancel button). Clicking Book opens a window asking for the patient’s information. This window is generated by the server, just like the rest of the page: the URL now contains the parameter [reserver=4], which is the number of the selected time slot:

After the booking, a message confirms the appointment:

Clicking “Cancel” prompts a confirmation (here by Dr. Pélissier, whose navigation bar does not include the administration menus):

docs.title: 11.2.3. The Patient Portal
docs.text:
A patient (role USER) arrives at “My Account”: their upcoming appointment, which they can cancel, and links to manage their account and view their calendar. Here, they do not yet have an appointment:

In the calendar, they do not see the names of other patients; these are replaced by “Reserved”: this name does not even appear in the page’s source code. They can book an available time slot:

The booking window does not prompt him to select a patient: he books the appointment for himself.

His dashboard now shows his upcoming appointment, which he can cancel:

Since he has an upcoming appointment, he cannot schedule another one: the “Book” button is not displayed, and on the calendar for another day or another doctor, a message explains why:

Account management: edit their information, change their password, or delete their account (and appointments). The current password is required for any changes:

A patient who attempts to open a page reserved for the administrator (here, [/medecins], typed manually) receives an error page:

The administrator has two additional menus, Doctors and Clients:

docs.title: 11.3. Installation and Execution
docs.text: The application is located in the [rdvmedecins2-laravel] folder, next to the [exemples] folder. It is a standalone project, with its own [composer.json] and [.env] files, and its own [vendor] folder. The [README.md] file in the folder contains all of the following. The introduction to this document has already described the installation of [PHP] and [Composer]; we’ll expand on that here.

docs.title: 11.3.1. Required Software
docs.text:
Three software programs are all you need:

  • [PHP] 8.4 or later, with the [pdo_mysql] extension (the application uses features introduced in version 8.4, such as [array_find]). Verify the installation in a terminal:
php -v
php -m

The second command lists the extensions: [pdo_mysql] should be listed there;

  • [Composer], the library manager for [PHP] (see appendices);
  • a [MySQL] 8 server, for example the one for [Laragon] under [Windows] (see appendices). [MariaDB] is also suitable: the application has been tested with it.

The recommended editor is [Visual Studio Code], with the extensions [PHP Intelephense] and [Laravel] (see appendices); however, everything can be done via the command line.

docs.title: 11.3.2. Install the libraries
docs.text:
The [vendor] folder is not provided: create it once and for all in a terminal window opened in the [rdvmedecins2-laravel] folder (you must be connected to the Internet):

composer install

[Composer] reads the file [composer.json] (discussed later), downloads [Laravel], [firebase/php-jwt], and the libraries they depend on, and generates the class loader [vendor/autoload.php].

docs.title: 11.3.3. Create the database
docs.text:
The [dbrdvmedecins2] database is created by the [database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] script. Using [Laragon], open the [HeidiSQL] tool (Database button), then run the script via the File / Run SQL menu. From the command line, in the application folder:

mysql -u root -p < database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql

The [-p] option prompts for the password for [root]; omit it if the account does not have a password (as is the case with [Laragon]). This is the same database as in other versions of the application: if it already exists, this step is optional. The script can be run at any time to revert to the original data.

docs.title: 11.3.4. Configure Database Access
docs.text: All installation configuration is contained in the file [.env] (discussed further below). By default, the application connects to [MySQL] on [127.0.0.1], port 3306, using the user [root] with no password: these are the default settings for [Laragon]. If your [root] account has a password, enter it in this file on the [DB_PASSWORD=] line. A system environment variable takes precedence over the file (example 25): this allows you to specify the password without writing it to a project file.

docs.title: 11.3.5. Run the application
docs.text:
In a terminal window open to the [rdvmedecins2-laravel] folder:

php artisan serve --port=8081

   INFO  Server running on [http://127.0.0.1:8081].

  Press Ctrl+C to stop the server

Next, open the URL [http://localhost:8081] in a browser, and stop the application using [Ctrl-C]. Port 8081 allows you to run a course example (port 8000) at the same time.

docs.title: 11.3.6. Demo Accounts
docs.text:
The password for each account is its username; you must also enter the characters from the image, in uppercase or lowercase:

[admin]ADMIN (the administrator)[pelissier], [tatou], [dupont]DOCTOR (the doctors)[martin], [durand], [bistrou], [german]USER (patients)

A guide to exploring the app:

  • [admin]: Calendar, Ms. Marie PELISSIER; today: a time slot is already booked by Ms. Brigitte BISTROU. Book a slot for Mr. Jean MARTIN, then try to book a second appointment for him (declined). Doctors and Clients menus: add, edit, delete (Dr. PELISSIER, who has appointments, cannot be deleted);
  • [pelissier]: his daily schedule is displayed directly; the address [/medecins], entered manually, returns a 403 error page;
  • [martin]: My Account, their appointment, the calendar where other patients appear as “Reserved”; Manage My Account;
  • login page: Create a customer account, then log in with the new account;
  • Buttons FR / EN: The entire interface changes languages, including dates.

docs.title: 11.3.7. Development Mode
docs.text:
The provided [.env] file configures the application for development:

  • [DB_LOG=true]: The server console displays every SQL command sent to the database, as well as each step of the transactions (example 28). For example, to display a calendar:
  select * from `medecins` order by `nom` asc, `prenom` asc []
  select * from `users` where `users`.`id` in (2, 3, 4) []
  select * from `medecins` where `medecins`.`id` = ? limit 1 [1]
  select * from `users` where `users`.`id` in (2) []
  select * from `rv` where `jour` = ? and exists (select * from `creneaux` where `rv`.`id_creneau` = `creneaux`.`id` and `id_medecin` = ?) ["2026-09-26",1]
  select * from `clients` where `clients`.`id` in (3) []
  select * from `creneaux` where `id_medecin` = ? order by `hdebut` asc, `mdebut` asc [1]
  2026-09-26 18:50:14 /agenda ...................................... ~ 0.10ms
  • [APP_DEBUG=true]: An unexpected exception displays the [Laravel] debug page (Example 03), showing the exception message and the call stack. In production, the application displays its own 500 error page instead;
  • there is nothing to restart after a change: each request re-reads the [PHP] files (Example 01), and a modified view is recompiled on the next request.

The [Xdebug] debugger also allows you to step through the application from [Visual Studio Code] ([PHP Debug] extension): This is an extension of [PHP], which must be installed separately (see xdebug.org).

docs.title: 11.3.8. A production server
docs.text:
The [php artisan serve] server is not intended for production use. In production, the application is served by a web server ([nginx], [Apache]), which forwards requests to [PHP-FPM], a process manager ([PHP]). The site root is the [public] folder: only its files are accessible from the browser; the [storage] and [bootstrap/cache] folders must be writable by the server. We set up the application with a few commands:

composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
php artisan key:generate
php artisan config:cache
php artisan route:cache
php artisan view:cache

[key:generate] writes a new encryption key to the file [.env]; the following three commands combine the configuration, routes, and compiled views into a few files, which load faster than the originals (this process must be repeated after each modification). In the [.env] file, you must also specify production mode, change the secret token key, and declare that the site is served via HTTPS:

APP_ENV=production
APP_DEBUG=false
JWT_SECRET=<une longue chaîne aléatoire>
COOKIE_SECURE=true

A suitable random string can be obtained using [PHP] itself: [php -r "echo bin2hex(random_bytes(32));"].

docs.title: 11.3.9. Common Issues
docs.text:
A [PHP] application fails to “start”: each request rebuilds the application (example 01). An inaccessible database therefore does not prevent the server from launching: the error appears on the first page that queries the database (the login page does not query the database; the login process itself does). With [APP_DEBUG=true], the error is displayed on the [Laravel] debug page; in all cases, it is logged in the [storage/logs/laravel.log] log. For example, with a database that does not exist:

[2026-09-26 18:55:12] local.ERROR: SQLSTATE[HY000] [1049] Unknown database 'dbinconnue' (Connection: mysql, Host: 127.0.0.1, Port: 3306, Database: dbinconnue, SQL: select * from `users` where `login` = admin limit 1) {"exception":"[object] (Illuminate\\Database\\QueryException(code: 1049): ...

The most common messages:

[Failed opening required '.../vendor/autoload.php']The command [composer install] was not executed[Your Composer dependencies require a PHP version ">= 8.4.0"]The version of [PHP] is earlier than 8.4[could not find driver]The [pdo_mysql] extension of [PHP] is not enabled (file [php.ini], or menu PHP / Extensions of [Laragon])[SQLSTATE[HY000] [2002] Connection refused][MySQL] has not started, or is not listening on [127.0.0.1:3306][SQLSTATE[HY000] [1045] Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost']The password for [MySQL] must be entered in [.env] (see “Configuring Database Access”)[SQLSTATE[HY000] [1049] Unknown database 'dbrdvmedecins2']The script [database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] was not executed[No application encryption key has been specified.]The variable [APP_KEY] in the file [.env] is empty: [php artisan key:generate][JWT_SECRET doit comporter au moins 32 caractères (cf. .env).]The secret key for the tokens is too short in [.env][Failed to listen on 127.0.0.1:8081 (reason: Address already in use)]Port 8081 is already in use (is another version of the application running?): Stop it, or choose a different port

docs.title: 11.4. Application Architecture
docs.text:
• The browser sends its requests to the server ([php artisan serve], or [nginx] + [PHP-FPM]), which forwards them to [Laravel] via the file [public/index.php]. Each request first passes through the middleware layers (see the chapter on the lifecycle): the request language ([FixerLangue]), cookies, the session, anti-CSRF protection, and then authentication: the user is identified based on the JWT token in their cookie, and protected pages are denied to visitors who do not have access ([Authenticate], [ExigerRoles]);
  • [Http/Controllers]: the web-layer controllers. They all pass through a single object, [ApplicationModel] (folder [Web]), which caches the lists of doctors and clients and forwards other requests to the business layer; [Http/Requests]: form validation;
  • [Auth]: tokens, JWT, CAPTCHA, attempt limits, and the account creation pass;
  • [Web]: what the controllers have in common: the cache and the [ApplicationModel] facade, flash messages, and a few utilities; [Vues]: view templates;
  • [Metier]: business rules and transactions;
  • [Dao]: the DAO layer, one class per table;
  • [Models]: the [Eloquent] models, which the DAO layer reads from and writes to the database; [Domain]: the calendar objects, calculated by the business layer;
  • [resources/views]: the [Blade] views, which generate the HTML pages; [lang]: the dictionaries; [public]: the stylesheet, the page script, and [Bootstrap];
  • [bootstrap/app.php] and [app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php] assemble everything; [.env] and the [config] folder: the configuration.

There are two differences from the examples: the application has its own [vendor] folder (the examples shared the one in the [exemples] folder), and a service provider ([app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php]), which is discussed further below. The application’s classes are organized in the [app] folder, according to the PSR-4 rule (Example 01): the [App\Metier\MetierService] class is in the [app/Metier/MetierService.php] file. [Laravel] does not enforce any of these folders (Example 06): [Http], [Models], and [Providers] are the ones in use; the others ([Auth], [Dao], [Metier]...) are part of the layered architecture in Example 28. [Bootstrap] is part of the application (folder [public/lib/bootstrap]) this time: the case study is self-contained.

docs.title: 11.5. The database
docs.text:
The [dbrdvmedecins2] database has five tables:

  • [users]: users authorized to log in;
  • [medecins] and [clients]: doctors and patients, each linked to their user account;
  • [creneaux]: each doctor’s available time slots;
  • [rv]: appointments, one client per time slot, on a given day.

docs.title: 11.5.1. database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql
docs.text:
-- =========================================================================
-- Database [dbrdvmedecins2] - MySQL 8
--
-- Changes to [dbrdvmedecins]:
--    1. The tables [medecins] and [clients] are added with a column named [user],
--       foreign key to users(id): every doctor and every client is
--       now also a user capable of logging in;
--    2. A third role appears: DOCTOR (in addition to ADMIN and USER);
--    3. The script creates a row [users] for each doctor (role DOCTOR)
--       and for each client (role USER):
--         -        login = name in lowercase
--         - password = name in lowercase, hashed with bcrypt (10 rounds)
--         - displ ay name = first name + last name
--
--    4. uniqueness constraints, all NOMMÉES (the application recognizes
--       the name of the violated constraint in the error message MySQL):
--         - unq_users         _login : a login belongs to only one account;
--         - unq_medecins_pren om_nom : Two doctors cannot have the
--                                      same first and last names;
--         - unq_clients_pren  om_nom : the same applies to clients.
--       Note: The utf8mb4_unicode_ci collation compares without taking into account
--       capital letters or accents—"Hélène DUPONT" and "helene dupont"
--       are therefore considered identical.
--
-- The table [users] must now be created AVANT [medecins] and [clients]
-- (they reference it), and delete APRÈS them.
-- =========================================================================

-- The script is written in UTF-8
SET NAMES utf8mb4;

-- we start with an empty database each time the script runs (useful during development)
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS dbrdvmedecins2 CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbrdvmedecins2;

-- Deletion order: from “child” tables to “parent” tables
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS rv;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS creneaux;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS clients;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS medecins;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [users]: users authorized to log in to the application
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE users (
  id       INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  login    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,                 -- login ID
  password VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,                -- HACHÉ password (bcrypt) — never stored in plain text
  nom      VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,                 -- display name after login
  role     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,                 -- 'ADMIN', 'DOCTOR', or 'USER'
   -- A login can only be associated with a single account
  CONSTRAINT unq_users_login UNIQUE (login)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [medecins]: the practice’s doctors
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE medecins (
  id      INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,      -- primary key (technical identifier)
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,               -- row version number (optimistic lock)
  titre   VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,                 -- Ms., Mrs., Mr.
  nom     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  prenom  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`  INT NOT NULL,                         -- Foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_medecins_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
   -- one account per doctor, and one doctor per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_medecins_user UNIQUE (`user`),
   -- Two doctors cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_medecins_prenom_nom UNIQUE (prenom, nom)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [clients]: doctors' patients
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE clients (
  id      INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  titre   VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
  nom     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  prenom  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`  INT NOT NULL,                         -- foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_clients_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
   -- One account per customer, and one customer per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_user UNIQUE (`user`),
   -- Two clients cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_prenom_nom UNIQUE (prenom, nom)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [creneaux]: each doctor’s appointment slots
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE creneaux (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  id_medecin INT NOT NULL,                      -- foreign key -> doctors(id)
  hdebut     INT NOT NULL,                       -- start time of the time slot
  mdebut     INT NOT NULL,                       -- start minute of the time slot
  hfin       INT NOT NULL,                       -- slot end hour
  mfin       INT NOT NULL,                       -- end minute of the time slot
  CONSTRAINT fk_creneaux_medecin FOREIGN KEY (id_medecin) REFERENCES medecins(id)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [rv]: appointments made by customers
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE rv (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  jour       DATE NOT NULL,                      -- appointment date
  id_creneau INT NOT NULL,                        -- foreign key -> time slots (id)
  id_client  INT NOT NULL,                        -- foreign key -> customers(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_rv_creneau FOREIGN KEY (id_creneau) REFERENCES creneaux(id),
  CONSTRAINT fk_rv_client  FOREIGN KEY (id_client)  REFERENCES clients(id),
   -- The same time slot on the same day can only be booked once
  CONSTRAINT unq1_rv UNIQUE (jour, id_creneau)
);

-- =========================================================================
-- Demo data
-- =========================================================================

-- Users: Passwords hashed with bcrypt (10 rounds of salting)
--    admin/admin (ADMIN)
--    One account (DOCTOR) per doctor, one account (USER) per client
--    (the demo account user/user has been removed: a USER account is
--    is now TOUJOURS, a client account that can make reservations and manage the account)
--    (login = password = name in lowercase)
INSERT INTO users (login, password, nom, role) VALUES
  ('admin',     '$2b$10$YSNBJXXHX9mp13nPZb6YGu8M1jR6uvPwO1s2X73z0QAqBR7TOQjoq', 'Administrateur',   'ADMIN'),
   -- doctors
  ('pelissier', '$2b$10$DnSDOK5ONrdMxTTr1NKCHOphR3WSp5QAyG9S9ueruw9HwlxI.16ba', 'Marie PELISSIER',  'DOCTOR'),
  ('tatou',     '$2b$10$PeovBO.gmJUKP4PglI/fwu4xtWOYSxoM5VTWjTj7uQ4wcd9P9.htS', 'Paul TATOU',       'DOCTOR'),
  ('dupont',    '$2b$10$az7wvPKC1h0EiAxXwu/PU.vYjzmB04rd5B7QnK0mvxp4niYIHVoc.', 'Sophie DUPONT',    'DOCTOR'),
   -- clients
  ('martin',    '$2b$10$GT6S5pp.WdGapFw/UmocXesbC6LEjJfZzgatCUyG9Sf4o1iBNlqZW', 'Jean MARTIN',      'USER'),
  ('durand',    '$2b$10$l2gl/zCder8E7Nh4VxGRX.0.SsO3FDiXt6YwqYq3v9nFzgC/jQCy6', 'Alice DURAND',     'USER'),
  ('bistrou',   '$2b$10$naeRp2YUU6c.QDl5itJMAum3Y5aHdUV6jwIcsbp0D.64jPG4F6E9m', 'Brigitte BISTROU', 'USER'),
  ('german',    '$2b$10$tTWxh3ROWF7NjhZOMnWDMOsZcnSWUiwwfy5C3G0.xhccTXALKyLeW', 'Luc GERMAN',       'USER');

-- doctors: the column [user] is retrieved based on the login,
-- rather than assuming the values of the primary keys in [users]
INSERT INTO medecins (titre, nom, prenom, `user`) VALUES
  ('Mme',  'PELISSIER', 'Marie',  (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'pelissier')),
  ('Mr',   'TATOU',     'Paul',   (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'tatou')),
  ('Melle','DUPONT',    'Sophie', (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'dupont'));

INSERT INTO clients (titre, nom, prenom, `user`) VALUES
  ('Mr',   'MARTIN',  'Jean',     (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'martin')),
  ('Mme',  'DURAND',  'Alice',    (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'durand')),
  ('Melle','BISTROU', 'Brigitte', (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'bistrou')),
  ('Mr',   'GERMAN',  'Luc',      (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'german'));

-- Dr. PELISSIER’s time slots (id_medecin = 1): from 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. in 20-minute increments
INSERT INTO creneaux (id_medecin, hdebut, mdebut, hfin, mfin) VALUES
  (1, 8, 0, 8, 20), (1, 8, 20, 8, 40), (1, 8, 40, 9, 0),
  (1, 9, 0, 9, 20), (1, 9, 20, 9, 40), (1, 9, 40, 10, 0),
  (1, 10, 0, 10, 20), (1, 10, 20, 10, 40), (1, 10, 40, 11, 0),
  (1, 11, 0, 11, 20), (1, 11, 20, 11, 40), (1, 11, 40, 12, 0);

-- Dr. TATOU’s time slots (id_medecin = 2): 2:00 PM to 6:00 PM in 20-minute increments
INSERT INTO creneaux (id_medecin, hdebut, mdebut, hfin, mfin) VALUES
  (2, 14, 0, 14, 20), (2, 14, 20, 14, 40), (2, 14, 40, 15, 0),
  (2, 15, 0, 15, 20), (2, 15, 20, 15, 40), (2, 15, 40, 16, 0),
  (2, 16, 0, 16, 20), (2, 16, 20, 16, 40), (2, 16, 40, 17, 0),
  (2, 17, 0, 17, 20), (2, 17, 20, 17, 40), (2, 17, 40, 18, 0);

-- an appointment already scheduled, to immediately see a slot that is occupied in the calendar
INSERT INTO rv (jour, id_creneau, id_client) VALUES
  (CURDATE(), 2, 3);
  • line 33: the database is created if it does not exist, with the character set [utf8mb4] and the collation [utf8mb4_unicode_ci], which compares strings without regard to uppercase letters or accents (example 28);
  • lines 37–41: The tables are dropped and then recreated; the script restores the database to its initial state. The order matters: a table cannot be dropped as long as another table references it via a foreign key;
  • lines 46–55: users: a login, a password hashed by [bcrypt] (example 25), the display name once logged in, and the role ([ADMIN], [DOCTOR], or [USER]). The constraint [unq_users_login] ensures that a username belongs to only one account;
  • Lines 60–72: Each table has a primary key [id], generated by the database, and a column [version], which is the optimistic lock (Example 28). The column [user] is a foreign key referencing [users(id)]: the database rejects any value that is not the ID of an existing user. Since [user] is a reserved word in SQL, it is surrounded by grave accents. Three constraints: [fk_medecins_user] (the foreign key), [unq_medecins_user] (one account per doctor, and one doctor per account), and [unq_medecins_prenom_nom] (no homonyms). All constraints are named: the application recognizes a violated constraint by its name;
  • lines 77–89: the customer table has exactly the same columns;
  • lines 94–103: a time slot belongs to a doctor; its start and end times are stored in hours and minutes;
  • lines 108–118: an appointment consists of a day (type [DATE], without a time), a time slot, and a client. The constraint [unq1_rv] prevents the same time slot from being booked twice on the same day: the database enforces this rule, even if two users attempt to book it at the same time;
  • Lines 130–140: Demo users, whose password is the login. The hashes begin with [$2b$10$]: the algorithm ([bcrypt], variant [2b]) and the cost (10). Next come the salt and the hash. These hashes were calculated by the [Flask] version of the application; [PHP] writes its own with the prefix [$2y$], but checks both equally (see [config/hashing.php], below);
  • lines 144–147: the [user] column for each doctor is retrieved via a subquery based on the login, rather than by assuming the values of the primary keys;
  • lines 170–171: an appointment already scheduled for today ([CURDATE()]) in Dr. PELISSIER’s second time slot for Ms. BISTROU: the calendar thus immediately shows a booked time slot.

Unlike with [Laravel], the database is not created through migrations ([PHP] classes that describe the creation and evolution of tables, executed by [php artisan migrate]): it is shared with the other versions of the application, and the SQL script is common to all of them.

docs.title: 11.6.1. composer.json
docs.text:
{
    "name": "rdvmedecins/rdvmedecins2-laravel",
    "description": "RdvMedecins : prise de rendez-vous médicaux, pages HTML fabriquées par le serveur (Laravel + Blade)",
    "type": "project",
    "license": "MIT",
    "require": {
        "php": "^8.4",
        "ext-pdo_mysql": "*",
        "laravel/framework": "^13.33",
        "firebase/php-jwt": "^7.0"
    },
    "autoload": {
        "psr-4": {
            "App\\": "app/"
        }
    },
    "scripts": {
        "post-autoload-dump": [
            "Illuminate\\Foundation\\ComposerScripts::postAutoloadDump",
            "@php artisan package:discover --ansi"
        ]
    },
    "config": {
        "optimize-autoloader": true,
        "sort-packages": true
    },
    "minimum-stability": "stable",
    "prefer-stable": true
}
  • Lines 6–11: the libraries required by the application and the constraints they must meet. [^13.33] reads “version 13.33 or a newer version of the same major version 13”: [Composer] accepts versions that fix bugs or add features, but not those that could break the application (version 14). The lines [php] and [ext-pdo_mysql] do not refer to libraries, but to environment requirements: [Composer] prevents installation if the version of [PHP] or the extension is incompatible, rather than allowing the application to fail later;
  • Lines 12–16: The application’s rule PSR-4: Classes in the [App] namespace are located in the [app] folder (Example 01: In the examples, [bootstrap/app.php] itself declared this rule to the class loader via [addPsr4]);
  • lines 18–21: commands that [Composer] executes after creating the class loader: [Laravel] lists the service providers for the installed libraries ([package:discover], in [bootstrap/cache]).

[composer install] installs the versions that meet these constraints and records the exact versions installed in a file named [composer.lock]. Subsequent installations (on another machine, for example) use this file: they install exactly the same versions. [composer update], on the other hand, searches for the most recent versions permitted by [composer.json] and updates [composer.lock]. The command [composer show] lists what is installed in the [vendor] folder.

# =========================================================================
# .env: settings specific to the CETTE installation (read by env('NOM') in the
# files in the config folder). This file is never published: it contains
# secrets. A system environment variable takes precedence over it.
# =========================================================================
APP_NAME=RdvMedecins
# local: development; production: in production
APP_ENV=local
# the Laravel encryption key (cookies, session). In production:
# php artisan key:generate (writes a new key to this file)
APP_KEY=base64:+UmYSB3+TOKSr/f/fiqPCyo5IXFgXOLrvO1II52r+q4=
# true: an unexpected exception displays the Laravel debug page, along with its
# call stack (JAMAIS in production); false: the application’s 500 error page
APP_DEBUG=true
APP_URL=http://localhost:8081

# ---- the database MySQL [dbrdvmedecins2] (script: database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql):
# the server, its port, the database, the username, and its password (those for
# Laragon: root, no password)
DB_CONNECTION=mysql
DB_HOST=127.0.0.1
DB_PORT=3306
DB_DATABASE=dbrdvmedecins2
DB_USERNAME=root
DB_PASSWORD=
# true: the SQL commands sent to the database are displayed in the console
DB_LOG=true

# ---- the Laravel session (flash messages, anti-CSRF token, re-entry
# refresh): stored in a cookie CHIFFRÉ; the server does not store anything
SESSION_DRIVER=cookie
SESSION_LIFETIME=120
# ---- the cache (lists of doctors and clients, CAPTCHAs,
# attempts, passes): files, in storage/framework/cache
CACHE_STORE=file
# the log: storage/logs/laravel.log
LOG_CHANNEL=single

# ---- authentication (see config/rdvmedecins.php)
# secret key for JWT tokens: at least 32 characters (HMAC-SHA256)
JWT_SECRET=ef1cfc9709f10b5b5d183b4deb6d5dbbe69518629c3b12a8
# token validity period, in minutes (120 min = 2 h)
JWT_DUREE_MINUTES=120
# true in production (site served as HTTPS): cookies are never transmitted in plain text
COOKIE_SECURE=false

# ---- protection against bots (see app/Auth/LimiteurTentatives.php)
LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS=5
LOGIN_BLOCAGE_MINUTES=15
INSCRIPTION_MAX_PAR_HEURE=10

The file containing settings specific to this installation (example 25): these vary from one machine to another (the database, its credentials) or are secret (the keys). It is never published; the file [.env.example], which contains no secrets, serves as its template.

  • Line 11: the encryption key for [Laravel]: it encrypts cookies (example 20), including the session cookie. The command [php artisan key:generate] writes a new one;
  • line 14: During development, an unexpected exception displays the [Laravel] debug page; in production ([false]), the application’s 500 error page;
  • lines 20–25: the connection to the database (example 28);
  • Line 31: The [Laravel] session (Example 23) is stored in an encrypted cookie rather than in files on the server. The application stores very little information there (flash messages, the anti-CSRF token, form data to be re-displayed): a single cookie is sufficient, and the server no longer needs to store anything between requests. [Laravel] uses two cookies: [rdvmedecins_session] contains the session ID, and a second cookie—named after that ID—contains the session data;
  • Line 35: The cache (example 20) is stored in files within the [storage/framework/cache] folder. The application stores lists of doctors and clients, CAPTCHAs, attempt counters, and access tokens there—information that must be shared across all requests. With multiple servers, a shared cache, such as [Redis], would be used;
  • lines 41–48: application-specific settings: the JWT tokens (example 25) and bot protection (example 27).

docs.title: 11.6.3. config/app.php, config/session.php, config/hashing.php, config/auth.php
docs.text:
The files in the [config] folder supplement the default configuration of [Laravel] (Example 25): only the keys they write are changed.

<?php
// config/app.php: this file (COMPLÈTE) contains Laravel’s default configuration
// (vendor/laravel/framework/config/app.php): only the keys listed here change
return [
     //: the default interface language (see lang/fr.json, lang/en.json), and the
     // fallback language (it is used only for PHP files in the lang folder: a key
     // that is missing from a JSON dictionary is displayed as-is)
    'locale' => 'fr',
    'fallback_locale' => 'fr',

     // the time zone: that of the doctor’s office. It sets the current date
     // (no past appointments; see app/Metier/Dates.php)
    'timezone' => 'Europe/Paris',
];
  • lines 8–9: the default interface language (Example 22) and the fallback language (which is used only for the [PHP] files in the [lang] folder; see Example 22);
  • line 13: the time zone. By default, [Laravel] operates in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC); however, the current date is used for a business rule: no appointments in the past. In Paris, between midnight and 2:00 a.m. in the summer, the day UTC is still the previous day: the firm’s time zone takes precedence.
<?php
// config/session.php: the Laravel session (complements the default configuration).
// [cookie] driver (see .env, SESSION_DRIVER): session data (messages
// flash messages, anti-CSRF token, form data to be re-displayed) are stored in a cookie CHIFFRÉ
return [
    'cookie' => 'rdvmedecins_session',
     // Application cookies are only transmitted in HTTPS in production
    'secure' => (bool) env('COOKIE_SECURE', false),
];

The name of the session cookie, and the [secure] option for session cookies, read from the [.env] file ([(bool)] converts the value to a Boolean; [env] already includes [false] and [true]).

<?php
// config/hashing.php: password hashing (complements the default configuration)
return [
    'driver' => 'bcrypt',
    'bcrypt' => [
         // 10 rounds, like the hashes in the SQL script
        'rounds' => 10,
         // By default, Laravel verifies that a stored hash is indeed a hash
         // bcrypt... as PHP writes it ($2y$). However, the dbrdvmedecins2 database is
         // shared with the Python ($2b$) and Java ($2a$) versions of the application,
         // for which PHP verifies the hashes correctly, without recognizing them as
         // "bcrypt." We therefore disable this check
        'verify' => false,
    ],
];

Password hashing: [bcrypt], 10 rounds, like the hashes in the SQL script. Line 13 disables a check that [Laravel] performs by default: before comparing a password to a hash, it verifies that the hash was indeed generated by the configured algorithm, as written by [PHP] ([$2y$]). The hashes in the database, generated by [Python] ([$2b$]) or by [Java] ([$2a$]), would fail this check, even though [PHP] is perfectly capable of verifying them. This is the price to pay for sharing a database with other applications.

<?php
// config/auth.php: authentication (complements the default configuration)
return [
     // the default "guard": the one that reads the JWT token from the cookie
    'defaults' => [
        'guard' => 'jwt',
    ],
    'guards' => [
         // a driver guard [jwt], defined by AppServiceProvider (Auth::viaRequest)
        'jwt' => [
            'driver' => 'jwt',
        ],
    ],
];

The guard [jwt], the default guard for driver [jwt]: exactly like Example 25.
