docs.title: 11.19.2. public/js/app.js
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// public/js/app.js - the application's SEUL JavaScript.
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The entire application works without JavaScript. This script adds a
// convenience feature: before submitting a form that includes the
// data-confirmation="...", a modal window asks "Are you sure?"
// (the window itself is located at: resources/views/fragments/confirmation.blade.php).
// If JavaScript is disabled, the form simply submits without
// confirmation—nothing breaks (the principle of “progressive enhancement”).
//
// Why not window.confirm()? Its input field doesn’t format properly, and its
// buttons remain in the browser’s language, not the page’s.
// =========================================================================

(() => {
  const modale = document.getElementById('modale-confirmation');
  if (!modale) {
    return;
  }
  const message = document.getElementById('modale-confirmation-message');
  const boutonNon = modale.querySelector('.modal-footer [data-action="non"]');

  let formulaireEnAttente = null; // the form to submit if you confirm
  let focusPrecedent = null; // the element to focus on when closing

  function ouvrir(formulaire) {
    formulaireEnAttente = formulaire;
    focusPrecedent = document.activeElement;
     // textContent (not innerHTML): the message is displayed as TEXTE,
     // never interpreted as HTML
    message.textContent = formulaire.dataset.confirmation;
    modale.classList.remove('d-none');
     // the focus moves to "No": accidentally pressing Enter does not delete anything
    boutonNon.focus();
  }

  function fermer() {
    modale.classList.add('d-none');
    formulaireEnAttente = null;
    if (focusPrecedent) {
      focusPrecedent.focus();
    }
  }

   // 1. We intercept the submission of forms requiring confirmation
  document.querySelectorAll('form[data-confirmation]').forEach((formulaire) => {
    formulaire.addEventListener('submit', (evenement) => {
      evenement.preventDefault();
      ouvrir(formulaire);
    });
  });

   // 2. The window’s buttons (Yes / No / close button)
  modale.addEventListener('click', (evenement) => {
    const action = evenement.target.closest('[data-action]')?.dataset.action;
    if (action === 'oui') {
      const formulaire = formulaireEnAttente;
      fermer();
       // formulaire.submit() submits the form SANS trigger again
       // the 'submit' event: no new confirmation request
      formulaire.submit();
    } else if (action === 'non') {
      fermer();
    } else if (evenement.target.classList.contains('modal')) {
      fermer(); // Click on the grayed-out background outside the window
    }
  });

   // 3. Keyboard: Esc closes the window; Tab keeps the focus on the window
   /   / (otherwise, the focus would move to the grayed-out page behind it)
  modale.addEventListener('keydown', (evenement) => {
    if (evenement.key === 'Escape') {
      fermer();
    } else if (evenement.key === 'Tab') {
      const boutons = [...modale.querySelectorAll('button')];
      const premier = boutons[0];
      const dernier = boutons[boutons.length - 1];
      if (evenement.shiftKey && document.activeElement === premier) {
        evenement.preventDefault();
        dernier.focus();
      } else if (!evenement.shiftKey && document.activeElement === dernier) {
        evenement.preventDefault();
        premier.focus();
      }
    }
  });
})();

The only [JavaScript] in the application—the one from Example 21—with a few additions. The entire application works without [JavaScript]: this script adds convenience by providing a confirmation before submitting a form that carries the [data-confirmation] attribute. If [JavaScript] is disabled, the form submits without confirmation: nothing breaks (principle of progressive enhancement).

  • Lines 15–21: The script is a function called as soon as it is defined ([(() => { ... })()]); its variables are not visible to the rest of the page. Without a confirmation window on the page, it does nothing;
  • Lines 26–35: Opening the window: The form to be submitted upon confirmation is stored, and the form’s message is displayed in the window. [textContent], not [innerHTML]: the message is displayed as text and is never interpreted as HTML. The focus moves to the “No” button: accidentally pressing Enter does not delete anything;
  • lines 37–43: closing the window; focus returns to the element that had it previously;
  • lines 46–50: the submission of each form to be confirmed is intercepted ([preventDefault] prevents it), and the window opens;
  • lines 54–67: the window’s buttons. A single handler for the entire window: [closest('[data-action]')] identifies the clicked button or the element containing it. “Yes” submits the form via [formulaire.submit()], which does not trigger the [submit] event: no new confirmation request is issued. Clicking on the grayed-out background outside the window closes it;
  • lines 71–86: the keyboard. Esc closes the window; the Tab key moves focus from one button to another without leaving the window (otherwise, it would move to the grayed-out page behind it): this is what users who navigate with the keyboard and screen readers expect.

docs.title: 12. Conclusion
docs.text:
This document has presented the development of a MVC web application using the [Laravel] framework: an application whose HTML pages are generated by the server, using [Blade] views, without a browser-side [JavaScript] framework. He followed the [Flask] course step by step, which itself builds on the [Spring MVC], [ASP.NET Core MVC], and [NestJS] courses: actions and routing to views, forms, internationalization, security, and data access, followed by a comprehensive case study.

The same 28 examples and the same application were thus written using five frameworks: in [TypeScript], in [C#], in [Java], in [Python], and in [PHP]. The concepts are the same; only the names and mechanisms differ. The correspondences between [Flask] and [Laravel]:

[Flask][Laravel]manufacturer [create_app], items stored in [app.extensions][bootstrap/app.php], service providers, container ([$singletons], injected by the manufacturer)[requirements.txt], virtual environment, [pip][composer.json], [composer.lock], folder [vendor], [Composer][config.py], variables [FLASK_...] ([app.config])file [.env], folder [config], functions [env] and [config]blueprints, [@bp.get], [@bp.post][routes/web.php], controllers, named routes, route groups[render_template], [redirect], [url_for][view], [redirect], [route][request.args], [request.form], converters ([<int:id>])object [Request], action parameters, constraints ([whereNumber]), model link[Pydantic]; [WTForms]: validators, [form.validate()], [form.errors][Validator], form requests ([FormRequest]), rules, [$errors], [old()]views [Jinja2], [{{ }}], [{% for %}], [{% if %}]views [Blade], [{{ }}], [@foreach], [@if][{% extends %}] and blocks, [{% include %}], macros[@extends] and sections, [@include], components ([<x-...>])context processor ([@app.context_processor])view composer ([View::composer])Flash messages ([flash]), in the signed session cookiesession flash data ([session()->flash], [with]), session stored in files or in an encrypted cookie[before_request], [after_request], [teardown_request]middleware (global, group, route), method [terminate][@app.errorhandler][withExceptions], [render], [abort][before_request] and hand-written decorators ([PyJWT], [bcrypt])guards ([Auth::viaRequest]), middleware [auth], [Gate], facade [Hash] ([firebase/php-jwt])[CSRFProtect] from [Flask-WTF][PreventRequestForgery] middleware, [@csrf] directive (419 response)dictionaries JSON, handwritten function [t(...)]folder [lang], function [__()], [App::setLocale][Babel][Carbon] ([isoFormat]), [Number] (extension [intl])in-memory dictionaries, [threading.Lock]cache ([Cache], [Cache::lock]), [RateLimiter][SQLAlchemy]: reporting entities, [select(...)], sessions[Eloquent]: templates, query builder, relationships ([belongsTo], [with])[with sessions.begin() as session:][DB::transaction(...)][version_id_col], managed by [SQLAlchemy][WHERE version = ?] and [version + 1], written to the DAO layer[python app.py] in debug mode (automatic reloading)[php artisan serve] (nothing to reload: each request re-reads the code)WSGI server: [Waitress], [Gunicorn]Web server ([nginx], [Apache]) and [PHP-FPM]

Regarding [Flask], the key points to note are:

  • [Laravel] is a full-stack framework: routing, views, validation, sessions, caching, authentication, translation, data access, email sending, task queues... everything is provided, and everything is designed to work together. This is the opposite of the micro-framework [Flask]: much less code to write, but a broader framework to learn, where many things happen “automatically” (sessions, encrypted cookies, anti-CSRF tokens, returning to the form after an input error). The chapter on the request lifecycle and the analysis of requests with [curl] served to make these processes visible;
  • the [PHP] application is rebuilt with each request (Example 01): nothing survives in memory from one request to the next. Anything that needs to persist goes into the session (a single user), the cache (all users), the database, or cookies. Conversely, code changes take effect without a restart, and a failed request never affects subsequent ones;
  • the service container creates controllers, middleware, and services, and provides them with their dependencies based on their constructor types: dependency injection is at the heart of the framework, as seen in [Spring] or [ASP.NET Core];
  • facades ([Cache::], [DB::], [Auth::], [Hash::]...) and global functions ([view], [redirect], [session], [config], [__]...) provide access to services anywhere, in a single line. This is very convenient; it’s also a way to hide a class’s dependencies, which constructor injection makes visible;
  • almost everything is middleware: cookies, sessions, anti-CSRF protection, authentication, authorizations, and our own controls (language, roles, pass). The same mechanism is used for all requests, for a group of routes, or for a single one;
  • [PHP] is a language with runtime type checking: the declared types of parameters, properties, and results ([int], [?Client], [Collection]) are checked on every call. Since version 8, classes such as [readonly], enumerations, constructor promotion, named arguments, and the null-safe operator ([?->]) have made it an expressive and safe language;
  • [Eloquent] follows the Active Record pattern: a model can read and write itself ([Medecin::find(1)], [$medecin->save()]), with very little code. Its queries closely resemble the SQL they generate, and monitoring the queries ([DB::listen]) allows you to verify what is being sent to the database. It is important to consider preloading the relationships ([with]); otherwise, you will quickly run into the “N+1 queries” problem again;
  • The [Blade] views are compiled into [PHP] and cached: they are fast, automatically escape the content they display, and their components ([<x-champ>]) keep the forms concise.

The case study shows that a classic HTML application, without the essential [JavaScript], remains a simple and robust solution: each page is a URL, the browser’s “Back” button works, and the server controls everything. The limited use of [JavaScript] (confirmation windows) enhances the user experience without being necessary for functionality. [Laravel] can also support more interactive applications, without leaving [PHP] ([Livewire]) or with a browser-side [JavaScript] framework ([Inertia], with [Vue.js] or [React]): this will be covered in other documents.

For further information, consult the [Laravel] documentation (laravel.com/docs), particularly the pages dedicated to the request lifecycle, the service container, validation, [Blade], and [Eloquent], as well as the documentation for [PHP] (php.net/manual/fr), the section on [Composer] (getcomposer.org/doc), and compare this application with its counterparts [Flask], [Spring MVC], [ASP.NET Core MVC], and [NestJS].

docs.title: 6. Data Scopes
docs.text:
A web application serves many users at once, and each user makes numerous requests. Data can therefore be shared at several levels, known as its scope:

  • application scope: the data is shared by all users throughout the application’s lifetime (the list of doctors, for example);
  • request scope: the data exists only for the duration of a request (a view’s model, the logged-in user as identified for that request);
  • session scope: the data is specific to a user and must persist from one request to the next (the selected language, a shopping cart);
  • client scope: data stored in the browser itself, in a cookie.

In [PHP], these scopes behave in a particular way because the application is rebuilt with every request (Example 01): nothing survives in memory from one request to the next. Any data that needs to last longer than a single request is therefore stored outside of [PHP]: in the cache, a database, files, or on the client’s side. This is the so-called “shared-nothing” architecture: each request is processed in isolation by a process that shares nothing with those processing other requests. This approach has significant advantages: an error affects only a single request, no data leaks from one user to another, and multiple identical servers can be run behind a load balancer, provided they share the same cache and database.

In [Laravel], each scope has its own container:

ScopeContainerLifetimeapplicationthe cache ([Cache] front end, example 20), or the databasethe selected duration, or unlimitedquerythe container’s objects (a singleton exists for only one query), the query’s attributes (example 12)processing a querysessionthe session ([$request->session()], [session()]), stored by the server and retrieved using a cookieDefault 2-hour inactivity period ([SESSION_LIFETIME])clienta cookie ([withCookie], example 22), encrypted by defaultthe cookie’s specified duration

The session for [Laravel] is a server-maintained session, like those for [Java] ([JSESSIONID]) or the classic [PHP] ([PHPSESSID]): its data is stored on the server (one file per session, with the configuration from our examples), and the browser only holds the identifier in an encrypted cookie (Example 20). This differs from [Flask], whose entire session is stored in a signed cookie on the client side.

docs.title: 6.1.1. The objects: app/Services/CompteurService.php and RequeteInfos.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Services/CompteurService.php: scope APPLICATION, a counter shared by
// all requests from all users, stored in the cache (see Example 20)

namespace App\Services;

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Cache;

class CompteurService
{
     // by one under the key [$cle]; the "file" cache does not increment a
     // number atomically: a lock protects read and write operations
    public static function suivant(string $cle): int
    {
        return Cache::lock("$cle-verrou", 10)->block(5, function () use ($cle) {
            $valeur = Cache::get($cle, 0) + 1;
            Cache::forever($cle, $valeur);
            return $valeur;
        });
    }

    public function incrementer(): int
    {
        return self::suivant('visites');
    }
}
  • Lines 13–20: an application scope counter: a number stored in the cache under a key and incremented by 1 on each call. The cache provides a method [Cache::increment], but with the “file” store used in our examples, it is not atomic: it reads the value, increments it, and then writes it, and two concurrent requests could read the same value—resulting in a lost visit. A lock (example 20) therefore protects both the read and the write operations. (With a store such as [Redis] or a database, [Cache::increment] is atomic, and the lock is unnecessary.) The function returns the value of the lock, which is the same as the value returned by the function it protects;
  • lines 22–25: the visit counter.
<?php
// app/Services/RequeteInfos.php: scope REQUÊTE, the information from a request

namespace App\Services;

class RequeteInfos
{
    public readonly int $numero;

    public readonly string $debut;

    public function __construct()
    {
         // a number generated by OBJET, derived from a counter shared by all requests
        $this->numero = CompteurService::suivant('instances');
         // the time, including milliseconds (v)
        $this->debut = now()->format('H:i:s.v');
    }
}
  • lines 8–10: properties declared as [readonly] one by one (rather than the entire class): they can only be assigned once, by the constructor;
  • lines 12–18: request-scope information: a number, derived from a counter shared by all requests (the counter from the previous class, under a different key), and the time of the request. The function [now()] returns the current time as a [Carbon] date; the format [v] specifies the milliseconds.

docs.title: 6.1.2. Configuration: bootstrap/app.php
docs.text:
<?php
// bootstrap/app.php: the application from Example 23

use App\Services\CompteurService;
use App\Services\RequeteInfos;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Middleware;

(require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php')->addPsr4('App\\', __DIR__.'/../app/');

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(
        web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php',
         // the route serving Bootstrap (see Example 15)
        then: fn () => require __DIR__.'/../../commun/bootstrap.php')
    ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
         // The cookie [mesVisites] is not encrypted (the others are)
        $middleware->encryptCookies(except: ['mesVisites']);
    })
    ->withExceptions()
     // only one instance of each class during request processing
    ->withSingletons([CompteurService::class])
    ->withScopedSingletons([RequeteInfos::class])
    ->create();
  • Line 18: The cookie [mesVisites] is not encrypted; all others are (Example 22);
  • Lines 22–23: Both services are registered with the container. [withSingletons] (example 06): a single object, created on the first request. [withScopedSingletons]: a single object per request. In a standard [PHP], the two are equivalent, since each request rebuilds the application and its container. The difference becomes apparent with [Laravel Octane], an application server that keeps the application in memory from one request to the next to improve performance: a singleton is shared by all requests, while a “scoped” singleton is recreated for each one. Declaring the desired scope ensures the code is correct in both cases.

docs.title: 6.1.3. The controller: app/Http/Controllers/PorteesController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/PorteesController.php: the four scopes of data

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Services\CompteurService;
use App\Services\RequeteInfos;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Http\Response;

class PorteesController
{
     // both objects are provided by the container (see bootstrap/app.php)
    public function afficher(Request $request, CompteurService $compteur, RequeteInfos $infos): Response
    {
         // APPLICATION: the shared counter
        $total = $compteur->incrementer();
         // SESSION: browser-specific data for CE, stored by SERVEUR
         // (a file in storage/framework/sessions), retrieved via the session cookie
        $visitesSession = $request->session()->increment('visites');
         // CLIENT: data stored by NAVIGATEUR in cookies,
         // sent back to the server with each request; one in plain text, the other encrypted
        $mesVisites = (int) $request->cookie('mesVisites') + 1;
        $mesVisitesChiffre = (int) $request->cookie('mesVisitesChiffre') + 1;
        return response()->view('portees.portees', [
            'total' => $total, 'instance' => $infos->numero,
            'visitesSession' => $visitesSession, 'mesVisites' => $mesVisites,
            'mesVisitesChiffre' => $mesVisitesChiffre,
        ])->withCookie(cookie('mesVisites', $mesVisites))
            ->withCookie(cookie('mesVisitesChiffre', $mesVisitesChiffre));
    }
}
  • line 14: the action receives the request and the two services, provided by the container;
  • line 17: the application scope;
  • line 20: the session scope. [$request->session()] returns the user’s session; its method [increment] increments the value of a key by 1 (or sets it to 0 if it does not exist), and returns the new value. A value is read using [get('visites')] and written using [put('visites', 3)]; the function [session('visites')] is a shortcut for reading. [Laravel] saves the session at the end of the request (the [StartSession] middleware from the [web] group);
  • lines 23–24: the client scope, with two cookies. Their values are strings provided by the browser and may therefore be missing or invalid: the [(int)] conversion returns 0 for [null] or for text that is not a number;
  • Lines 25–30: To set a cookie, you need the response object: [response()->view(...)] constructs it from the view (Example 13), and then [withCookie] adds the cookies to it. Without an expiration time, a cookie lasts until the browser is closed (this is a “session” cookie, as defined by browsers).

docs.text:

  • Line 13: The [@inject] directive requests an object from the container, from within the view, and stores it in a variable (here, [$infos]). During the same request, this is the same [RequeteInfos] object as the one from the action: the view displays its number, which must be the one received from the action;
  • Line 18: The session is also accessible in the views.

docs.title: 6.1.5. Execution
docs.text:
After a few visits in a browser:

Let’s track the requests with [curl], which acts as a first browser by storing its cookies in the file [a.txt]:

curl -i -c a.txt -b a.txt http://localhost:8000/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: mesVisites=1; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
Set-Cookie: mesVisitesChiffre=eyJpdiI6IlNYLzF1MnBiUS82L2NjenE4K01RQnc9PSIsInZhbHVlIjoiejRQTC94clIy...; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
Set-Cookie: XSRF-TOKEN=eyJpdiI6IlVCeGJtSTU4SVV2aTFvS1Ryb3A2SlE9PSIsInZhbHVlIjoicWM4RGQ1ZXNi...; expires=...; Max-Age=7200; path=/; samesite=lax
Set-Cookie: exemple23_session=eyJpdiI6IngrbWJBelphY3oyUDlYZkpFV1pKeVE9PSIsInZhbHVlIjoiRklyYWlN...; expires=...; Max-Age=7200; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
...
      <li>application : 1 visite(s) du site, tous navigateurs confondus</li>
      <li>requête : objet n° 1 (n° 1 dans la vue),
        requête reçue à 16:19:05.709</li>
      <li>session : 1 visite(s) de ce navigateur (1 dans la vue)</li>
      <li>client : 1 visite(s) de ce navigateur (cookie en clair),
        1 (cookie chiffré)</li>
...

The response sets four cookies. The first, [mesVisites], contains the value in plain text. The second, [mesVisitesChiffre], contains the same value, encrypted: the visible part is a Base64-encoded string (JSON), which contains the encryption initialization vector ([iv]), the encrypted value ([value]), and an authentication code ([mac]), which ensures that the value has not been altered. The last two are for the session and anti-CSRF protection (example 20). A second visit, with the same cookies:

curl -i -c a.txt -b a.txt http://localhost:8000/

...
Set-Cookie: mesVisites=2; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
...
      <li>application : 2 visite(s) du site, tous navigateurs confondus</li>
      <li>requête : objet n° 2 (n° 2 dans la vue),
        requête reçue à 16:19:05.731</li>
      <li>session : 2 visite(s) de ce navigateur (2 dans la vue)</li>
      <li>client : 2 visite(s) de ce navigateur (cookie en clair),
        2 (cookie chiffré)</li>
...

A second “browser,” with its own cookie file, which is initially empty:

curl -c b.txt -b b.txt http://localhost:8000/

      <li>application : 3 visite(s) du site, tous navigateurs confondus</li>
      <li>requête : objet n° 3 (n° 3 dans la vue),
        requête reçue à 16:19:05.747</li>
      <li>session : 1 visite(s) de ce navigateur (1 dans la vue)</li>
      <li>client : 1 visite(s) de ce navigateur (cookie en clair),
        1 (cookie chiffré)</li>

The application counter continued running; the session and cookies for the second browser start over at 1. Each request had its own [RequeteInfos] object, and in each one, the action and view were the same. Finally, a malicious user forges their own cookies: 1,000 visits in [mesVisites], 999 in [mesVisitesChiffre], and a session ID of their own invention:

curl -b "mesVisites=1000;mesVisitesChiffre=999;exemple23_session=abc" http://localhost:8000/

      <li>application : 4 visite(s) du site, tous navigateurs confondus</li>
      ...
      <li>session : 1 visite(s) de ce navigateur (1 dans la vue)</li>
      <li>client : 1001 visite(s) de ce navigateur (cookie en clair),
        1 (cookie chiffré)</li>

The unencrypted cookie was accepted as is: 1,001 visits. The cookie [mesVisitesChiffre], however, could not be decrypted: [Laravel] ignored it, as if it were absent. The same applies to the session cookie: the user cannot choose another user’s session and is assigned a new one. This is the key difference between a regular cookie and an encrypted cookie. Let’s remember the rule: data coming from the client is trustworthy only if it is protected by the server (encrypted, as here, or signed, like the token in the chapter on authentication); data that has nothing to hide, and whose value is verified by the server (the language in Example 22), can remain in plaintext.

The case study brings them together into a complete, realistic-sized application (about 100 files, approximately 5,800 lines, including comments). It was written with the same care as the examples: each file begins with a comment explaining its role, and tricky sections are annotated in the code. Each main folder also contains a file named [README.md] that lists its files. The document’s comments highlight what the examples did not show and refer to them for the rest.

docs.title: 5. Internationalization
docs.text:
An internationalized application displays its text in the user’s language. The case study is in French and English. The principle is simple: the views no longer contain text, but keys ([MENU.ACCUEIL]), and a dictionary for each language associates a text with each key. The selected language is stored in a cookie.

[Laravel] has its own translation system, which we already encountered in Example 09 for validation messages. It accepts two types of dictionaries, stored in the [lang] folder: [PHP] files, one per theme and per language ([lang/fr/validation.php]), which return an array of keys; and JSON files, one per language ([lang/fr.json]), where each key is an arbitrary string. We use the second format: apart from the parameter syntax, these are the same dictionaries as those in versions [ASP.NET Core MVC], [NestJS], [Spring MVC], and [Flask] from the case study, and their format can be read and written without any special tools. The formatting of dates and amounts remains the same as in Example 16.

docs.title: 5.1.1. The Dictionaries
docs.text:
The file [lang/fr.json]:

{
    "MENU.ACCUEIL": "Accueil",
    "MENU.PRODUITS": "Produits",
    "ACCUEIL.TITRE": "Bienvenue",
    "ACCUEIL.BONJOUR": "Bonjour :nom !",
    "ACCUEIL.DATE": "Nous sommes le :date.",
    "PRODUITS.TITRE": "Nos produits",
    "PRODUITS.NOM": "Produit",
    "PRODUITS.PRIX": "Prix",
    "PRODUITS.NOMBRE": ":n produit(s) au catalogue."
}

A JSON dictionary is an object in which each pair associates a key with its text. Keys are grouped by theme based on their prefix: the menu text “Home” has the key [MENU.ACCUEIL]. A text may contain placeholders, written as [:nom], which are replaced during translation. (The dictionaries in the other versions of the case study nest the objects JSON — [{"MENU": {"ACCUEIL": "Accueil"}}] — and write the parameters as [{nom}]; those in [Laravel] are “flat” and use the [:nom] syntax.) The [lang/en.json] file has exactly the same keys:

{
    "MENU.ACCUEIL": "Home",
    "MENU.PRODUITS": "Products",
    "ACCUEIL.TITRE": "Welcome",
    "ACCUEIL.BONJOUR": "Hello :nom!",
    "ACCUEIL.DATE": "Today is :date.",
    "PRODUITS.TITRE": "Our products",
    "PRODUITS.NOM": "Product",
    "PRODUITS.PRIX": "Price",
    "PRODUITS.NOMBRE": ":n product(s) in the catalogue."
}

If a key is missing from the JSON dictionary for the current language, it is searched for in the [PHP] files in that language’s folder ([lang/fr/*.php], example 09), and then in those for the fallback language ([APP_FALLBACK_LOCALE], English by default). There is no backup dictionary (JSON): a key missing from the current language’s dictionary (JSON) and from these files is displayed as-is. This way, any omission is immediately visible on the screen.

docs.title: 5.1.2. The language of each request: app/Http/Middleware/DefinirLangue.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Middleware/DefinirLangue.php: the language of each request

namespace App\Http\Middleware;

use Closure;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\App;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

class DefinirLangue
{
     // the supported languages; the first is the default language
    public const LANGUES = ['fr', 'en'];

    public const COOKIE = 'langue';

     // the language of the [langue] cookie, if supported; otherwise, French
    public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next): Response
    {
        $langue = $request->cookie(self::COOKIE);
        App::setLocale(in_array($langue, self::LANGUES, true) ? $langue : self::LANGUES[0]);
        return $next($request);
    }
}
  • lines 14–16: the supported languages and the cookie name: public class constants, accessible from other classes ([DefinirLangue::LANGUES]);
  • lines 21–22: Before each action, the request language: the language specified in the [langue] cookie if one exists and is supported; otherwise, French. [$request->cookie(nom)] returns the value of a cookie sent by the browser, or [null]. [in_array], with [true] as the third parameter, also compares the types ([===]). [App::setLocale] (example 16) sets the application language for the request: this is the language used for translations and formatting.

docs.title: 5.1.3. The configuration: bootstrap/app.php
docs.text:
<?php
// bootstrap/app.php: the application from Example 22

use App\Http\Middleware\DefinirLangue;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Middleware;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Blade;

(require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php')->addPsr4('App\\', __DIR__.'/../app/');

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(
        web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php',
         // the route serving Bootstrap (see Example 15)
        then: fn () => require __DIR__.'/../../commun/bootstrap.php')
    ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
         // the cookie [langue] is not encrypted: it contains nothing confidential, and
         // the server only accepts supported languages
        $middleware->encryptCookies(except: [DefinirLangue::COOKIE]);
         // the language of each request: the one in the [langue] cookie, or French otherwise
        $middleware->web(append: DefinirLangue::class);
    })
    ->withExceptions()
    ->booted(function () {
         // in views: @currency($prix) (see Example 16)
        Blade::directive('monnaie', fn (string $expression) =>
            "<?php echo e(\\App\\Aides\\Formats::monnaie($expression)); ?>");
    })
    ->create();
  • Line 19: By default, [Laravel] encrypts all cookies it sets and decrypts those it receives (this is the role of the [EncryptCookies] middleware in the [web] group; see Example 20): The user cannot read or create an encrypted cookie. The [langue] cookie contains no secret information, and the server accepts only supported languages: we exclude it from encryption, which allows us to view (and create) it using [curl]. The following example will revisit this encryption;
  • line 21: the language middleware, at the end of the [web] group (Example 16): it runs after [EncryptCookies] and therefore reads cookies that have already been decrypted;
  • lines 26–27: the [@monnaie] directive from Example 16.

The class [App\Aides\Formats] is the one from Example 16, with one difference: the date is formatted in the “long” format for each language:

<?php
// app/Help/Formats.php: dates and amounts, formatted in the request language (see Example 16)

namespace App\Aides;

use Brick\Math\BigDecimal;
use Carbon\CarbonInterface;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\App;
use Illuminate\Support\Number;

class Formats
{
     // an amount in euros
    public static function monnaie(BigDecimal $montant): string
    {
        return Number::currency($montant->toFloat(), in: 'EUR', locale: App::getLocale());
    }

     // a date written out in full. The "dddd LL" format: the day of the week, followed by the
     // date in the language’s “long” format: “mercredi 23 septembre 2026” in French,
     // "Wednesday, September 23, 2026" in English
    public static function dateLongue(CarbonInterface $jour): string
    {
        return $jour->locale(App::getLocale())->isoFormat('dddd LL');
    }
}
  • Line 24: [LL] is a localized format: each language has its own ([23 septembre 2026] in French, [September 23, 2026] in English), whereas [D MMMM YYYY] would impose the French order on all languages. [dddd] adds the day of the week.

docs.title: 5.1.4. Language selection: app/Http/Controllers/LangueController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/LangueController.php: the language selection

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Http\Middleware\DefinirLangue;
use Illuminate\Http\RedirectResponse;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;

class LangueController
{
     // GET /language/en: stores the selection in a cookie, then returns to the previous page
    public function changer(Request $request, string $code): RedirectResponse
    {
        abort_unless(in_array($code, DefinirLangue::LANGUES, true), 404);
         // the cookie: one year lifetime (in minutes), unreadable by the JavaScript of the
         // page (httpOnly), never sent with a POST request originating from another site (sameSite)
        return redirect(self::pageDOrigine($request))
            ->withCookie(cookie(DefinirLangue::COOKIE, $code, 365 * 24 * 60, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax'));
    }

     // the page from which the request originated (Referer header), of which only the path is retained:
     // redirecting to a full URL from the request would allow
     // to send the user to another site (“open redirect” vulnerability)
    private static function pageDOrigine(Request $request): string
    {
         // parse_url breaks down a URL into its components (path, parameters, etc.)
        $url = parse_url($request->header('Referer', ''));
        $chemin = $url['path'] ?? '';
         // "//site.com/..." would be interpreted by the browser as a URL
         // on a AUTRE site: also rejected
        if (! str_starts_with($chemin, '/') || str_starts_with($chemin, '//')) {
            return '/';
        }
        return isset($url['query']) ? "$chemin?{$url['query']}" : $chemin;
    }
}
  • line 15: an unknown language code: 404;
  • lines 18–19: the action responds with a redirect to the page the user came from; the user is taken back to that page in the new language. The response includes a cookie, which the browser will send back with every request: the function [cookie] creates it, and the method [withCookie] adds it to the response. Its parameters: the name, the value, the lifetime in minutes (one year), and two named parameters: [httpOnly: true] makes it invisible to the [JavaScript] on the page; [sameSite: 'lax'] prevents the browser from sending it with a POST request originating from another site;
  • lines 25–36: the original page is specified by the [Referer] header in the request (the misspelled version, with a single [r], is the one used in the HTTP standard), which the browser fills in with the URL from the page that contained the link. But this header comes from the client, which can put anything in it. Blindly redirecting to this address would turn our application into an *open redirect*: a malicious link bearing our domain name could send the user to a malicious site. Therefore, we retain only the path and parameters from URL (the [parse_url] function from [PHP] breaks it down into its components, storing them in an associative array), and we reject any path that begins with [//], which the browser would interpret as the address of another site. [Laravel] also provides [redirect()->back()] (or [back()]), which redirects to the previous page stored in the session (example 20), and not to the header [Referer]: we will use this in the case study.

docs.title: 5.1.5. Actions: app/Http/Controllers/PagesController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/PagesController.php: Actions are not language-aware:
// they provide data, the views translate and format it

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Models\Produit;
use Brick\Math\BigDecimal;
use Carbon\CarbonImmutable;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class PagesController
{
    public function accueil(): View
    {
        return view('pages.accueil', ['nom' => 'Marie',
            'aujourdhui' => CarbonImmutable::create(2026, 9, 23)]);
    }

    public function produits(): View
    {
        return view('pages.produits', ['produits' => [
            new Produit('Clavier', BigDecimal::of('25')),
            new Produit('Souris', BigDecimal::of('12.5')),
            new Produit('Écran', BigDecimal::of('1149')),
        ]]);
    }
}

Actions are language-agnostic: they provide raw data (a name, a date, amounts). Translation and formatting are handled by the views.

  • line 3: the page’s [lang] attribute specifies its language to browsers, search engines, and screen readers;
  • line 7: the page title is provided by the page itself, already translated (section [titre]).
<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">

  • lines 4–5: The function [__] (with two underscores) returns the translation of a key in the language of the request;
  • Lines 9–12: One button per language, which triggers the [/langue/{code}] action. The current language is highlighted ([btn-primary], solid button): [app()->isLocale($code)] checks the language of the request.

docs.text:
The home page, in French (the default language), then in English after clicking the “EN” button:

The products page, in both languages. The amounts follow the conventions of each language:

The language switch, as seen with [curl]. The option [-H] provides the header [Referer] that the browser would send:

curl -i -H "Referer: http://localhost:8000/produits" http://localhost:8000/language/en

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: http://localhost:8000/products
Set-Cookie: langue=en; expires=Sun, 26 Sep 2027 16:18:24 GMT; Max-Age=31536000; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax

The redirect takes you back to the original page, and the cookie is set for one year, in plain text. A [Referer] that points to another site does not redirect you there: only its path is retained.

curl -i -H "Referer: https://pirate.example/piege" http://localhost:8000/language/en
curl -i -H "Referer: http://localhost:8000//pirate.example/x" http://localhost:8000/language/fr

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: http://localhost:8000/trap
...
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: http://localhost:8000

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The document’s PDF is |HERE|.

The document’s codes are |HERE|.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s IA Claude. It follows the document “Step-by-Step Introduction to the [Flask] Web Framework” (2026), which itself followed the documents “Step-by-Step Introduction to the [Spring MVC] Web Framework,” "Step-by-Step Introduction to the [ASP.NET Core MVC] Web Framework," and "Step-by-Step Introduction to the [NestJS] Web Framework" (2026). This document adapts the [Flask] course to the [PHP] environment:

  • the [Flask] framework and the [Python] language are replaced by the [Laravel] 13 framework and the [PHP] language (version 8.4 or later);
  • the [Jinja2] views are replaced by [Blade] views, the view engine for [Laravel];
  • validation by [Pydantic] and [WTForms] is replaced by that of [Laravel]: validation rules and form queries ([FormRequest]);
  • The few dozen lines of hand-written security code for [Flask] are replaced by the authentication system for [Laravel] (guards, middleware, [Gate], [Hash] facade, attempt limiter), supplemented by the [firebase/php-jwt] library for JWT tokens;
  • ORM and [SQLAlchemy] are replaced by ORM and [Laravel], [Eloquent], still based on [MySQL].

The document closely follows the structure of the [Flask] course: first, numerous small projects, each focused on a specific concept, followed by a comprehensive case study—a web application for scheduling appointments at a medical practice—with all files fully commented. The examples have the same numbers and cover the same topics as in courses [Flask], [Spring MVC], and [ASP.NET Core MVC]: a reader familiar with any of these courses can compare the frameworks example by example. However, this is not necessary: this document stands on its own and assumes no prior knowledge of these frameworks. The only prerequisites are a basic understanding of web programming (the HTTP protocol, the HTML language) and the fundamentals of the [PHP] language (variables, arrays, functions, classes). The course “Introduction to the PHP7 Language Through Examples” (2019) introduces the language itself for those who need to learn it first; the new features of [PHP] 8 used here (promoted properties, [readonly] classes, enumerations, named arguments, the nullsafe operator, etc.) are explained when they first appear.

docs.title: 1.1. Laravel’s Role in a Web Application
docs.text:
A web application is often built in layers, with each layer communicating only with its neighboring layers:

  • the web layer receives requests HTTP from the browser and returns pages HTML to it. This is the layer that [Laravel] helps us write;
  • the business layer contains the application’s business rules (e.g., “a patient can have only one upcoming appointment”). It knows nothing about the web: it could just as easily serve a command-line application;
  • the data access layer (DAO layer, for *Data Access Object*) reads from and writes to the database. We will use [Eloquent], the ORM (*Object Relational Mapper*) of [Laravel], which maps table rows to [PHP] objects.

The web layer itself follows the MVC (*Model-View-Controller*) pattern:

  • the controller (C) is a class [PHP] whose methods, called actions, each handle a specific type of request (for example, [GET /agenda]). An action reads the request parameters, processes the request through the business layer, and then selects the view to display;
  • the model (M) is the set of data that the action passes to the view;
  • the view (V) is a [Blade] file (extension [.blade.php]): a HTML page that contains [{{ ... }}] expressions and [@if], [@foreach]... directives, which the [Blade] engine replaces with data from the template.

A note on terminology, to avoid confusion: in [Laravel], the word “model” (*model*) usually refers to a [Eloquent] model, a class that represents a database table ([app/Models] file). This document uses the word in both senses, specifying which one is meant each time: the view model (the data passed to a view) and the [Eloquent] model (as discussed in the chapter on data access). The word “template” refers to the common view from which other pages inherit (chapter on views).

The processing of a request follows the numbered steps in the diagram:

  • 1: The browser sends a request HTTP, for example, [GET /agenda?idMedecin=1&jour=2026-09-26];
  • 2: The web server receives the request and passes it to the [Laravel] application via the [public/index.php] file. During development, this server is the one that includes [PHP], launched by the command [php artisan serve]; in production, it will be a server such as [nginx] or [Apache], associated with [PHP-FPM]. The request passes through middleware components—classes that handle all requests (cookies, sessions, security, etc.)—and then [Laravel] compares the requested path to the application’s routes and selects the action responsible for handling that request: this is routing;
  • 3: The action requests the data it needs from the business layer; if necessary, the business layer contacts the DAO layer, which queries the [MySQL] database via SQL;
  • 4: The action constructs the view’s M model and instructs the [Blade] engine to generate the page (function [view]);
  • 5: The page HTML generated by the view is the action’s response, which [Laravel] returns to the browser.

[Laravel] is by far the most widely used web framework in the [PHP] world, ahead of [Symfony] (on whose components it is, incidentally, built). Free and open-source, created in 2011 by Taylor Otwell, it works anywhere that [PHP] ([Windows], [Linux], [macOS]), and [PHP] works with almost all web hosting providers. It is a comprehensive framework: routing, views, validation, sessions, caching, authentication, translation, database access, email sending, background tasks... everything is provided and designed to work together. This is the opposite of the micro-framework [Flask] from the previous lesson, which left it up to the developer to assemble their own components: [Laravel] does a lot on its own, with very little code, and one of the goals of this document is to reveal what happens “behind the scenes .” [Laravel] can create servers that return JSON to a client ([JavaScript], [Angular], [React], [Vue.js], [Flutter]...) as well as traditional web applications, where the server generates the HTML pages and the browser simply displays them. It is this second use case that this document examines.

A specific feature of [PHP] explains a great deal about [Laravel]: the application is rebuilt with each request and then discarded (Example 01). We will return to this point frequently.

docs.title: 1.2. Tools Used
docs.text:
The examples were written and tested using the following tools (installation instructions are provided in the appendix):

  • [PHP] 8.4 (any version 8.4 or later is suitable), with the extensions [intl], [mbstring], [openssl], and [pdo_mysql];
  • [Composer] 2, the library manager from [PHP];
  • the editor [Visual Studio Code], with the extensions [PHP Intelephense] (code analysis) and [Laravel] (views [Blade]);
  • a recent browser ([Chrome], [Firefox], [Edge]);
  • the command-line tool [curl], which displays the raw HTTP responses (it is included with [Windows] 10 and 11);
  • SGBD [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]), for example, that of [Laragon] under [Windows], starting with the chapter on data access, and for the case study. Under [Windows], [Laragon] installs [PHP], [Composer], and [MySQL] all at once.

[Laravel] and the other libraries are not part of [PHP]: [Composer] downloads them from the [Packagist] repository during installation (so you must be connected to the Internet on that day) and places them in a [vendor] folder. Each project describes its libraries in a [composer.json] file. The following table lists the main ones, along with the versions used:

[laravel/framework]the framework: routing, middleware, controllers, views ([Blade]), validation, session, cache, authentication, translation, [Eloquent]...13.33.0[symfony/*]the [Symfony] components on which [Laravel] is built (HTTP requests and responses, routing, console), installed along with it8.1[nesbot/carbon]dates (e.g., 12), installed with [Laravel]3.14.0[brick/math]exact decimal numbers (example 06), installed with [Laravel]1.0.0[firebase/php-jwt]tokens JWT (section on authentication)7.2.0

[Laravel] is typically installed by creating a complete project using the command:

composer create-project laravel/laravel mon-projet

[Composer] then downloads the skeleton of a [Laravel] application (about fifty files and folders: configuration, service providers, migrations, tests, [JavaScript] build tools...), then its libraries, and creates an encryption key. This is how you start a real project. For learning purposes, this skeleton has one drawback: it contains many files whose purpose you don’t yet understand. The examples in this document therefore start from the other end: Example 01 is the smallest possible [Laravel] application, and each example adds only the files it needs. The case study at the end has the structure of a standard [Laravel] application.

docs.title: 1.3.1. Installing Laragon
docs.text:
The case study requires SGBD, MySQL, a PHP interpreter, and the PHP and [composer] package installer. Laragon can provide all of this and more. As of September 2026, Laragon is available at URL and [Download Laragon – Fast & Modern Dev Environment ]. Laragon comes with tools that allow you to install a PHP server and the SGBD and [MySQL]:

  • in [1], an Apache web server;
  • in [2], the SGBD and [MySQL];
  • on [3], a messaging tool that we will not use;
  • [4] starts all services (Apache, [MySQL], MailPit);
  • [5] displays the web page for URL and [http://localhost]. By default, this URL refers to the <laragon-install>\www folder, where <laragon-install> is the Laragon installation folder;
  • in [6], launches the HeidiSQL tool, which allows you to manage MySQL databases. We will use this tool to create the database used by the tax calculation server;
  • In [7], open a terminal; all the binaries needed for Laragon are located in PATH;
  • In [8], open a Windows Explorer window in the folder associated with URL and [http://localhost];

The Laragon installation folder contains the following items:

  • In [1], the [bin] folder contains numerous applications:
  • In [1], the Apache web server;
  • in [2], a command-line terminal;
  • in [3], a [git] client that allows you to manage different versions of a project;
  • in [4], a database manager;
  • in [5], a mail manager;
  • in [6], the SGBD and [MySQL];
  • [7], another web server;
  • in [8], [node.js] to run JavaScript scripts;
  • [9], a text editor;
  • [10], the PHP interpreter;
  • [11], the [Python] interpreter;
  • [12], a cache server;

Laragon comes with a comprehensive development environment. In this course, we will use:

  • SGBD, [MySQL], [6], and the [heidisql] tool for graphical management;
  • the PHP 8.5 interpreter;
  • the [composer] package installer;

The README from the case study indicates that you must enter the following commands in a terminal:

composer install

to install the PHP packages required for the examples and the case study.

php -S localhost:8000 -t public

to run either one of the examples or the case study. If you use a [PowerShell] terminal within VSCode, you will encounter the following problem: Neither [composer] nor [php] are present in the PATH directory on the Windows machine after installing Laragon. Therefore, these commands will not be recognized in a VSCode terminal.

To include [composer] and [php] in the PATH on the Windows machine, open a PowerShell terminal in [administrateur] mode, then type the following commands:


[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path",[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine") + ";C:\laragon\bin\composer","Machine")


[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path",[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine") + ";C:\laragon\bin\php\php-8.5.11-nts-Win32-vs17-x64","Machine")

Adjust the two highlighted paths to match your environment.

You will need to restart VSCode for these changes to take effect.

To create the [MySQL] database required for the case study, proceed as follows:

  • In [1], all services must be started;
  • in [2], the [Database] option allows you to manage the database;

The [Database] option launches a utility called HeidiSQL:

  • In [1], you can select various SGBD options. The default value provided is SGBD MySQL. This is acceptable;
  • in [2], you log in to HeidiSQL;
  • In [1-2], run the SQL file, then select the [dbrdvmedecins2.sql] file, which you’ll find in the [symfony-sept-202-] folder:

Running the [3] file will create the [dbrdvmedecins2] database used by the case study. To view it, run F5 within HeidiSQL to refresh the display:

Editor's note: The following screenshots show a database named [dbrdvmedecins], whereas the database in the case study is named [dbrdvmedecins2]. The two databases are virtually identical, so we determined that it was unnecessary to take new screenshots.

End of note

The database [dbrdvmedecins] has been created. Here is its content:

  • in [1-3], the table [clients];
    • [id] is the primary key of the table;
    • [version] is the row’s version number. This number increments each time the row is modified;
    • [titre, nom, prenom] identifies the person;

  • in [1-3], the table [medecins];
    • [id] is the primary key of the table;
    • [version] is the version number of the row;
    • [titre, nom, prenom] identifies the person;

  • In [1-3], the table of doctors’ appointment time slots:
    • [id]: primary key;
    • [version]: row version number;
    • [id-medecin]: foreign key referencing the doctor’s primary key;
    • [hdebut, mdebut]: hour and minutes of the appointment start time. Thus, [8,20] means 8:20 a.m.
    • [hfin, mfin]: hour and minutes of the end of the consultation.

  • In [1-3], the [rv] table of scheduled appointments;
    • [id]: primary key;
    • [version]: version number;
    • [jour]: appointment date;
    • [id_creneau]: foreign key referencing the primary key of the appointment time slot. Since a time slot is linked to a doctor, we know which doctor is handling this appointment;
    • [id_client]: foreign key to the number (primary key) of the patient attending the appointment;

  • in [1-3], the table [users] lists the users authorized to use the application [NestJS];
    • [id, version]: primary key, version number;
    • [login, password]: user credentials;
    • [nom]: user name;
    • [role]: the user’s role. [ADMIN] has full access rights. [USER] has read-only access. This user can view a doctor’s schedule but cannot schedule or cancel an appointment;

docs.title: 1.3.2. Running the Case Study
docs.text:
Reviewer’s note: I advise the reader to run the case study immediately as described below. Once you fully understand the purpose of this appointment scheduling application, ask your favorite IA to modify the application as follows: from now on, each doctor will be able to:

  • set their own appointment slots between two dates. This will allow them to adjust their schedule as needed;
  • remove certain time slots from the calendar for a given day—for example, if they are unavailable for personal reasons;

The modification is not straightforward because it involves a change to the database structure. Ask IA to provide you with the new application code and the SQL script to create the new database. To do this, you’ll need to provide them with the ZIP file containing the complete project as well as the SQL script for the old database.

Also, I haven’t reviewed the course created by Claude. He had already produced the courses [NestJS], [ASP.NET Core MVC], [Spring MVC], and [Flask], all of which were perfect. I assumed the same was true for this one. If you run into a problem understanding something, the solution is always the same: ask your favorite IA to explain what you don’t understand. Claude, for example, is very good at this. You may need to “upload” the example you don’t understand to him.

End of note.

The case study at the end of this document is a complete application. Readers will likely want to see it in action before delving into the details of the framework: here’s how to run it. It’s located in the [rdvmedecins2-laravel] folder, next to the [exemples] folder:

laravel-sept-2026/
├── exemples/
└── rdvmedecins2-laravel/

You must have installed [PHP] (version 8.4 or later), [Composer], [Visual Studio Code], and [MySQL] (see appendices). Then:

  • Create the [dbrdvmedecins2] database by running the [rdvmedecins2-laravel/database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] script. With [Laragon], open the [HeidiSQL] tool (Database button), then run the script via the File / Run SQL menu. At the command line, from the [rdvmedecins2-laravel] folder:
mysql -u root < database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql
  • Open the [rdvmedecins2-laravel] folder in [Visual Studio Code] (File menu / Open Folder), then open a terminal (Terminal menu / New Terminal);
  • Install the application libraries: [Composer] reads the file [composer.json], downloads [Laravel] and the other libraries, and places them in the application’s [vendor] folder (takes a few tens of seconds):
composer install
  • Check the connection to the database. The application connects to [MySQL] on [127.0.0.1], port 3306, using the user [root] without a password (the default settings for [Laragon]). If your [root] account has a password, enter it in the application’s [.env] file, on the [DB_PASSWORD=] line (for example, [DB_PASSWORD=monMotDePasse]);
  • Run the application:
php artisan serve --port=8081
  • [Laravel] displays:
   INFO  Server running on [http://127.0.0.1:8081].

  Press Ctrl+C to stop the server

The development server listens on port 8081 at the address [127.0.0.1] (i.e., [localhost]). Each request received will be logged in the console, along with the SQL commands it sends to the database;

  • Open the address [http://localhost:8081] in a browser:

  • Log in with one of the demo accounts, whose password is the same as the username: [admin] (administrator), [pelissier], [tatou], [dupont] (doctors), [martin], [durand], [bistrou], [german] (patients). You must also enter the characters from the image, in uppercase or lowercase.

An application named [PHP] fails to read the database upon startup: a connection error only appears on the first page that queries the database—that is, at the time of connection. [Laravel] then displays its debug page and logs the error in the [storage/logs/laravel.log] file. If the message is [SQLSTATE[HY000] [2002] Connection refused], it means that [MySQL] has not started; with [[1045] Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost'], it means the password is incorrect; with [[1049] Unknown database 'dbrdvmedecins2'], it means the script SQL was not executed; with [could not find driver], that the [pdo_mysql] extension of [PHP] is not enabled. If the [php artisan serve] command itself fails with the message [Failed opening required '.../vendor/autoload.php'], it means that [composer install] was not executed; with [Failed to listen on 127.0.0.1:8081 (reason: Address already in use)], it means that port 8081 is already in use (by another version of the application, for example). The application’s [README.md] file describes other scenarios. Stop the application using [Ctrl-C] in the terminal.

The case study at the end of the document describes how to use the application and then explains each of its files.

docs.title: 1.4. Examples
docs.text:
The examples are stored in the [exemples] folder, with one subfolder per example:

exemples/
├── 01-structure/
├── 02-routage/
├── ...
├── 28-couches/
├── commun/
│   ├── bootstrap/
│   └── bootstrap.php
└── composer.json

Each example is a small application ([Laravel]) that runs on its own. All examples use the same libraries, described in the file [exemples/composer.json]:

{
    "name": "cours/laravel-exemples",
    "description": "Les 28 exemples du cours [Introduction étape par étape au framework web Laravel] : un seul dossier vendor, partagé par tous les exemples",
    "type": "project",
    "license": "MIT",
    "require": {
        "php": "^8.4",
        "ext-intl": "*",
        "ext-pdo_mysql": "*",
        "laravel/framework": "^13.33",
        "firebase/php-jwt": "^7.0"
    },
    "config": {
        "optimize-autoloader": true,
        "sort-packages": true
    },
    "minimum-stability": "stable",
    "prefer-stable": true
}
  • Lines 6–12: What the examples require: [PHP] 8.4 or later, the extensions [intl] (language-specific number formatting, Example 16), and [pdo_mysql] (access to [MySQL], example 28), [Laravel], and [firebase/php-jwt] (the tokens JWT, example 25). [^13.33] reads “version 13.33, or a newer version of major version 13”;
  • the other lines configure the behavior of [Composer]: the class loader is optimized, libraries are sorted by name, and only stable versions are accepted.

To run the examples, first install their libraries—once and for all—in a terminal window open to the [exemples] folder:

composer install

[Composer] creates the [exemples/vendor] folder, shared by all 28 examples, and the [composer.lock] file, which records the exact versions installed (see case study). The [commun] folder contains the CSS framework, [Bootstrap] ([commun/bootstrap]), shared by the examples that format their pages (starting with Example 15), and the route that serves it ([commun/bootstrap.php]; see Example 15).

Almost all of the examples have the same structure—that of a standard [Laravel] application, stripped down to the essentials. For example, the one in Example 13:

13-premiere-vue/
├── app/
│   ├── Http/
│   │   └── Controllers/
│   │       └── VuesController.php
│   └── Models/
│       └── PageModele.php
├── bootstrap/
│   ├── app.php
│   └── cache/
├── public/
│   └── index.php
├── resources/
│   └── views/
│       └── vues/
│           ├── inconnu.blade.php
│           └── index.blade.php
├── routes/
│   └── web.php
├── storage/
├── .env
├── artisan
└── composer.json
  • [public/index.php]: the entry point for all requests; [bootstrap/app.php]: the application structure; [artisan]: the command-line tool for [Laravel] (Example 01);
  • [routes/web.php]: routes, which associate URL with actions (Example 02);
  • [app]: the application’s classes: controllers ([app/Http/Controllers]), models, services...;
  • [resources/views]: the views [Blade] (from the chapter on views);
  • [.env]: settings specific to the example (Example 01); [storage] and [bootstrap/cache]: the files that [Laravel] writes itself (compiled views, cache, sessions, log).

To run an example, open a terminal in its folder (in [Visual Studio Code]: right-click the example folder, then select “Open in the built-in terminal”), and type:

php artisan serve

All examples listen on port 8000: you can only run one at a time (or you must change the port: [php artisan serve --port=8001]). Stop the server by entering [Ctrl-C] in the terminal. It is not necessary to restart the server after modifying a [PHP] file or a view: the change takes effect with the next request (example 01).

When you open the [exemples] folder within [Visual Studio Code], the [PHP Intelephense] extension analyzes all files, including those from [Laravel] in the [vendor] folder: In each file, you can take advantage of code completion, navigation to the definition of a class or method ([F12] key), and error reporting. Since all examples have their classes in the [App] namespace, the extension may flag “duplicate” classes: this has no effect on execution, since each example runs independently. To avoid these warnings, simply open the example’s folder itself.

docs.text:
The document proceeds as follows:

Actions, routing, responsesFrom request to action: routes, controllers, responses, redirects, shared services01 to 06The Action ModelRequest parameters: binding, conversion, validation, forms POST07 to 12The view and its template[Blade], template, components, forms, validation, PRG, anti-CSRF protection13 to 21InternationalizationAn application in French and English22Data Scopequery, session, cache, cookies23The lifecycle of a requestmiddleware, parameter binding, exception handlers24Authentication and authorizationJWT in a cookie, guards, roles, CAPTCHA, attempt limits25–27Layered architecture and data accessWeb / Business / DAO with [Eloquent] and [MySQL]28Case StudyThe RdvMedecins application, explained file by file-

Each example introduces only a few new concepts, and the chapters build on one another: it is best to read them in order. The case study, meanwhile, draws on all the concepts from the previous chapters: whenever relevant, its commentary refers to the example where the concept was introduced. The appendices describe how to install the tools: [PHP], [Composer], [Visual Studio Code] and its extensions, [MySQL] along with [Laragon], and [curl].

docs.title: 9. Layered Architecture and Data Access
docs.text:
The previous examples stored their data in memory or in the cache. A real application stores it in a database and is organized into layers (see the diagram in the introduction):

  • the web layer (controllers, views): read the request, call the business layer, select the view;
  • the business layer: business rules;
  • the DAO layer (*Data Access Object*): database queries.

Each layer is aware only of the layer below it, and as few details about it as possible: the web layer is unaware of the SQL layer, and the business layer is unaware of the HTML layer. This separation makes each layer easier to understand, test, and evolve. Example 28 applies this to managing a list of people: it is, on a smaller scale, the management of doctors and clients from the case study.

In [PHP], database access is organized across several layers:

  • the PDO extension (*PHP Data Objects*) of [PHP] defines an interface common to all SGBD modules: opening a connection, executing a SQL command, and reading rows. Each SGBD has its own driver: [pdo_mysql] for [MySQL] (and [MariaDB]), included with [PHP];
  • the query builder (*query builder*) of [Laravel] ([DB] facade) constructs the SQL commands from method calls ([where], [orderBy]...), regardless of the SGBD, and manages connections and transactions;
  • Eloquent, the ORM (*Object-Relational Mapper*) of [Laravel], maps classes (models, as defined by [Eloquent]) to database tables and transforms the retrieved rows into objects. It follows the so-called *Active Record* model: each object knows how to read and save itself ([Personne::find(1)], [$personne->save()]).

This is the equivalent of converting [JDBC], [JPA], and [Hibernate] to [Java], [Entity Framework Core] to [C#], or [SQLAlchemy] to [Python]. Note a consequence of how [PHP] works: since nothing survives the request, each request opens its own connection to the database (upon its first SQL request) and closes it upon termination. There is no connection pool as in [Java] or [Python]; opening a connection to [MySQL] on the same machine takes only a fraction of a millisecond.

This example requires a [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]) server to be running: the appendix explains how to install one using [Laragon].

docs.title: 9.1.1. The database
docs.text:
The [dbpersonnes] database is created by the SQL script. Using [Laragon], you can run it, for example, in the [HeidiSQL] tool (File menu / Run a SQL file), or from the command line, from the example folder:

mysql -u root < database/dbpersonnes.sql

The [database/dbpersonnes.sql] file:

-- Example 28 database: a single table, [personnes]
-- The script is written in UTF-8
SET NAMES utf8mb4;
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS dbpersonnes;
CREATE DATABASE dbpersonnes CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbpersonnes;

CREATE TABLE personnes (
  id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
   -- the row version, incremented with each modification (see layer DAO)
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  prenom VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  nom VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  age INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id),
   -- Two people cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_personnes_prenom_nom UNIQUE (prenom, nom)
) ENGINE = InnoDB;

INSERT INTO personnes (prenom, nom, age) VALUES
  ('Marie', 'Pélissier', 42),
  ('Jacques', 'Bromard', 35),
  ('Philippe', 'Jandot', 58);
  • Line 3: The script is written in [UTF-8]; this is specified to the server so that the accents in the data ([Pélissier]) remain intact;
  • line 5: the character set [utf8mb4] accepts all characters (accents, emojis, etc.). The [utf8mb4_unicode_ci] collation compares strings without regard to uppercase letters or accents: for [MySQL], [pelissier], and [Pélissier] are equal;
  • line 11: a version number, incremented each time the line is modified (see “optimistic lock,” below);
  • line 17: a named uniqueness constraint: the database does not allow two people with the same first and last names. The name will be used to identify the error.

[Laravel] can also create the tables itself, using migrations: [PHP] classes that describe, step by step, the creation and modifications of each table (command [php artisan migrate]). We maintain a script, SQL, which is common to all versions of the case study and shows exactly what the database contains.

docs.title: 9.1.2. Configuration
docs.text:
The database connection is defined in the file [.env]:

# Database connection: SGBD MySQL, on this machine (127.0.0.1), port 3306,
# the `dbpersonnes` database, the `root` user without a password (Laragon settings)
DB_CONNECTION=mysql
DB_HOST=127.0.0.1
DB_PORT=3306
DB_DATABASE=dbpersonnes
DB_USERNAME=root
DB_PASSWORD=
# true: SQL commands sent to the database are displayed in the console
DB_LOG=false

[DB_CONNECTION] refers to one of the connections described by the configuration in [Laravel] ([mysql], [mariadb], [pgsql], [sqlite], [sqlsrv]); the following lines configure it. If your server has a password, enter it in [DB_PASSWORD]. The [mysql] connection communicates with the server using [utf8mb4], the database character set. [DB_LOG] is a variable we define, read by [bootstrap/app.php]:

<?php
// bootstrap/app.php: the application from Example 28

use Illuminate\Database\Events\QueryExecuted;
use Illuminate\Database\Events\TransactionBeginning;
use Illuminate\Database\Events\TransactionCommitted;
use Illuminate\Database\Events\TransactionRolledBack;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Event;

(require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php')->addPsr4('App\\', __DIR__.'/../app/');

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(
        web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php',
         // the route used by Bootstrap (see Example 15)
        then: fn () => require __DIR__.'/../../commun/bootstrap.php')
    ->withMiddleware()
    ->withExceptions()
    ->booted(function () {
         // DB_LOG=true (.env file): each SQL command and each step of a
         // transaction is displayed in the server console
        if (env('DB_LOG')) {
            DB::listen(fn (QueryExecuted $q) =>
                error_log($q->sql.' '.json_encode($q->bindings, JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE)));
            Event::listen(TransactionBeginning::class, fn () => error_log('BEGIN'));
            Event::listen(TransactionCommitted::class, fn () => error_log('COMMIT'));
            Event::listen(TransactionRolledBack::class, fn () => error_log('ROLLBACK'));
        }
    })
    ->create();
  • Lines 24–30: If [DB_LOG] equals [true], each SQL command is displayed in the console. [DB::listen] registers a function called after each SQL command, with a [QueryExecuted] object (the command text, its parameters, and its duration). [Event::listen] logs a function called for each event of a given type: [Laravel] thus signals, among other things, the start, confirmation, and cancellation of transactions. Events are another way—along with middleware—to intervene in the framework’s operation. (We read [env] directly, for brevity; a typical application would use a configuration file; see Example 25.)

There is nothing else to configure: the classes of the three layers are created by the [Laravel] container, which injects the layer below into each one (the controller receives the business layer, and the business layer receives the DAO layer).

docs.title: 9.1.3. The Person Model
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Models/Personne.php: a row in the [personnes] table, an Eloquent “model”

namespace App\Models;

use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model;

// Model: the parent class of Eloquent entities, Laravel’s ORM. The columns
// in the table automatically become properties of the object ($p->name)
class Personne extends Model
{
     // the table name (Eloquent would infer this from the class name: `people`)
    protected $table = 'personnes';

     // the table does not have the columns created_at and updated_at, which Eloquent maintains by default
    public $timestamps = false;

     // the columns that can be filled in bulk: new Person([...]), update([...])
    protected $fillable = ['prenom', 'nom', 'age'];

     // type conversions, column by column
    protected function casts(): array
    {
        return ['age' => 'integer', 'version' => 'integer'];
    }
}
  • Line 10: A model named [Eloquent] inherits from the class [Model]. The table columns are not declared: [Eloquent] reads the row, and each column becomes a property of the object ([$p->nom], [$p->version]). The primary key is, by default, the column [id], generated by the database ([AUTO_INCREMENT]);
  • line 13: the table associated with the class. [Eloquent] would derive it itself from the class name by putting it in the plural (in English);
  • line 16: By default, [Eloquent] maintains two columns, [created_at] and [updated_at], which it assumes are present in every table. Ours does not have them;
  • line 19: the columns that can be filled in “in bulk” from an array ([Personne::create([...])]). This is a precaution: an array from a form might contain other columns ([version], [id]...), which we do not want to be filled in this way;
  • Lines 22–25: Type conversions: the driver converts certain numeric columns to strings; [casts] ensures they are integers. There are conversions for Booleans, dates ([Carbon] objects), decimals, arrays (a JSON column)...

docs.title: 9.1.4. The DAO layer
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Dao/PersonnesDao.php: the DAO layer, queries, no business rules

namespace App\Dao;

use App\Metier\DonneesPersonne;
use App\Models\Personne;
use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Collection;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;

class PersonnesDao
{
     // SELECT * FROM people ORDER BY last name, first name
    public function lister(): Collection
    {
        return Personne::orderBy('nom')->orderBy('prenom')->get();
    }

     // SELECT * FROM people WHERE id = ? LIMIT 1; null if the person does not exist
    public function lire(int $id): ?Personne
    {
        return Personne::find($id);
    }

     // a person with the same first and last name, other than [$saufId]:
     // SELECT * FROM person WHERE first name = ? AND last name = ? AND ID <> ? LIMIT 1
    public function homonyme(string $prenom, string $nom, int $saufId = 0): ?Personne
    {
        return Personne::where('prenom', $prenom)->where('nom', $nom)
            ->where('id', '<>', $saufId)->first();
    }

     // INSERT INTO people (first name, last name, age) VALUES (?, ?, ?) ; the database generates
     // the ID, which Eloquent stores in the object
    public function ajouter(DonneesPersonne $donnees): Personne
    {
        return Personne::create(['prenom' => $donnees->prenom, 'nom' => $donnees->nom,
            'age' => $donnees->age]);
    }

     // the VERROU OPTIMISTE: UPDATE ... SET ..., version = version + 1
     // WHERE id = ? AND version = ? ; returns the number of modified lines (0: the
     // row has been modified or deleted since it was read)
    public function modifier(int $id, int $version, DonneesPersonne $donnees): int
    {
        return Personne::where('id', $id)->where('version', $version)->update([
            'prenom' => $donnees->prenom, 'nom' => $donnees->nom, 'age' => $donnees->age,
             // DB::raw: a SQL expression, written as-is in the SQL order
            'version' => DB::raw('version + 1'),
        ]);
    }

     // DELETE FROM people WHERE id = ?
    public function supprimer(int $id): void
    {
        Personne::whereKey($id)->delete();
    }
}

The DAO layer contains only queries, with no business logic. Each method uses the connection for the current query and participates in the open transaction, if there is one, initiated by the business layer.

  • Lines 14–17: [Personne::orderBy(...)] initiates a query on the people table; the methods are chained together ([orderBy] adds a sort), and [get()] executes the query. The result is a collection [Eloquent] (example 03) of objects [Personne];
  • lines 20–23: [find]: retrieval by primary key, or [null];
  • lines 27–31: [where(colonne, valeur)] adds an equality condition; [where(colonne, opérateur, valeur)] adds any condition. The values are passed to the database as parameters of the SQL command (the [?] commands), and are never copied into its text, which makes injection via SQL impossible. [first()] returns the first line ([LIMIT 1]) or [null];
  • lines 35–39: [Personne::create] creates the object from an array (within the scope of [$fillable]) and inserts it into the database; [Eloquent] stores the ID generated by the database in the object;
  • lines 44–51: the update, with an optimistic lock. The [UPDATE] command has two conditions: the person’s ID and the version read when the form was displayed. It increments the version by 1: [DB::raw] inserts an expression SQL as-is ([version + 1]), instead of a value. If another query has modified the row in the meantime, its version has changed, and [UPDATE] does not modify any rows: [update] returns the number of modified rows, which is 0 in this case. This is the principle of optimistic locking: nothing is locked, but concurrent modifications are detected. ([Eloquent] does not manage a version number itself, unlike [Hibernate] or [SQLAlchemy]: the condition is written by hand.);
  • lines 54–57: a [DELETE], constructed in the same way ([whereKey]: a condition on the primary key).

// message is intended for the user

namespace App\Metier;

use RuntimeException;
