An exception class specific to the business layer: a business rule rejects the operation, and the exception message is intended for the user. It inherits from [RuntimeException] without adding anything to it—only its name matters.

<?php
// app/Metier/PersonnesMetier.php: the MÉTIER layer, the business rules, and they
// alone. Each operation that writes to a TRANSACTION is validated (COMMIT) if the
// function completes normally, rolled back (ROLLBACK) if an exception occurs

namespace App\Metier;

use App\Dao\PersonnesDao;
use App\Models\Personne;
use Exception;
use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Collection;
use Illuminate\Database\QueryException;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;

class PersonnesMetier
{
    private const HOMONYME = 'Une personne porte déjà ces prénom et nom.';

    private const MODIFIEE = 'Cette fiche a été modifiée entre-temps : rechargez-la.';

    private const INCONNUE = "Cette personne n'existe pas (ou plus).";

    public function __construct(private PersonnesDao $dao)
    {
    }

    public function lister(): Collection
    {
        return $this->dao->lister();
    }

    public function lire(int $id): Personne
    {
        return $this->dao->lire($id) ?? throw new MetierException(self::INCONNUE);
    }

    public function ajouter(DonneesPersonne $donnees): Personne
    {
        try {
             // DB::transaction: the function is executed within a transaction
            return DB::transaction(function () use ($donnees) {
                 // Rule 1: No two people can have the same first and last names
                if ($this->dao->homonyme($donnees->prenom, $donnees->nom)) {
                    throw new MetierException(self::HOMONYME);
                }
                return $this->dao->ajouter($donnees);
            });
        } catch (QueryException $e) {
            throw self::traduire($e);
        }
    }

    public function modifier(int $id, int $version, DonneesPersonne $donnees): Personne
    {
        try {
            return DB::transaction(function () use ($id, $version, $donnees) {
                $personne = $this->lire($id);
                 // Rule 2: Do not modify a record that has been modified in the meantime by someone else
                if ($personne->version !== $version) {
                    throw new MetierException(self::MODIFIEE);
                }
                if ($this->dao->homonyme($donnees->prenom, $donnees->nom, $id)) {
                    throw new MetierException(self::HOMONYME);
                }
                 // The UPDATE "WHERE id = ... AND version = ..." did not modify any rows:
                 // Another query has modified the record since it was read
                if ($this->dao->modifier($id, $version, $donnees) === 0) {
                    throw new MetierException(self::MODIFIEE);
                }
                 // the record, read again: its new values and new version
                return $this->lire($id);
            });
        } catch (QueryException $e) {
            throw self::traduire($e);
        }
    }

    public function supprimer(int $id): Personne
    {
        return DB::transaction(function () use ($id) {
            $personne = $this->lire($id);
            $this->dao->supprimer($id);
            return $personne;
        });
    }

     // two simultaneous additions: the database's uniqueness constraint rejected the
     // second one; getMessage() contains the message from MySQL, including the constraint name
    private static function traduire(QueryException $e): Exception
    {
        if (str_contains($e->getMessage(), 'unq_personnes_prenom_nom')) {
            return new MetierException(self::HOMONYME, previous: $e);
        }
        return $e;
    }
}
  • lines 17–21: the business rule messages;
  • lines 32–35: a nonexistent person is a business error. The operator [??] accepts an expression [throw] on the right-hand side: if the person is [null], the exception is thrown;
  • lines 37–51: Rule No. 1: No two people may have the same first and last names. [DB::transaction] executes the function within a transaction: if the function completes normally, the transaction is committed ([COMMIT]), and [DB::transaction] returns the function’s value; if an exception is thrown, the transaction is rolled back ([ROLLBACK]): none of the changes made within the function are retained, and the exception proceeds. The business layer thus determines the scope of transactions: one business operation, one transaction. The rule is checked before writing, and a [MetierException] is raised if it is not followed. But this check is not sufficient: two simultaneous queries could both verify that there is no duplicate, and then both insert the data. The database’s uniqueness constraint then rejects the second [INSERT], and [Laravel] triggers a [QueryException], which the [traduire] method transforms into the same [MetierException]. The database is the last line of defense;
  • lines 53–76: Rule No. 2: Do not modify a record that has been modified in the meantime by someone else. The update form carries the version of the record that was read (in a hidden field); if it differs from the current version, the record has changed since it was displayed. Here again, the database (via the optimistic lock in layer DAO) detects when a concurrent modification occurs between the read operation and the [UPDATE] transaction: the [UPDATE] transaction then does not modify any rows. The record is then read again, with its new values;
  • lines 78–85: The deletion marks the person as deleted for the confirmation message;
  • lines 89–95: [getMessage()] contains the message from [MySQL], including the name of the violated constraint. Another error is returned as-is: this is not a business error, but a programming error. The parameter named [previous] attaches the original exception to the new one for the log.

namespace App\Http\Requests;

class PersonneRequest extends FormRequest

            'age' => 'required|integer|between:0,150',
             // the record version, carried by a hidden field (update only)
            'version' => 'nullable|integer',
        ];

    {
        return [
            'prenom.required' => 'Le prénom est obligatoire.',
            'prenom.max' => '30 caractères au plus.',

The form request (Example 19). The hidden field [version] is optional (add form). The method [donnees] returns the validated data in the format expected by the business layer.

<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/PersonnesController.php: the WEB layer; it only recognizes the business layer

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Http\Requests\PersonneRequest;
use App\Metier\MetierException;
use App\Metier\PersonnesMetier;
use Illuminate\Http\RedirectResponse;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class PersonnesController
{
    public function __construct(private PersonnesMetier $metier)
    {
    }

    public function accueil(): RedirectResponse
    {
        return redirect()->route('personnes.liste');
    }

    public function liste(): View
    {
        return view('personnes.liste', ['personnes' => $this->metier->lister()]);
    }

    public function ajout(): View
    {
        return view('personnes.formulaire', ['titre' => 'Ajouter une personne',
            'action' => route('personnes.ajouter'), 'personne' => null]);
    }

     // PersonneRequest: an invalid form does not reach this point (see Example 19)
    public function ajouter(PersonneRequest $request): RedirectResponse
    {
        try {
            $p = $this->metier->ajouter($request->donnees());
        } catch (MetierException $e) {
             // A business rule rejects the form: return to the form, with the entered data and the
             // message at the bottom of the page
            return back()->withInput()->with('erreur', $e->getMessage());
        }
        return redirect()->route('personnes.liste')->with('succes', "$p->prenom $p->nom a été ajouté(e).");
    }

    public function modification(int $id): View|RedirectResponse
    {
        try {
            $p = $this->metier->lire($id);
        } catch (MetierException $e) {
            return redirect()->route('personnes.liste')->with('erreur', $e->getMessage());
        }
        return view('personnes.formulaire', ['titre' => 'Modifier une personne',
            'action' => route('personnes.modifier', $id), 'personne' => $p]);
    }

    public function modifier(PersonneRequest $request, int $id): RedirectResponse
    {
        try {
            $p = $this->metier->modifier($id, (int) $request->validated('version'), $request->donnees());
        } catch (MetierException $e) {
            return back()->withInput()->with('erreur', $e->getMessage());
        }
        return redirect()->route('personnes.liste')->with('succes', "$p->prenom $p->nom a été modifié(e).");
    }

    public function supprimer(int $id): RedirectResponse
    {
        try {
            $p = $this->metier->supprimer($id);
        } catch (MetierException $e) {
             // No form to redisplay: the error is also displayed in a pop-up message
            return redirect()->route('personnes.liste')->with('erreur', $e->getMessage());
        }
        return redirect()->route('personnes.liste')->with('succes', "$p->prenom $p->nom a été supprimé(e).");
    }
}
  • line 14: the business layer, the only layer known to the controller;
  • lines 35–45: the addition process, in three steps: form validation (input errors), performed before the action is called by the form request; the call to the business layer (business rules); then the PRG schema, with a success flash message. A [MetierException] returns to the form: [back()] redirects to the previous page (the form page), [withInput()] preserves the input for [old] (example 19), and [with('erreur', ...)] returns the error message, which the template will display at the bottom of the page. This is exactly what [Laravel] does for an invalid form: input errors and business logic errors are handled the same way;
  • lines 47–56: the edit form, pre-filled with the retrieved person. If the person does not exist, the user is redirected to the list with a pop-up error message;
  • lines 58–66: the update, following the same pattern as the add operation;
  • lines 68–77: deletion. There is no form to redisplay: any error is also conveyed in a pop-up message, [erreur].

The web layer contains neither SQL nor any business rules: it translates the request into a call to the business layer and the result into a page. The routing table:

<?php
// routes/web.php: the routes from Example 28

use App\Http\Controllers\PersonnesController;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::controller(PersonnesController::class)->name('personnes.')->group(function () {
    Route::get('/', 'accueil');
    Route::get('personnes', 'liste')->name('liste');
    Route::get('personnes/ajout', 'ajout')->name('ajout');
    Route::post('personnes/ajout', 'ajouter')->name('ajouter');
    Route::get('personnes/{id}/modification', 'modification')->whereNumber('id')->name('modification');
    Route::put('personnes/{id}', 'modifier')->whereNumber('id')->name('modifier');
    Route::delete('personnes/{id}', 'supprimer')->whereNumber('id')->name('supprimer');
});

docs.title: 9.1.8. The commands SQL
docs.text:
Let’s restart the application with the environment variable [DB_LOG=true] (under [Linux] and [macOS]: [DB_LOG=true php artisan serve]; for [Windows]: [$env:DB_LOG="true"] before [php artisan serve]; or by modifying the file [.env]), and then monitor the SQL commands for a modification in the console. The display of the modification form for person #1:

  select * from `personnes` where `personnes`.`id` = ? limit 1 [1]

A read operation using the primary key, whose value is passed as a parameter ([?]), without a transaction: an isolated read does not require one. Saving the record with a new age:

  BEGIN
  select * from `personnes` where `personnes`.`id` = ? limit 1 [1]
  select * from `personnes` where `prenom` = ? and `nom` = ? and `id` <> ? limit 1 ["Marie","Pélissier",1]
  update `personnes` set `prenom` = ?, `nom` = ?, `age` = ?, `version` = version + 1 where `id` = ? and `version` = ? ["Marie","Pélissier",44,1,1]
  select * from `personnes` where `personnes`.`id` = ? limit 1 [1]
  COMMIT

In a single transaction, we can see: the read of the master record, the search for a namesake, the [UPDATE], and the re-read. The [UPDATE] increments the version ([version + 1], written as-is thanks to [DB::raw]), and sets the optimistic lock condition ([and version = ?], with the read version, here 1). [Laravel] surrounds table and column names with grave accents ([personnes]), which is how these names are written in [MySQL]. Now let’s submit the same form a second time, still with version 1:

  BEGIN
  select * from `personnes` where `personnes`.`id` = ? limit 1 [1]
  ROLLBACK

The version being read (2) is not the same as the one in the form (1): the business layer raised a [MetierException], which rolled back the transaction ([ROLLBACK]), and the page displays “This record has been modified in the meantime: please reload it.” Similarly, the process of adding a namesake stops after the namesake search, without a [INSERT].

docs.title: 3. The Action Template
docs.text:
An action requires information sent by the browser: the parameters of the URL ([?nom=martin&age=42]), form fields, the request body JSON, and sometimes a request header HTTP. The original course refers to all of this information as the action model. This chapter shows how an action [Laravel] retrieves this information, converts it to the correct type, and validates it. This process is called data binding.

[Laravel] provides access to the request information via the [Request] object (Example 05), in the form of character strings, along with a few conversion methods. To verify the data, it has a comprehensive validation system: the expected data is described using rules (“required,” “an integer between 0 and 150,” etc.), and [Laravel] checks that the data complies with them. We’ll first read the parameters manually (example 07), then use these rules to validate them (examples 08 through 12). In the next chapter, the same system will validate the HTML forms.

Note on terminology: In the next chapter, the word “model” will primarily refer to the data that an action passes to its view. An action’s model, as used in this chapter, is what it receives. [Laravel] also uses the word *model* for the classes that represent database tables (Chapter 9): this is a third meaning.

Examples 07 through 12 are run in the same way as those in the previous chapter: open a terminal in the example directory, [php artisan serve]; [Ctrl-C] stops the server. Their [bootstrap/app.php] files are all similar: they add the [JsonLisible] middleware from Example 03, resulting in a readable JSON file. We will only comment on them when they introduce something new.

docs.title: 3.1. Example 07: The parameters of URL
docs.text:
The parameters for URL are the part that follows [?]: [?nom=martin&age=42]. This part is called the query string (*query string*). Each parameter is a pair of [nom=valeur]; the pairs are separated by [&]. The controller [ParametresController]:

<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/ParametresController.php: the parameters of URL (the "query string")

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use Illuminate\Http\Request;

class ParametresController
{
     // /settings/action01?name=martin: the query returns the parameter's value, or
     // null if it is missing
    public function action01(Request $request): string
    {
        $nom = $request->query('nom');
        return "nom = [$nom], de type ".get_debug_type($nom);
    }

     // /parameters/action02?age=42: integer CONVERTIT the value (a string) as
     // integer; a missing parameter, or one that is not an integer, returns 0
    public function action02(Request $request): string
    {
        $age = $request->integer('age');
        return "age = [$age], de type ".get_debug_type($age);
    }

     // /parameters/action03?age=42: a parameter OBLIGATOIRE; if it is missing, or if a
     // value that is not an integer, stops the action with a 400 (Bad Request) response
    public function action03(Request $request): string
    {
        $texte = $request->query('age');
        if ($texte === null) {
             // abort throws an exception, which Laravel converts into an error response
            abort(400, 'le paramètre [age] est obligatoire');
        }
         // we are responsible for the conversion: filter_var returns the integer or false
        $age = filter_var($texte, FILTER_VALIDATE_INT);
        if ($age === false) {
            abort(400, "[$texte] n'est pas un nombre entier");
        }
        return "age = [$age], de type ".get_debug_type($age);
    }

     // /parameters/action04?page=2: a default value if the parameter is missing
    public function action04(Request $request): string
    {
        $page = $request->integer('page', 1);
        return "page = [$page]";
    }

     // /parameters/action05?q=laravel: the name of the parameter in URL is not necessarily
     // the same as that of the variable PHP
    public function action05(Request $request): string
    {
        $recherche = $request->query('q');
        return "recherche = [$recherche]";
    }

     // /settings/action06?name=martin&age=42: all parameters at once, in an array
    public function action06(Request $request): array
    {
        return $request->query();
    }
}
  • line 14: the [query] method in the request returns the value of a parameter from URL, which has already been decoded, or [null] if it is missing; it never causes an error;
  • Line 15: The action displays the value and its type: the [get_debug_type] function returns the name of a value’s type. A value retrieved from URL is always a string ([string]). The operator [.] concatenates the interpolated string and the type;
  • line 22: the method [integer] reads the parameter and converts it to an integer. If the conversion fails ([abc]), or if the parameter is missing, it returns 0: the action cannot distinguish these cases from an age of 0 that was actually entered, and the input error goes unnoticed. Similarly, there are [float], [boolean] ([1], [true], [on], [yes] are valid), [string], [date] (example 12), [enum];
  • lines 30–40: a required parameter and a manual conversion that distinguishes between the two possible errors. [abort(400, message)] terminates the action with a 400 response (*Bad Request*, the request is invalid), accompanied by the message (see example 03). The function [filter_var] of [PHP], with the filter [FILTER_VALIDATE_INT], returns the integer contained in the string, or [false] if the string is not an integer;
  • line 46: the second parameter of [integer] is a default value, used if the parameter is missing. This is typically the case for a page number in a list;
  • line 54: There is no requirement to name the variable [PHP] the same as the parameter of URL. Search engines often use a short parameter, such as [q] (*query*);
  • line 61: without a parameter, [query] returns all the parameters of URL in an associative array, which the action returns: [Laravel] transforms it into JSON (see example 03).

The routing table declares the six routes using a loop:

<?php
// routes/web.php: the routes from Example 07

use App\Http\Controllers\ParametresController;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::prefix('parametres')->controller(ParametresController::class)->group(function () {
    foreach (['action01', 'action02', 'action03', 'action04', 'action05', 'action06'] as $action) {
        Route::get($action, $action);
    }
});
  • Line 8: The loop [foreach] iterates through an array: on each iteration, the variable [$action] takes on the value of the next element. Each route is named after its action: [Route::get('action01', 'action01')]... The routing table is just another [PHP] file: you can write any code you want in it.

Let’s test each action with [curl]. A parameter present, then absent:

curl -i "http://localhost:8000/parametres/action01?nom=martin"
curl http://localhost:8000/settings/action01

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

nom = [martin], de type string
nom = [], de type null

The quotation marks around "URL" are necessary in a terminal: without them, the shell would interpret [&] (which runs a command in the background under [Linux]) and [?]. The value [null], when inserted into a string, becomes an empty string. A value containing spaces or special characters must be encoded in URL: a space becomes [%20], and [&] becomes [%26] (otherwise, it would separate two parameters). The browser handles this automatically; with [curl], you have to write it out. [PHP] decodes the value before the action reads it:

curl "http://localhost:8000/parametres/action01?nom=jean%20dupont%20%26%20fils"

nom = [jean dupont & fils], de type string

Conversion using [integer]—successful, failed, then without parameters:

curl "http://localhost:8000/parametres/action02?age=42"
curl "http://localhost:8000/parametres/action02?age=abc"
curl http://localhost:8000/settings/action02

age = [42], de type int
age = [0], de type int
age = [0], de type int

The required parameter for action 03 is missing, then invalid. We request a response JSON (header [Accept], see example 03), which contains the message from [abort]:

curl -i -H "Accept: application/json" http://localhost:8000/settings/action03
curl -H "Accept: application/json" "http://localhost:8000/parametres/action03?age=abc"

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "message": "le paramètre [age] est obligatoire",
    "exception": "Symfony\\Component\\HttpKernel\\Exception\\HttpException",
    ...
}
{
    "message": "[abc] n'est pas un nombre entier",
    "exception": "Symfony\\Component\\HttpKernel\\Exception\\HttpException",
    ...
}

In a browser, in debug mode, a 400 response displays the error page for [Laravel], with the message:

The default value and the renamed parameter:

curl http://localhost:8000/settings/action04
curl "http://localhost:8000/parametres/action04?page=3"
curl "http://localhost:8000/parametres/action05?q=laravel"

page = [1]
page = [3]
recherche = [laravel]

Finally, all the parameters at once. The parameter [nom] appears twice:

curl "http://localhost:8000/parametres/action06?nom=martin&age=42&nom=durand"

{
    "nom": "durand",
    "age": "42"
}

The parameter [nom] retains only its last value: this is a rule for [PHP], which we’ll see again in Example 10. The age remained a string (["42"], enclosed in quotation marks within JSON): no conversion was requested. In a browser (here, [Chromium]), the JSON is displayed exactly as the server formatted it; the “Pretty-print” checkbox would indent it if it were not already indented. The address bar also shows the encoding of accented characters in URL ([é] becomes [%C3%A9], with its two bytes in [UTF-8]):

This first example illustrates the limitations of the manual approach: for each parameter, you must write the reading, conversion, and handling of missing values and errors. With ten parameters, the action’s code would be overwhelmed by these checks. It is better to describe what is expected and let the framework verify it. That is the purpose of the following example.

docs.title: 3.2. Example 08: An action model described by a class
docs.text: [Laravel] validates request data using validation rules. A rule has a name ([required], [integer], [email]...), and sometimes parameters ([min:2], [between:0,150]); the rules for a field are written as a string, separated by [|], or as an array. [Laravel] provides about a hundred of them. The natural place to describe an action’s model is a form request (*form request*): a class that inherits from [FormRequest], and whose [rules] method returns the rules for each parameter.

docs.title: 3.2.1. The model: app/Http/Requests/PersonneRequest.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Requests/PersonneRequest.php: the action model, a class that
// describes the expected parameters and their constraints

namespace App\Http\Requests;

use App\Models\Personne;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Http\FormRequest;

class PersonneRequest extends FormRequest
{
     // the validation rules, parameter by parameter
    public function rules(): array
    {
        return [
             // required, a string of 2 to 20 characters
            'nom' => 'required|string|min:2|max:20',
             // required, an integer between 0 and 150
            'age' => 'required|integer|between:0,150',
             // only one of these three values
            'titre' => 'required|in:Mr,Mme,Melle',
             // optional (nullable); if present, a valid email address
            'email' => 'nullable|email',
        ];
    }

     // the validated parameters, in the form of a typed object
    public function personne(): Personne
    {
        $valeurs = $this->validated();
        return new Personne($valeurs['nom'], (int) $valeurs['age'], $valeurs['titre'],
            $valeurs['email'] ?? null);
    }
}
  • Line 10: The class ([extends]) inherits from [FormRequest], which itself inherits from [Request]: A [PersonneRequest] object is a query, with all the methods from Example 07, plus validation rules;
  • lines 13–24: the rules, in an associative array: for each parameter, the string containing its rules;
  • line 17: [required]: the parameter is required (if missing or empty, it is rejected); [string]: a string; [min:2] and [max:20]: for a string, its length must be between 2 and 20 characters;
  • line 19: [integer]: the value must be an integer (["42"] is valid, ["abc"] is not); [between:0,150]: For a number, its value must be between 0 and 150. The rules [min], [max], and [between] thus adapt to the value’s type: a length for a string, a value for a number, and a number of elements for an array (e.g., 10);
  • line 21: [in:Mr,Mme,Melle]: one of the three values listed, and only those;
  • line 23: [nullable]: the parameter is optional (it is accepted if absent or empty); [email]: if present, a valid email address;
  • lines 28–33: a method added to the class: it returns the validated data in the form of a [Personne] object (see below). [$this->validated()] returns only the data that has been validated: a parameter without a rule is not included. The validation performed by [Laravel] checks the data but does not convert it: the validated age is still the string ["42"]. It is the conversion operator [(int)] that converts it to an integer. The operator [??] returns its left operand if it exists and is not [null]; otherwise, it returns the right operand: [$valeurs['email'] ?? null] evaluates to [null] if the address is not in the array.

This template describes the expected data; it contains no validation instructions. This is known as a declarative style. The class [Personne] is an immutable class, modeled after the one in Example 03:

<?php
// app/Models/Personne.php: a person

namespace App\Models;

readonly class Personne
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $nom,
        public int $age,
        public string $titre,
        public ?string $email,
    ) {
    }
}
  • line 12: [?string]: a string, or [null].

docs.title: 3.2.2. The action: app/Http/Controllers/PersonnesController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/PersonnesController.php: an action whose model is a class FormRequest

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Http\Requests\PersonneRequest;

class PersonnesController
{
     // /people/action01?name=martin&age=42&title=Mr
     // The parameter of type PersonneRequest is VALIDÉ by Laravel AVANT when calling
     // the action: an invalid model raises a ValidationException error, which is converted to
     // a 400 response by bootstrap/app.php, and the action is never called
    public function action01(PersonneRequest $request): array
    {
        $personne = $request->personne();
        return [
            'recu' => $request->validated(),
            'personne' => $personne,
            'typeAge' => get_debug_type($personne->age),
        ];
    }
}
  • Line 14: The action requires a parameter of type [PersonneRequest], whereas Example 07 required a [Request]. [Laravel] then creates a [PersonneRequest] object from the current request and validates it before calling the action: it checks each rule for each parameter. If all rules are met, the action is called. Otherwise, [Laravel] throws a [ValidationException] exception, which contains a list of all errors (not just the first one), and the action is never called: it therefore does not have to deal with invalid data;
  • Lines 16–20: The action returns the validated data as-is, then as a [Personne] object, along with the age type, to illustrate the difference.

Who handles the [ValidationException] exception? By default, [Laravel] itself, and its response depends on the client. For a request expecting JSON (header [Accept: application/json]), the response is a 422 (*Unprocessable Content*), which describes the errors in JSON. For a regular request originating from a HTML form, the response is a redirect to the previous page, with the errors preserved for the form that will be redisplayed (we’ll cover this in the next chapter). Here, we want an error response in JSON, in all cases, with the 400 code. That is the role of [bootstrap/app.php].

docs.title: 3.2.3. Error handling: bootstrap/app.php
docs.text:
<?php
// bootstrap/app.php: the application from Example 08

use App\Http\Middleware\JsonLisible;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Exceptions;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Middleware;
use Illuminate\Validation\ValidationException;

(require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php')->addPsr4('App\\', __DIR__.'/../app/');

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php')
    ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
        $middleware->append(JsonLisible::class);
    })
    ->withExceptions(function (Exceptions $exceptions): void {
         // an invalid template: the exception ValidationException becomes, for
         // TOUTE the application, a 400 response that details the errors
        $exceptions->render(function (ValidationException $e) {
            $erreurs = [];
             // errors(): field -> list of its error messages
            foreach ($e->errors() as $champ => $messages) {
                foreach ($messages as $message) {
                    $erreurs[] = ['champ' => $champ, 'message' => $message];
                }
            }
            return response()->json(['statut' => 400, 'erreurs' => $erreurs], 400);
        });
    })
    ->create();
  • Lines 17–30: The [withExceptions] method is now passed a function, which receives the [$exceptions] object describing the application’s exception handling;
  • lines 20–29: The [render] method registers an exception handler: a function that [Laravel] calls when an action throws an exception of the same type as its parameter (here, [ValidationException] or a derived class), and whose return value is the response sent. [Laravel] identifies the type of the exception being handled based on the function’s parameter type. Declared in [bootstrap/app.php], the handler applies to all actions in the application: every action that validates a model benefits from it, without having to write a single line of error-handling code;
  • Lines 23–27: [$e->errors()] returns errors in an associative array: for each field with an error, the list of its error messages. The [foreach ($tableau as $cle => $valeur)] loop iterates through both the keys and the values. [$erreurs[] = ...] adds an element to the end of the [$erreurs] array;
  • line 28: a response JSON, with status code 400.

docs.title: 3.2.4. Execution
docs.text:
A valid template:

curl -i "http://localhost:8000/personnes/action01?nom=martin&age=42&titre=Mr"

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "recu": {
        "nom": "martin",
        "age": "42",
        "titre": "Mr"
    },
    "personne": {
        "nom": "martin",
        "age": 42,
        "titre": "Mr",
        "email": null
    },
    "typeAge": "int"
}

The validated data contains only the received parameters; the age is in string format; the [Personne] object contains the age as an integer (without quotes in JSON), and the missing address is [null]. A name surrounded by spaces ([%20]) and a present address:

curl "http://localhost:8000/personnes/action01?nom=%20%20martin%20&age=42&titre=Mme&email=martin@exemple.fr"

{
    "recu": {
        "nom": "martin",
        "age": "42",
        "titre": "Mme",
        "email": "martin@exemple.fr"
    },
    "personne": {
        "nom": "martin",
        "age": 42,
        "titre": "Mme",
        "email": "martin@exemple.fr"
    },
    "typeAge": "int"
}

The spaces surrounding the name have disappeared without us asking for it: two middleware components, executed by [Laravel] for all requests, transform the received parameters before an action reads them. [TrimStrings] removes the spaces surrounding each string; [ConvertEmptyStringsToNull] replaces each empty string with [null]. There are now no parameters: the three required fields are missing.

curl -i http://localhost:8000/people/action01

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "statut": 400,
    "erreurs": [
        {
            "champ": "nom",
            "message": "The nom field is required."
        },
        {
            "champ": "age",
            "message": "The age field is required."
        },
        {
            "champ": "titre",
            "message": "The titre field is required."
        }
    ]
}

Four invalid fields at once:

curl "http://localhost:8000/personnes/action01?nom=m&age=abc&titre=Mlle&email=xx"

{
    "statut": 400,
    "erreurs": [
        {
            "champ": "nom",
            "message": "The nom field must be at least 2 characters."
        },
        {
            "champ": "age",
            "message": "The age field must be an integer."
        },
        {
            "champ": "titre",
            "message": "The selected titre is invalid."
        },
        {
            "champ": "email",
            "message": "The email field must be a valid email address."
        }
    ]
}

All errors are reported at once, allowing the user to correct everything in one go. For the age field [abc], only rule [integer] is flagged: rule [between] does not apply to a value that is not a number. The messages are in English, the default language of [Laravel]. The following example replaces them with French messages.

docs.title: 3.3. Example 09: Validation Performed by the Action
docs.text:
In Example 08, an invalid model terminates the action, and the application handler responds. This is convenient for a API, whose clients are programs that expect a standardized error response. However, a web page often prefers to redisplay the form with the error messages: in this case, the action must decide how to handle an invalid model. The classes [PersonneRequest] and [Personne] are the ones from Example 08.

09-validation-action/
├── app/
│   ├── Http/
│   │   ├── Controllers/
│   │   │   └── PersonnesController.php
│   │   └── Requests/
│   │       └── PersonneRequest.php
│   └── Models/
│       └── Personne.php
├── lang/
│   └── fr/
│       └── validation.php
└── ...

docs.title: 3.3.1. French messages: lang/fr/validation.php
docs.text:
The error messages for [Laravel] are not hard-coded: each message is identified by a key, and a language file associates text with each key. The English files are included with the framework; for other languages, the application provides its own files in the [lang] folder, with one subfolder per language. The application’s language is set by the [.env] file:

APP_LOCALE=fr

The validation message file is named [validation.php]:

<?php
// lang/fr/validation.php: validation error messages in French.
// Each message is identified by the name of its RÈGLE (required, min...). The markers
// :attribute, :min, :max... are replaced by the field name and the
// rule parameters
return [
    'required' => 'le champ est obligatoire',
    'string' => 'une chaîne de caractères est attendue',
    'integer' => 'un nombre entier est attendu',
    'email' => 'adresse électronique invalide',
    'in' => 'valeur inconnue',
     // Some rules have one message per value type: for a string, min
     // refers to its length; for a number, to its value; for an array, to
     // the number of elements
    'min' => [
        'string' => ':min caractère(s) au moins',
        'numeric' => 'la valeur doit être supérieure ou égale à :min',
        'array' => ':min élément(s) au moins',
    ],
    'max' => [
        'string' => ':max caractère(s) au plus',
        'numeric' => 'la valeur doit être inférieure ou égale à :max',
    ],
    'between' => [
        'numeric' => 'la valeur doit être comprise entre :min et :max',
    ],
    'array' => 'une liste est attendue',
];
  • Line 6: A language file is a [PHP] file that returns an associative array: for each key, its corresponding text;
  • lines 7–11: The key for a validation message is the name of the rule that failed. This technique (translating based on the error name rather than its English text) is the one used in the case study: the texts there are identified by keys, which are translated into the user’s language;
  • lines 15–19: Rules that adapt to the value type (e.g., 08) have a message for each type: [string], [numeric], [array]. The identifiers [:min] and [:max] are replaced by the rule’s parameters ([min:2] means “at least 2 characters”). The tag [:attribute], which we do not use, would be replaced by the field name.

A key missing from this file retains its English message: [Laravel] falls back to the fallback language, [APP_FALLBACK_LOCALE], which is English by default. Complete translations of the messages in [Laravel], in many languages, are published by the community (the [laravel-lang] package).

docs.title: 3.3.2. The action: app/Http/Controllers/PersonnesController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/PersonnesController.php: This is the action that determines what to do with an invalid model

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Http\Requests\PersonneRequest;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Validator;

class PersonnesController
{
    public function action01(Request $request): string
    {
         // a VALIDATEUR: the data to be validated, and the rules (those of the
         // PersonneRequest class from Example 08)
        $validateur = Validator::make($request->query(), (new PersonneRequest())->rules());
        if ($validateur->fails()) {
             // Errors, field by field: errors()->messages() lists them
            $items = '';
            foreach ($validateur->errors()->messages() as $champ => $messages) {
                $items .= "<li>$champ : $messages[0]</li>";
            }
            return "<p>Le formulaire contient des erreurs :</p><ul>$items</ul>";
        }
         // Validated data
        $personne = $validateur->validated();
         // e(): the entered name is inserted into HTML; its characters < > & " '
         // are replaced by < >... (otherwise, user input could inject HTML)
        return "<p>Bienvenue {$personne['titre']} ".e($personne['nom'])
            ." ({$personne['age']} ans)</p>";
    }
}
  • Line 16: The [Validator] facade creates a validator—an object that applies rules to data. The data consists of the parameters of URL; the rules are those of the [PersonneRequest] class from Example 08. A form request is a class like any other: you can create an instance of it, via [new], to read its rules;
  • line 17: [fails()] performs validation and returns [true] if at least one rule fails. The action itself determines what happens next: no exception is thrown;
  • Lines 19–23: Errors, field by field. [errors()] returns a [MessageBag] object (a “bag” of messages), whose [messages()] method returns the associative array field → list of messages. For each field, the first message, [$messages[0]], is stored in a [<li>] tag. The [.=] operator appends one string to the end of another;
  • line 26: the validated data, in an associative array;
  • lines 29–30: if successful, a welcome message. Within a string enclosed in quotation marks, [{$personne['titre']}] inserts an array element (curly braces delimit the expression). The name is passed through the [e] function of [Laravel] (for *escape*), which replaces characters that have special meaning in HTML ([<], [>], [&], ["], [']) with their entities ([<], [>]...): they will be displayed as-is instead of being interpreted. Without this precaution, a user could enter a “name” containing HTML, or even [JavaScript], which would execute in the browser of anyone viewing the page. This is the most common security vulnerability on the web: script injection (*XSS*, *cross-site scripting*). The title and age do not require this protection: their values have been validated by the rules (one of three allowed values, an integer). In the next chapter, the [Blade] view engine will perform this escaping automatically for any value inserted into a page.

A valid entry, followed by an entry containing four errors:

The raw response to the second query, and the response for a name containing HTML:

curl "http://localhost:8000/personnes/action01?nom=m&age=abc&titre=Mx&email=xx"
curl "http://localhost:8000/personnes/action01?nom=%3Cb%3Emartin%3C/b%3E&age=42&titre=Mr"

<p>Le formulaire contient des erreurs :</p><ul><li>nom : 2 caractère(s) au moins</li><li>age : un nombre entier est attendu</li><li>titre : valeur inconnue</li><li>email : adresse électronique invalide</li></ul>
<p>Bienvenue Mr <b>martin</b> (42 ans)</p>

The name [<b>martin</b>] (encoded as [%3Cb%3E...] in URL) is displayed as-is, without being bolded: its tags have been neutralized. Note that the response this time is a 200 status code: this is the action that chose to return a normal page containing the errors.

docs.title: 3.4. Example 10: Multiple Parameters
docs.text:
The same parameter may appear multiple times in a URL: [?couleur=rouge&couleur=vert]. This is what a browser sends for a group of checkboxes with the same name, or a multi-select list (see the next chapter). [PHP] handles this case in its own way. The [TableauxController] controller:

<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/TableauxController.php: a parameter that appears multiple times in URL

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Validator;

class TableauxController
{
     // /tableaux/action01?color=red&color=green: for PHP, the second parameter
     // REMPLACE the first: only the DERNIÈRE value is retained
    public function action01(Request $request): array
    {
        return ['couleur' => $request->query('couleur'), 'brut' => $request->server('QUERY_STRING')];
    }

     // /tables/action02?color[]=red&color[]=green: the square brackets require
     // PHP to store TOUTES the values in an array
    public function action02(Request $request): array
    {
         // array: the parameter in the form of an array (empty if absent)
        $couleurs = $request->array('couleur');
        return ['couleur' => $couleurs, 'nombre' => count($couleurs)];
    }

     // /arrays/action03?color[]=red: an array, validated element by element
    public function action03(Request $request): array
    {
        $couleurs = $request->array('couleur');
        $validateur = Validator::make(['couleur' => $couleurs], [
             // a list with at least one element
            'couleur' => 'array|min:1',
             // each element (*): "red", "green", or "blue"
            'couleur.*' => 'in:rouge,vert,bleu',
        ]);
        $erreurs = [];
        foreach ($validateur->errors()->messages() as $champ => $messages) {
            $erreurs[] = "$champ : $messages[0]";
        }
        return ['couleurs' => $couleurs, 'valide' => ! $erreurs, 'erreurs' => $erreurs];
    }
}
  • line 15: for [PHP], the parameters of URL form an associative array, where each key has only one value: a repeated parameter replaces the previous one, and only the last value is retained. The action also returns, for comparison, the raw parameter string as sent by the browser: [$request->server(...)] reads the variables that the web server transmits to [PHP], including [QUERY_STRING];
  • lines 20–24: To retrieve all values, the parameter name must end with square brackets: [?couleur[]=rouge&couleur[]=vert]. [PHP] then stores the values in an array, and the value of the parameter [couleur]. The [array] method of the query returns the parameter as an array: empty if it is absent, with a single element if it has only one value without square brackets;
  • Lines 31–36: The array is validated against rules. [array|min:1]: an array with at least one element (the rule [min] applies to the number of elements in an array; see Example 08). The key [couleur.*] identifies each element of the array: each must be one of the three colors;
  • line 41: the operator [!] (not) evaluates to [true] for an empty array, which evaluates to “false” in a condition.

The file [lang/fr/validation.php] is the one from Example 09. The results:

curl "http://localhost:8000/tableaux/action01?couleur=rouge&couleur=vert"
curl -g "http://localhost:8000/tableaux/action02?couleur[]=rouge&couleur[]=vert"
curl http://localhost:8000/tables/action02

{
    "couleur": "vert",
    "brut": "couleur=rouge&couleur=vert"
}
{
    "couleur": [
        "rouge",
        "vert"
    ],
    "nombre": 2
}
{
    "couleur": [],
    "nombre": 0
}

The [-g] option in [curl] prevents it from interpreting the square brackets in URL on its own. A browser, on the other hand, encodes them ([couleur%5B%5D=rouge]), which [PHP] also understands. As for HTML, all you need to do is name the checkboxes in a group [couleur[]]: that’s what Example 18 will do. This rule applies specifically to [PHP]: frameworks for other languages ([Flask], [Spring MVC], [ASP.NET Core]) retain all values of a repeated parameter, without square brackets.

Validation: successful, then failed due to an unknown color, then due to an empty list:

curl -g "http://localhost:8000/tableaux/action03?couleur[]=rouge&couleur[]=bleu"
curl -g "http://localhost:8000/tableaux/action03?couleur[]=rouge&couleur[]=jaune"
curl http://localhost:8000/tables/action03

{
    "couleurs": [
        "rouge",
        "bleu"
    ],
    "valide": true,
    "erreurs": []
}
{
    "couleurs": [
        "rouge",
        "jaune"
    ],
    "valide": false,
    "erreurs": [
        "couleur.1 : valeur inconnue"
    ]
}
{
    "couleurs": [],
    "valide": false,
    "erreurs": [
        "couleur : 1 élément(s) au moins"
    ]
}

The error regarding the unknown color refers to [couleur.1]: the field and index of the problematic element in the array (the second one, with indices starting at 0).

docs.title: 3.5. Example 11: Parameters of a POST query
docs.text:
The previous examples used GET queries, whose parameters are contained in the URL. A POST query carries its data in its body, in two main forms:

  • fields from a HTML form: the body has the same syntax as a query string ([nom=martin&age=42]), and its type (header [Content-Type]) is [application/x-www-form-urlencoded];
  • a JSON document, sent by a program ([JavaScript] on a page, client of a API...): the type is [application/json].

The [PostController] controller:

<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/PostController.php: the parameters of a request POST

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Http\Requests\PersonneRequest;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Validator;
use JsonException;

class PostController
{
     // the fields of a form HTML (body application/x-www-form-urlencoded):
     // post() returns the request parameters from CORPS as an array
    public function action01(Request $request): array
    {
        return [
            'typeRecu' => $request->header('Content-Type'),
            'champs' => $request->post(),
        ];
    }

     // a JSON body: json() deserializes it; isJson() checks the declared type
    public function action02(Request $request): array
    {
        if (! $request->isJson()) {
            abort(415, 'le corps de la requête doit être du JSON');
        }
         // json_decode, with JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR: an invalid JSON raises an exception
        try {
            $corps = json_decode($request->getContent(), true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
        } catch (JsonException $e) {
            abort(400, 'JSON mal formé : '.$e->getMessage());
        }
        return ['typeRecu' => $request->header('Content-Type'), 'corps' => $corps,
            'nom' => $request->input('nom')];
    }

     // a single form field
    public function action03(Request $request): string
    {
        $nom = $request->input('nom');
        return "nom = [$nom]";
    }

     // form fields, validated by the rules of the PersonneRequest class
    public function action04(Request $request): array
    {
        $validateur = Validator::make($request->post(), (new PersonneRequest())->rules());
        $erreurs = [];
        foreach ($validateur->errors()->messages() as $champ => $messages) {
            $erreurs[] = "$champ : $messages[0]";
        }
        sort($erreurs);
        return ['personne' => $erreurs ? null : $validateur->validated(),
            'valide' => ! $erreurs, 'erreurs' => $erreurs];
    }
}
  • line 18: the [Content-Type] header of the request;
  • line 19: the method [post] returns the parameters from the request body in an associative array; [post('nom')] would return a single parameter. Form fields follow the rules in Example 10: a repeated field must have a name ending in [[]];
  • lines 26–27: [isJson()] checks the type declared by the [Content-Type] header. A body that is not declared as JSON is rejected with a 415 error (*Unsupported Media Type*);
  • lines 30–34: [getContent()] returns the raw body of the request, a string; the function [json_decode] from [PHP] deserializes it: the text JSON becomes a value [PHP] (the second parameter, [true], requires associative arrays for JSON objects). With the [JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR] option (a named parameter), malformed text raises a [JsonException] exception, which the [try] / [catch] intercepts to return a 400 error. The [json()] method of the request would do the same thing, but for a malformed JSON, it would simply return an empty result;
  • Line 36: The [input] method searches for a parameter everywhere: in the request body—whether it’s a form or JSON—and then in the URL. This is the method most commonly used, because it does not depend on the format of the request;
  • line 42: a form field, read by [input];
  • lines 49–56: the rules of the [PersonneRequest] class from Example 08, applied this time to the form fields. The code is the same as for the parameters of URL: only the data source changes. [sort] sorts the messages to ensure a consistent response. The ternary operator [condition ? a : b] returns [a] if the condition is true, and [b] otherwise.

The routing table declares routes POST, and [bootstrap/app.php] disables CSRF protection for these URL, as shown in Example 02:

<?php
// routes/web.php: the routes from Example 11

use App\Http\Controllers\PostController;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::prefix('post')->controller(PostController::class)->group(function () {
    Route::post('action01', 'action01');
    Route::post('action02', 'action02');
    Route::post('action03', 'action03');
    Route::post('action04', 'action04');
});

<?php
// bootstrap/app.php: the application from Example 11

use App\Http\Middleware\JsonLisible;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Middleware;

(require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php')->addPsr4('App\\', __DIR__.'/../app/');

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php')
    ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
        $middleware->append(JsonLisible::class);
         // The requests POST sent by curl would not pass the protection
         // anti-CSRF protection (Example 21)
        $middleware->preventRequestForgery(except: ['post/*']);
    })
    ->withExceptions()
    ->create();

With [curl], the [-d] (*data*) option sends a body; the request then becomes a POST request, of type [application/x-www-form-urlencoded], unless the option [-H] (*header*) specifies a different type. The option [-X POST] explicitly sets the method (it is optional here). The fields of a form, including a repeated field:

curl -i -g -X POST -d "nom=martin&age=42&loisir[]=tennis&loisir[]=piano" http://localhost:8000/post/action01

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "typeRecu": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
    "champs": {
        "nom": "martin",
        "age": "42",
        "loisir": [
            "tennis",
            "piano"
        ]
    }
}

A JSON body, which contains an integer and an array:

curl -i -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"nom\": \"martin\", \"age\": 42, \"enfants\": [\"léa\", \"tom\"]}" http://localhost:8000/post/action02

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "typeRecu": "application/json",
    "corps": {
        "nom": "martin",
        "age": 42,
        "enfants": [
            "léa",
            "tom"
        ]
    },
    "nom": "martin"
}

The quotation marks in JSON are preceded by [\] to prevent the command string from ending; In the case of [Linux] and [macOS], you can also enclose JSON in apostrophes: [-d '{"nom": "martin"}']. Unlike form fields, the JSON carries data types: age is already an integer. A body that is not JSON, followed by a malformed JSON (requesting a JSON response to view the message):

curl -i -H "Accept: application/json" -d "nom=martin" http://localhost:8000/post/action02
curl -i -H "Accept: application/json" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"nom\": " http://localhost:8000/post/action02

HTTP/1.1 415 Unsupported Media Type
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "message": "le corps de la requête doit être du JSON",
    ...
}
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "message": "JSON mal formé : Syntax error",
    ...
}

A single field, then the same URL requested as GET:

curl -d "nom=jean%20dupont" http://localhost:8000/post/action03
curl -i "http://localhost:8000/post/action03?nom=martin"

nom = [jean dupont]
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
allow: POST
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
...

URL exists, but not for the GET method: [Laravel] returns a 405 (*Method Not Allowed*), and its header [allow] lists the accepted methods. Finally, the rules applied to the form fields, which were first satisfied and then not:

curl -d "nom=martin&age=42&titre=Mr" http://localhost:8000/post/action04
curl -d "nom=m&age=200" http://localhost:8000/post/action04

{
    "personne": {
        "nom": "martin",
        "age": "42",
        "titre": "Mr"
    },
    "valide": true,
    "erreurs": []
}
{
    "personne": null,
    "valide": false,
    "erreurs": [
        "age : la valeur doit être comprise entre 0 et 150",
        "nom : 2 caractère(s) au moins",
        "titre : le champ est obligatoire"
    ]
}

docs.title: 3.6. Example 12: Custom Binding and Validation
docs.text:
Standard types and rules are not always sufficient. This example shows three ways to extend binding and validation:

  • a type bound to a route parameter: a date in French format, [23-09-2026], in the path of URL;
  • middleware that provides the action with a parameter that does not come from the URL, but from a HTTP header;
  • a custom validation rule (no spaces), and the conversion of a date [jj/mm/aaaa].
12-liaison-perso/
├── app/
│   ├── Http/
│   │   ├── Controllers/
│   │   │   └── ExemplesController.php
│   │   └── Requests/
│   │       └── RechercheRequest.php
│   └── Liaison/
│       ├── DetecterLangue.php
│       ├── JourFr.php
│       └── SansEspace.php
├── lang/
│   └── fr/
│       └── validation.php
└── ...

docs.title: 3.6.1. A type linked to a route parameter: app/Liaison/JourFr.php
docs.text:
We saw in Example 02 that a route parameter is passed to the action as a string, or as an integer if the action’s parameter is of type [int]. [Laravel] can also convert a route parameter into an object if the action requires a parameter whose class implements the [UrlRoutable] interface. This is the route binding (*route model binding*), which [Laravel] primarily uses for database entities (an identifier in URL becomes the corresponding object; see Chapter 9). We use it here for a date.

<?php
// app/Liaison/JourFr.php: a French date "23-09-2026" in the path of URL

namespace App\Liaison;

use Carbon\CarbonImmutable;
use Illuminate\Contracts\Routing\UrlRoutable;

// a type that knows how to LIER to a route parameter (resolveRouteBinding) and
// to revert to a segment of URL (getRouteKey): the UrlRoutable interface
class JourFr implements UrlRoutable
{
    public function __construct(public ?CarbonImmutable $date = null)
    {
    }

     // path text -> JourFr object; null: the value is invalid (error 404)
    public function resolveRouteBinding($valeur, $champ = null): ?static
    {
         // the "!" in "!d-m-Y" sets the time to zero (otherwise, it would be the current time)
        $date = CarbonImmutable::createFromFormat('!d-m-Y', $valeur);
         // createFromFormat accepts "31-02-2026" (and actually converts it to March 3): we verify
         // that the formatted date correctly reflects the received text
        if ($date === null || $date->format('d-m-Y') !== $valeur) {
            return null;
        }
        return new static($date);
    }

     // subject JourFr -> path text (used by the route function)
    public function getRouteKey(): string
    {
        return $this->date->format('d-m-Y');
    }

    public function getRouteKeyName(): string
    {
        return 'jour';
    }

    public function resolveChildRouteBinding($typeEnfant, $valeur, $champ): ?static
    {
        return null;
    }
}
  • line 11: the class implements the [UrlRoutable] interface, whose four methods are as follows;
  • line 13: the date, a [CarbonImmutable] object. [Carbon] is the date library for [Laravel]; It extends the [DateTime] class from [PHP] with hundreds of methods. The [Immutable] version creates a new object with each modification ([$date->addDay()] returns a new date), rather than modifying the existing object. The constructor has a default value, [null]: [Laravel] must be able to create an empty [JourFr] object, whose [resolveRouteBinding] method it will then call;
  • Lines 18–27: [resolveRouteBinding] converts the path text into an object: it returns the linked object, or [null] if the value is invalid. [CarbonImmutable::createFromFormat] parses a string according to a format: [d] for the day, [m] for the month, and [Y] for the four-digit year; the initial [!] sets the hour to zero. [createFromFormat] is tolerant: it accepts [31-02-2026] and interprets it as March 3. The validation on line 24 rejects this case: the date, after reformatting, must exactly match the received text. [new static(...)] creates an object of the current class. When the method returns [null], [Laravel] responds with a 404 error: URL does not refer to anything;
  • lines 31–34: the inverse operation, used by the [route] function to construct a URL from a [JourFr] object. [format] formats a date;
  • lines 36–41: The last two methods of the interface, which are used for database entities, have no role here.

docs.title: 3.6.2. A parameter provided by middleware: app/Liaison/DetecterLangue.php
docs.text:
An action [Laravel] receives as parameters the route parameters and the objects that the container can provide (the request, the services). To provide it with additional information, calculated from the request, we can have it calculated by a middleware (example 03), which includes it in the request before the action:

<?php
// app/Liaison/DetecterLangue.php: a middleware component that CALCULE provides information for the action

namespace App\Liaison;

use Closure;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

class DetecterLangue
{
    public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next): Response
    {
         // the "Accept-Language: fr-FR,fr;q=0.9,en;q=0.8" header -> "fr": the browser's
         // the browser’s preferred language from among those offered (the first one by default)
        $langue = $request->getPreferredLanguage(['fr', 'en']);
         // the ATTRIBUTS fields in the request: information that the application stores there
         // for the functions that will process the request afterward
        $request->attributes->set('langue', $langue);
        return $next($request);
    }
}
  • Line 16: The request header [Accept-Language] specifies the user’s languages, in order of preference: [fr-FR,fr;q=0.9,en;q=0.8] (the coefficient [q] measures the preference, on a scale from 0 to 1). [getPreferredLanguage] selects, from among the languages offered by the application, the one the user prefers; if no header is provided, it is the first one on the list;
  • line 19: the request has attributes—an array of information that the application stores there for the functions that will process the request afterward. The language is stored there under the name [langue];
  • Line 20: The request continues on to the action.

The action will receive this information via an attribute named [PHP] placed before its parameter (see the controller).

docs.title: 3.6.3. A "custom" rule and a conversion: SansEspace.php and RechercheRequest.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Liaison/SansEspace.php: a "custom" validation rule

namespace App\Liaison;

use Closure;
use Illuminate\Contracts\Validation\ValidationRule;

class SansEspace implements ValidationRule
{
     // the value is invalid: $echec is called with the error message
    public function validate(string $attribut, mixed $valeur, Closure $echec): void
    {
        if (str_contains((string) $valeur, ' ')) {
            $echec("le champ ne doit pas contenir d'espace");
        }
    }
}
  • Line 9: A "custom" validation rule is a class that implements the [ValidationRule] interface;
  • Lines 12–17: Its method [validate] takes the field name, its value, and a function, [$echec], which it calls with the error message if the value is invalid. [str_contains] checks for the presence of text in a string; [(string)] converts the value to a string. The type [mixed] refers to any type.

The rule is used by the search form query:

<?php
// app/Http/Requests/RechercheRequest.php: the search template

namespace App\Http\Requests;

use App\Liaison\SansEspace;
use Carbon\CarbonImmutable;
use Illuminate\Contracts\Validation\Validator;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Http\FormRequest;
use Illuminate\Http\Exceptions\HttpResponseException;

class RechercheRequest extends FormRequest
{
    public function rules(): array
    {
        return [
             // a "custom" rule: an object in a list of rules
            'motCle' => ['nullable', new SansEspace()],
             // date_format: a date in dd/mm/yyyy format
            'depuis' => 'nullable|date_format:d/m/Y',
        ];
    }

     // the date, CONVERTIE as a date object (null if absent)
    public function depuis(): ?CarbonImmutable
    {
        return $this->date('depuis', 'd/m/Y')?->toImmutable();
    }

     // the response to a failed validation, for class CETTE only: the message
     // the first error, in plain text, with code 400
    protected function failedValidation(Validator $validateur): never
    {
        throw new HttpResponseException(response($validateur->errors()->first(), 400,
            ['Content-Type' => 'text/plain; charset=utf-8']));
    }
}
  • line 18: A field’s rules can be specified in an array rather than as a string; this is essential for a “custom” rule, which is an object;
  • line 20: the rule [date_format:d/m/Y] verifies that the value is a date in the specified format and that this date exists;
  • Lines 25–28: Date conversion: The [date] method of a query reads a parameter and converts it to a date ([Carbon]) according to the specified format; it returns [null] if the parameter is missing. The operator [?->] calls a method if the object is not [null], and returns [null] otherwise; [toImmutable] converts the date to [CarbonImmutable];
  • lines 32–36: the method [failedValidation], inherited from [FormRequest], is called when validation fails; the method in [FormRequest] throws the exception [ValidationException] (example 08). We redefine it, for this class only: it throws a [HttpResponseException], an exception that carries a predefined response, which [Laravel] sends as-is. The response contains the first error message ([first()]), in plain text, with status code 400. This is a way to handle validation errors for an action differently from those in the rest of the application.

The message for rule [date_format] is localized into French by the file [lang/fr/validation.php]:

<?php
// lang/fr/validation.php: validation error messages in French
return [
     // :input: the received value
    'date_format' => "[:input] n'est pas une date jj/mm/aaaa valide",
];
  • Line 5: The tag [:input] is replaced by the received value. The text contains an apostrophe; it is enclosed in quotation marks.

docs.title: 3.6.4. The controller: app/Http/Controllers/ExemplesController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/ExemplesController.php: custom binding and validation

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Http\Requests\RechercheRequest;
use App\Liaison\JourFr;
use Illuminate\Container\Attributes\RequestAttribute;

class ExemplesController
{
     // /examples/calendar/23-09-2026: the route parameter {day} is bound to an object
     // JourFr, because the action requires a parameter of this type
    public function agenda(JourFr $jour): string
    {
         // route() uses the method getRouteKey from JourFr: object -> "23-09-2026"
        return "agenda du jour [{$jour->date->toDateString()}], de type "
            .get_debug_type($jour->date).', URL : '.route('agenda', $jour, false);
    }

     // /examples/hello: a parameter that does not come from URL, but from a header,
     // calculated by the DetecterLangue middleware and stored in the request attributes
    public function bonjour(#[RequestAttribute('langue')] string $langue): string
    {
        return $langue === 'en' ? 'Hello!' : 'Bonjour !';
    }

     // /examples/search?motCle=laravel&since=01/09/2026
    public function recherche(RechercheRequest $request): string
    {
        $motCle = $request->validated('motCle');
        $depuis = $request->depuis()?->toDateString();
        return "recherche de [$motCle] depuis le [$depuis]";
    }
}
  • Lines 14–18: The parameter [$jour] is of type [JourFr]: [Laravel] binds the route parameter [{jour}] to an object [JourFr] using its method [resolveRouteBinding]. [toDateString()] writes the date in international format ([2026-09-23]). The function [route] constructs the URL for this same action from the object, using its method [getRouteKey]; its third parameter, [false], requests a relative URL (without the protocol or the machine);
  • Lines 23–25: The parameter [$langue] is preceded by an attribute [PHP], written as [#[...]]: information attached to the code, which [PHP] ignores but which the libraries read (the equivalent of the annotations in [Java]). The [RequestAttribute('langue')] attribute instructs the container to provide, for this parameter, the [langue] attribute of the request, calculated by the [DetecterLangue] middleware;
  • Lines 29–33: The action receives the form request, which has already been validated (Example 08). [validated('motCle')] returns a single validated field; [depuis()] returns the converted date.

The routing table:

<?php
// routes/web.php: the routes from Example 12

use App\Http\Controllers\ExemplesController;
use App\Liaison\DetecterLangue;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::prefix('exemples')->controller(ExemplesController::class)->group(function () {
     // where: only a path fragment in the form dd-mm-yyyy is provided to JourFr
    Route::get('agenda/{jour}', 'agenda')->name('agenda')
        ->where('jour', '[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4}');
     // middleware: DetecterLangue runs before the action
    Route::get('bonjour', 'bonjour')->middleware(DetecterLangue::class);
    Route::get('recherche', 'recherche');
});
  • lines 10–11: the calendar route is named (for function [route]), and its parameter is constrained by a regular expression: [[0-9]] denotes a single digit, [{2}] denotes the repetition of the preceding pattern: two digits, a hyphen, two digits, a hyphen, four digits. A path segment with a different format does not match the route (404), without even consulting [JourFr];
  • line 13: the method [middleware] associates a middleware with a route: it runs only for that route, before the action. We’ll see this process throughout the course: middlewares that require a logged-in user, in the chapter on authentication, are associated with routes in the same way.

docs.title: 3.6.5. Execution
docs.text:
The type associated with the route parameter:

curl "http://localhost:8000/exemples/agenda/23-09-2026"
curl -i "http://localhost:8000/exemples/agenda/31-02-2026"

agenda du jour [2026-09-23], de type Carbon\CarbonImmutable, URL : /exemples/agenda/23-09-2026
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
...

The date is displayed in international format, but the URL constructed by [route] has reverted to the French format. February 31 does not exist: 404. A date in international format, [2026-09-23], does not match the pattern described by the regular expression: 404 as well.

The middleware. The [-H] option of [curl] sets the header [Accept-Language]:

curl -H "Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9,fr;q=0.8" http://localhost:8000/examples/hello
curl -H "Accept-Language: fr-FR,fr;q=0.9" http://localhost:8000/examples/hello
curl http://localhost:8000/examples/hello

Hello!
Bonjour !
Bonjour !

Without the [Accept-Language] header ([curl] does not send one), it is the first language in the list. The chapter on internationalization will revisit this issue, with the user selecting the language.

The “house” rule and date conversion:

curl "http://localhost:8000/exemples/recherche?motCle=laravel&depuis=01/09/2026"
curl "http://localhost:8000/exemples/recherche"
curl -i "http://localhost:8000/exemples/recherche?motCle=laravel%20mvc"
curl "http://localhost:8000/exemples/recherche?depuis=2026-09-01"
curl "http://localhost:8000/exemples/recherche?depuis=31/02/2026"

recherche de [laravel] depuis le [2026-09-01]
recherche de [] depuis le []
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

le champ ne doit pas contenir d'espace
[2026-09-01] n'est pas une date jj/mm/aaaa valide
[31/02/2026] n'est pas une date jj/mm/aaaa valide

docs.title: 3.6.6. Conclusion
docs.text:
Let’s summarize the methods available to an action for obtaining its template:

Route parametersthe action’s parameters, which share the same name; converted by their type ([int $id]), constrained by [whereNumber], [where]...; bound to an object by [UrlRoutable]Parameters of URL[$request->query(...)], [integer], [array], [date]...; a repeated parameter is written as [nom[]]Fields in a POST form[$request->post(...)], or [$request->input(...)], which searches everywhereBody JSON[$request->input(...)], [$request->json()], or [json_decode($request->getContent())]Headers[$request->header(...)], and methods that parse them, such as [getPreferredLanguage]Validationof rules: a [FormRequest] (validation before the action) or [Validator::make] (validation by the action); "custom" rules ([ValidationRule])Messagesthe files [lang/xx/validation.php] and the language file [APP_LOCALE]Common errors[$exceptions->render(...)] in [bootstrap/app.php] (entire application), [failedValidation] (a form request)Calculated parameterA middleware component that stores information in the request attributes, [#[RequestAttribute]]

The HTML forms, on the other hand, require more than just validation: they must be displayed, re-displayed with the user’s input and any errors, and protected against forged requests. This is the subject of the next chapter, once views have been introduced.

docs.title: 7. The Lifecycle of a Request
docs.text:
Between the arrival of a request and the dispatch of its response, [Laravel] goes through several stages, and the application can intervene at each one. We’ve already encountered several of these: middleware (examples 03, 12, 16, 22), route parameter binding (example 12), and exception handlers (examples 08 and 12). This chapter brings them together in a single example, which displays a message in the console at each step so you can observe their order:

  • 1 and 7. Global middleware, executed for all requests, even before routing. A middleware component wraps the rest of the processing: it sees the request pass through before it and the response after it (example 03). [Laravel] installs several by default (empty strings become [null], maintenance mode, requests become CORS...), in the order of the global middleware list;
  • Routing. [Laravel] searches for the route that matches the URL and the method. If none match, a [NotFoundHttpException] exception is thrown (404);
  • The group and route middlewares, in order: first those of the [web] group (cookies, session, form errors, anti-CSRF protection, parameter binding), then those of the route. One of them, [SubstituteBindings], binds the route parameters (2, example 12). The route middleware (3 and 4) is the right place for checks specific to certain actions: this is how the [auth] middleware in the next chapter works. If one of them returns a response without calling [$next] (or throws an exception), processing stops there: the action is not called;
  • 5. The action, and the view it generates;
  • 6. The end of the middleware chain, in reverse order: each component receives the response from [$next], can modify it (add a header or a cookie), and must return it;
  • 8. The [terminate] methods of the middleware components that have one, executed after the response is sent to the browser. They can no longer modify the response: they are used for processing tasks that can wait (writing a log, sending statistics, etc.), without making the user wait;
  • x. Exception handlers: An exception thrown by a middleware component, an action, or a view is passed to the handler ([render], in [bootstrap/app.php]) registered for its class, which constructs an error response. This response is then passed back up through the middleware components, just like a regular response.

This is equivalent to the filters in [Java] and the interceptors in [Spring MVC], the action filters in [ASP.NET Core MVC], and the functions [before_request] / [after_request] from [Flask]. The distinctive feature of [Laravel] is that almost everything in it is middleware: the same concept is used to process all requests (global middleware), a family of routes (groups), or a few routes.

docs.title: 7.1. Example 24: The steps in processing a request
docs.text:
24-cycle-de-vie/
├── app/
│   └── Http/
│       ├── Controllers/
│       │   └── CalculController.php
│       └── Middleware/
│           ├── Bloquer.php
│           ├── Chrono.php
│           └── Journal.php
├── bootstrap/
│   └── app.php
├── resources/
│   └── views/
│       ├── calcul/
│       │   └── resultat.blade.php
│       ├── erreur.blade.php
│       └── layout.blade.php
├── routes/
│   └── web.php
└── ...

The application has only one action, which calculates the square of an integer: [/carre/7]. Depending on URL, it either succeeds or fails in various ways. Messages are written to the server console by the [error_log] function of [PHP], which is displayed by the [php artisan serve] command.

docs.title: 7.1.1. The global middleware: app/Http/Middleware/Journal.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Middleware/Journal.php: a GLOBAL middleware, the first of them all: it
// intercepts every request AVANT as it passes through the rest of the application, and the response APRÈS

namespace App\Http\Middleware;

use Closure;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

class Journal
{
    public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next): Response
    {
         // error_log: a message in the development server console
        error_log('--- '.$request->method().' '.$request->getRequestUri());
        error_log('1. middleware global Journal (avant)');
         // the rest of the process: the other middleware components, routing, the action, the view
        $reponse = $next($request);
        error_log('7. middleware global Journal (après : code '.$reponse->getStatusCode().')');
        return $reponse;
    }
}
  • lines 16–17: the middleware displays the request ([getRequestUri()]: the path and parameters). This is message #1: nothing has happened yet in [Laravel], not even routing;
  • line 19: the rest of the processing takes place within this call;
  • line 20: message #7, once everything else has been completed. [getStatusCode()] is the response code.

A global middleware does not know the chosen route, since routing has not yet taken place. It is used for processing that applies to all requests: logging, compression, and handling a proxy (the [TrustProxies] middleware from [Laravel] corrects the client’s address when the application is located behind a proxy server; the case study discusses this in relation to the clients’ IP address).

docs.title: 7.1.2. The parameter mapping: routes/web.php
docs.text:
<?php
// routes/web.php: the routes from Example 24

use App\Http\Controllers\CalculController;
use App\Http\Middleware\Bloquer;
use App\Http\Middleware\Chrono;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

// a parameter LIAISON: any route parameter named {integer} is transformed
// by this function before being applied: an integer, or null if it is
// an integer (in which case the action decides)
Route::bind('entier', function (string $valeur) {
    error_log("2. liaison du paramètre (valeur reçue : \"$valeur\")");
    $n = filter_var($valeur, FILTER_VALIDATE_INT);
    return $n === false ? null : $n;
});

// the route: two route middlewares, executed in this order, before the action
Route::get('carre/{entier}', [CalculController::class, 'carre'])->name('carre')
    ->middleware([Bloquer::class, Chrono::class]);
  • lines 12–16: [Route::bind] registers an explicit binding: any route parameter named [{entier}] passes through this function, which receives the text from URL and returns the value that the action will receive. It accepts any text and converts it to an integer, or to [null] if it is not one: unlike [whereNumber] (Example 02), which would return a 404 page for [/carre/abc], here it is the action that will decide. It displays message #2. This is the other form of the route binding from Example 12, which bound a parameter to a class ([UrlRoutable]);
  • Lines 19–20: The route, named [carre], has two route middlewares, which will execute in that order, after those in the [web] group.

docs.title: 7.1.3. The route middlewares: Bloquer.php and Chrono.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Middleware/Bloquer.php: a middleware module from ROUTE, executed only for
// routes that request it
