namespace App\Http\Middleware;

use Closure;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

class Bloquer
{
    public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next): Response
    {
         // $request->route(): the route selected by the routing process; getName(): its name
        error_log('3. middleware Bloquer (route : '.$request->route()->getName().')');
        if ($request->has('bloquer')) {
             // an exception: the subsequent step (Chrono, the action) is not executed
            abort(403);
        }
        return $next($request);
    }
}
  • Line 16: Message No. 3. A route middleware knows the selected route: [$request->route()] returns the route, and [getName()] returns its name;
  • Lines 17–19: The parameter [?bloquer] of URL ([has] checks for its presence) causes a 403 error (*Forbidden*, access denied): [abort] throws an exception, which interrupts processing.
<?php
// app/Http/Middleware/Chrono.php: a route middleware that triggers AVANT and APRÈS
// the action, then one last time APRÈS sending the response (terminate)

namespace App\Http\Middleware;

use Closure;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

class Chrono
{
    public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next): Response
    {
        error_log('4. middleware Chrono (avant)');
         // the start time (hrtime: a precise clock, in nanoseconds), stored
         // in the request attributes (request scope, see Example 12)
        $request->attributes->set('debut', hrtime(true));
        $reponse = $next($request);
        error_log('6. middleware Chrono (après : code '.$reponse->getStatusCode().')');
        return $reponse;
    }

     // terminate: called at the very end, APRÈS sending the response to the browser;
     // it can no longer modify the response
    public function terminate(Request $request, Response $reponse): void
    {
        $debut = $request->attributes->get('debut');
         // the measurement has not started if the request was blocked before this middleware
        if ($debut !== null) {
            $ms = round((hrtime(true) - $debut) / 1e6);
            error_log("8. terminate Chrono (fin, $ms ms)");
        }
    }
}
  • lines 15–18: message #4, and the start time, stored in the request attributes (example 12). [hrtime(true)] is a precise clock, in nanoseconds, designed to measure durations;
  • Line 20: Message No. 6, after the action, with the response code;
  • Lines 26–34: the [terminate] method, called by [Laravel] after the response is sent, with the request and response: message #8, with the time elapsed since message #4. [Laravel] calls it for all middleware components in the route, even if they have not been executed (when a previous middleware component interrupted processing): the check on line 30 verifies that the measurement has started.

docs.title: 7.1.4. Error handling: bootstrap/app.php
docs.text:
<?php
// bootstrap/app.php: the application from Example 24

use App\Http\Middleware\Journal;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Exceptions;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Middleware;
use Symfony\Component\HttpKernel\Exception\HttpExceptionInterface;

(require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php')->addPsr4('App\\', __DIR__.'/../app/');

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(
        web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php',
         // the route used by Bootstrap (see Example 15)
        then: fn () => require __DIR__.'/../../commun/bootstrap.php')
    ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
         // prepend: the global Journal middleware passes AVANT all others
        $middleware->prepend(Journal::class);
    })
    ->withExceptions(function (Exceptions $exceptions): void {
         // an “unexpected” exception of a given type: DomainException and its subclasses
        $exceptions->render(function (DomainException $e) {
            error_log("x. render DomainException ({$e->getMessage()})");
             // instead of the default error page, our view [erreur], with status code 500
            return response()->view('erreur', ['code' => 500], 500);
        });
         // errors HTTP (abort(400), abort(403), unknown page -> 404...):
         // HttpExceptionInterface is the interface for all HTTP exceptions
        $exceptions->render(function (HttpExceptionInterface $e) {
            error_log("x. render HttpException (code {$e->getStatusCode()})");
            return response()->view('erreur', ['code' => $e->getStatusCode()], $e->getStatusCode());
        });
    })
    ->create();
  • line 19: [prepend] places the global middleware at the top of the list: it runs before all others and sees the response after all others;
  • Lines 23–27: An exception handler for the [DomainException] class (and its subclasses; see Example 08): an “unexpected” error is converted into a custom error page with status code 500 (*Internal Server Error*). The exception message is displayed in the console, but not on the page: it may contain internal details that are not relevant to the user;
  • lines 30–33: a handler for all HTTP errors. [abort(400)], [abort(403)], a URL for a missing route (404), a forbidden method (405): all of them throw an exception that implements the [HttpExceptionInterface] interface from [Symfony], and which contains its code ([getStatusCode()]). This single handler therefore replaces all English-language error pages from [Laravel] with ours.

[Laravel] passes an exception to the first handler whose parameter type matches it. An exception that has no handler becomes a 500 error: in debug mode, this is the detailed page (example 03); without debug mode, it is the standard 500 error page. There is another, even simpler way to replace error pages: a view named [resources/views/errors/404.blade.php] replaces the 404 error page, and the same applies to every error code (Example 26 uses this approach). The [render] handlers, on the other hand, allow for any type of handling: a log message, a JSON response, a redirect...

docs.title: 7.1.5. The controller and the error page
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/CalculController.php: an action protected by two middleware components

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use DomainException;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class CalculController
{
     // $n: the route parameter {integer}, bound via Route::bind (see routes/web.php);
     // a parameter bound to null is not passed to the action: hence the default value
    public function carre(?int $n = null): View
    {
        error_log("5. action carre($n)");
        if ($n === null) {
            abort(400);    // a 400 error: see bootstrap/app.php
        }
        if ($n === 13) {
            throw new DomainException('13 porte malheur');    // an “unexpected” error
        }
        return view('calcul.resultat', ['n' => $n, 'carre' => $n * $n]);
    }
}
  • Line 13: The parameter [$n] receives the value bound by [Route::bind]. [Laravel] does not pass a parameter bound to [null] to the action: the action’s parameter therefore has a default value, [null], which will be its value in this case;
  • line 17: a parameter that is not an integer: error 400;
  • line 20: the number 13 causes an “unexpected” error. [DomainException] is an exception class from the standard library of [PHP];
  • line 22: the normal case.
@extends('layout')
{{-- la page d'erreur ; son modèle : le code d'erreur --}}

@section('contenu')
  <div class="alert alert-danger">
    <h1 class="h4">Erreur {{ $code }}</h1>
    <p class="mb-0">
      @switch($code)
        @case(400) Requête incorrecte. @break
        @case(403) Accès refusé. @break
        @case(404) Page introuvable. @break
        @default Erreur interne du serveur.
      @endswitch
    </p>
  </div>
@endsection

The error page receives the error code and displays an appropriate message. The [@switch] directive selects a block based on a value: [@case] specifies a value, [@break] ends the block, and [@default] handles the other values. The view [calcul/resultat.blade.php] simply displays the result.

docs.title: 7.1.6. Execution
docs.text:
The normal case, [/carre/7]:

The server console displays the eight steps, in order:

  --- GET /carre/7
  1. middleware global Journal (avant)
  2. liaison du paramètre (valeur reçue : "7")
  3. middleware Bloquer (route : carre)
  4. middleware Chrono (avant)
  5. action carre(7)
  6. middleware Chrono (après : code 200)
  7. middleware global Journal (après : code 200)
  8. terminate Chrono (fin, 5 ms)
  2026-09-26 18:19:51 /carre/7 ..................................... ~ 0.35ms

The last line is the development server log, written once the request is complete. A blocked access, [/carre/7?bloquer]:

  --- GET /carre/7?bloquer
  1. middleware global Journal (avant)
  2. liaison du paramètre (valeur reçue : "7")
  3. middleware Bloquer (route : carre)
  x. render HttpException (code 403)
  7. middleware global Journal (après : code 403)

The first route middleware threw an exception: the second middleware and the action were not executed. The error response, generated by the handler, is passed up to the global middleware. [terminate] was called but did not display anything, as the measurement did not start. A parameter that is not an integer, [/carre/abc]:

  --- GET /carre/abc
  1. middleware global Journal (avant)
  2. liaison du paramètre (valeur reçue : "abc")
  3. middleware Bloquer (route : carre)
  4. middleware Chrono (avant)
  5. action carre()
  x. render HttpException (code 400)
  6. middleware Chrono (après : code 400)
  7. middleware global Journal (après : code 400)
  8. terminate Chrono (fin, 6 ms)

This time, the action was called with [null] (which is rendered as an empty string: [carre()]), and it was this action that raised the 400 error. An “unexpected” error, [/carre/13]:

  --- GET /carre/13
  1. middleware global Journal (avant)
  2. liaison du paramètre (valeur reçue : "13")
  3. middleware Bloquer (route : carre)
  4. middleware Chrono (avant)
  5. action carre(13)
  x. render DomainException (13 porte malheur)
  6. middleware Chrono (après : code 500)
  7. middleware global Journal (après : code 500)
  8. terminate Chrono (fin, 3 ms)

The exception was handled by its handler: the user sees the "custom" error page, not the detailed page, even though debug mode is enabled. The exception is still logged in the [storage/logs/laravel.log] log: [Laravel] distinguishes between an exception report (*report*, its entry in the log) and its rendering (*render*, the response). Finally, a URL that does not correspond to any route, [/inconnu]:

  --- GET /inconnu
  1. middleware global Journal (avant)
  x. render HttpException (code 404)
  7. middleware global Journal (après : code 404)

Routing failed: no connection, no route middleware, no action. The 404 page is ours:

curl http://localhost:8000/unknown

...
        <div class="alert alert-danger">
    <h1 class="h4">Erreur 404</h1>
    <p class="mb-0">
       Page introuvable.     </p>
  </div>
...

Let’s focus on the essentials. Route middleware is the right place for checks common to many actions (is the user logged in? Do they have permission to access this action?): the next chapter uses it for authentication. Exception handlers and views ([errors/...]) ensure that the user never sees a technical page, regardless of the error: the case study takes advantage of this.

docs.title: 4. The View and Its Model
docs.text:
Up to this point, actions have generated their own responses: text, JSON, and a few HTML tags written as a string of characters. In a MVC application, this is the role of a view: a file that describes the page HTML, with placeholders for the data passed to it by the action—the view’s model.

[Laravel] comes with its own view engine, [Blade]. A [Blade] view is a file whose name ends with [.blade.php], stored in the application’s [resources/views] folder. It is a text file—in this case, HTML—in which three types of tags are interpreted on the server:

  • [{{ expression }}]: the value of a [PHP] expression, inserted into the page;
  • [@instruction]: a directive: condition ([@if]), loop ([@foreach]), template inheritance ([@extends], [@section]), inclusion ([@include])... A directive begins with [@], followed by its name;
  • [{{-- commentaire --}}]: a comment, which does not appear on the generated page.

Everything else is copied as-is. Expressions are written in [PHP]: there is no second language to learn. [Blade] thus resembles [Razor], the view engine of [ASP.NET Core MVC], which also mixes HTML and code, and which also uses the character [@]; it differs from [Thymeleaf] ([Spring MVC]), whose views are valid HTML files enriched with [th:] attributes. A [Blade] view is not executed as-is: upon its first use, [Blade] compiles it into a standard [PHP] file, stored in [storage/framework/views], which it then reuses as long as the view remains unchanged. We’ll see what this file looks like.

docs.title: 4.1. Example 13: A First View
docs.text:
13-premiere-vue/
├── app/
│   ├── Http/
│   │   └── Controllers/
│   │       └── VuesController.php
│   └── Models/
│       └── PageModele.php
├── resources/
│   └── views/
│       └── vues/
│           ├── inconnu.blade.php
│           └── index.blade.php
├── routes/
│   └── web.php
└── ...

docs.title: 4.1.1. The view template: app/Models/PageModele.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Models/PageModele.php: the view model, the data that the action passes to the view

namespace App\Models;

readonly class PageModele
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $titre,
        public string $message,
        public string $heure,
    ) {
    }
}

The view model is a simple immutable class (see Example 03): the three pieces of information that the view will display. There’s no requirement to define a view’s model as a class: you could pass three separate variables to the view. However, a class documents what the view expects and allows the editor to verify the action’s code. This is the approach the case study will follow, where each view has its own model class.

docs.title: 4.1.2. The controller: app/Http/Controllers/VuesController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/VuesController.php: actions that return a VUE

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Models\PageModele;
use Illuminate\Http\Response;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class VuesController
{
     // view: the Blade engine renders the page from the view
     // resources/views/views/index.blade.php and variables passed into the
     // array (in this case, a single one: [modele]); the generated page is the response to the action
    public function index(): View
    {
        $modele = new PageModele(
            'Ma première vue',
            'Cette page a été fabriquée par Blade, sur le serveur.',
            date('H:i:s'));
        return view('vues.index', ['modele' => $modele]);
    }

     // the same view with a different template; or another view, with a 404 error
    public function bonjour(string $nom): View|Response
    {
        if ($nom === 'inconnu') {
             // the page, sent with a 404 error
            return response()->view('vues.inconnu', ['nom' => $nom], 404);
        }
        $modele = new PageModele(
            "Bonjour $nom",
            "Cette fois, le titre de la page vient de l'URL.",
            date('H:i:s'));
        return view('vues.index', ['modele' => $modele]);
    }
}
  • Lines 17–20: The action builds the view model. The function ***[date] from *[PHP] formats the current time: [H] for the hours, [i] for the minutes, and [s]** for the seconds;
  • Line 21: The function [view] causes [Blade] to generate the page. The first parameter is the view name: the file path, relative to the [resources/views] folder, where the [/]s are replaced by dots, and without the [.blade.php] extension: [vues.index] refers to the file [resources/views/vues/index.blade.php]. The second parameter is an associative array, where each key becomes a variable in the view—in this case, a single one: [$modele]. [view] returns an object [View], which [Laravel] transforms into a response (of type [text/html]) by generating the page;
  • Line 29: another view, with a different variable ([$nom]). [response()->view(...)] generates a response from a view, using the specified code—in this case, 404—to display a custom error page. The action type [View|Response] means: either a [View] or a [Response];
  • lines 31–35: the same view as the [index] action, but with a different template. This is the benefit of separating actions from views: a single view can be used by multiple actions.

docs.title: 4.1.3. The view: resources/views/vues/index.blade.php
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  {{-- {{ ... }} : la valeur d'une expression, insérée dans la page --}}
  <title>{{ $modele->titre }}</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>{{ $modele->titre }}</h1>
  <p>{{ $modele->message }}</p>
  <p>Page fabriquée à {{ $modele->heure }}.</p>
</body>
</html>
  • line 5: a comment [Blade];
  • line 6: [{{ $modele->titre }}] inserts the value of the [titre] property of the [$modele] variable. Between the curly braces, you can write any [PHP] expression.

Everything inserted by [{{ }}] is escaped: the characters [<], [>], [&], ["], and ['] are replaced by their entities HTML. This is the role that the [e] function played in Example 09, but this time it is automatic: a view therefore cannot inadvertently insert the HTML provided by a user into the page.

docs.title: 4.1.4. The view: resources/views/vues/inconnu.blade.php
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Inconnu</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Personne ne s'appelle [{{ $nom }}] ici.</h1>
</body>
</html>

A view is not required to receive an object: the variable [$nom] is a string.

docs.title: 4.1.5. Execution
docs.text:
The displayed time is in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), with the default time zone set to [Laravel]; the case study will show how to change this. The raw output shows the processing done by [Blade]: the [{{ }}] tags have been replaced with their values, and the comment has been removed (a blank line remains in its place).

curl -i http://localhost:8000/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">

  <title>Ma première vue</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Ma première vue</h1>
  <p>Cette page a été fabriquée par Blade, sur le serveur.</p>
  <p>Page fabriquée à 16:04:07.</p>
</body>
</html>

The “home” error page, followed by a name containing HTML ([<b>martin], encoded in URL):

curl -i http://localhost:8000/hello/unknown
curl http://localhost:8000/hello/%3Cb%3Emartin

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Inconnu</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Personne ne s'appelle [inconnu] ici.</h1>
</body>
</html>
...
  <title>Bonjour <b>martin</title>
...
  <h1>Bonjour <b>martin</h1>
...

The [<b>] tag was escaped, even though neither the action nor the view had anything to do with it. Here, finally, is the view compiled by [Blade], as found in the [storage/framework/views] folder (under a calculated name, such as [bfadc851307fb914e48325630a6c9191.php]):

<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">

  <title><?php echo e($modele->titre); ?></title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1><?php echo e($modele->titre); ?></h1>
  <p><?php echo e($modele->message); ?></p>
  <p>Page fabriquée à <?php echo e($modele->heure); ?>.</p>
</body>
</html>
<?php /**PATH .../13-first-view/resources/views/views/index.blade.php ENDPATH**/ ?>

Each [{{ expression }}] has become [<?php echo e(expression); ?>]: the conversion is performed by the [e] function from Example 09. A [Blade] view is therefore just a more elegant way of writing a [PHP] file that generates HTML. [PHP] was originally designed as a page language, where the code is inserted into the HTML file between [<?php] and [?>]; [Blade] retains its efficiency and corrects its flaws (notably the missing escape sequence).

docs.title: 4.2. Example 14: The Blade Language
docs.text: This example brings together the main constructs of [Blade] in a single view.

docs.title: 4.2.1. The Model and the Action
docs.text:
The view’s model is described by three immutable classes, each in its own file ([PHP] does not require one class per file, but the class loader in [Composer] does look for the class [App\Models\Produit] in the file [app/Models/Produit.php]):

<?php
// app/Models/Produit.php: a product

namespace App\Models;

readonly class Produit
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $nom,
        public float $prix,
        public bool $enStock,
    ) {
    }
}

<?php
// app/Models/Adresse.php: an address

namespace App\Models;

readonly class Adresse
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $rue,
        public string $ville,
    ) {
    }
}

<?php
// app/Models/BasesModele.php: the view model for Example 14

namespace App\Models;

readonly class BasesModele
{
    /**
     * @param list<Produit> $produits
     * @param list<Produit> $panier
     */
    public function __construct(
        public string $titre,
        public string $nom,
        public ?string $surnom,
        public string $html,
        public bool $connecte,
        public string $devise,
        public array $produits,
        public array $panier,
        public Adresse $adresse,
    ) {
    }
}

The model contains values of various types: strings, [null], Booleans, arrays of objects, empty arrays, and objects containing other objects. The prices here are of type [float], to simplify calculations in the view (Example 06 showed why an exact decimal is preferred).

<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/BasesController.php: a view that uses the main Blade constructs

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Models\Adresse;
use App\Models\BasesModele;
use App\Models\Produit;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class BasesController
{
    public function index(): View
    {
        $modele = new BasesModele(
            titre: 'Les bases de Blade',
            nom: 'Martin',
            surnom: null,
            html: '<b>ceci est du HTML</b>',
            connecte: true,
            devise: '€',
            produits: [
                new Produit('Clavier', 25, true),
                new Produit('Souris', 12.5, false),
                new Produit('Écran', 149, true),
            ],
            panier: [],
            adresse: new Adresse('12 rue des Lilas', 'Angers'));
        return view('bases.index', ['modele' => $modele]);
    }
}

The action constructs the model using named parameters (see Example 01): each value is preceded by the name of the parameter it is intended for, which makes the call readable despite the number of parameters.

docs.title: 4.2.2. The view: resources/views/bases/index.blade.php
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>{{ $modele->titre }}</title>
</head>
<body>
  {{-- du code PHP dans la vue, entre les deux instructions qui suivent ; ici, deux variables --}}
  @php
    $total = collect($modele->produits)->sum('prix');
    $nombre = count($modele->produits);
  @endphp
  <h1>{{ $modele->titre }}</h1>
  {{-- 1. afficher une valeur du modèle ; null s'affiche comme une chaîne vide ;
       l'opérateur ?? remplace une valeur null. Ce commentaire Blade n'apparaît
       pas dans la page produite --}}
  <p>1. Nom : {{ $modele->nom }} - surnom : [{{ $modele->surnom }}] [{{ $modele->surnom ?? 'aucun' }}]</p>
  {{-- 2. {{ }} échappe le HTML ; {!! !!} l'insère tel quel --}}
  <p>2a. {{ $modele->html }}</p>
  <p>2b. {!! $modele->html !!}</p>
  {{-- 3. une condition --}}
  @if ($modele->connecte)
    <p>3. Vous êtes connecté.</p>
  @else
    <p>3. Vous n'êtes pas connecté.</p>
  @endif
  {{-- 4. une boucle : $loop décrit l'état de la boucle --}}
  <p>4. Nos produits :</p>
  <ul>
    @foreach ($modele->produits as $produit)
      <li>n° {{ $loop->index }} : {{ $produit->nom }}, {{ $produit->prix }} {{ $modele->devise }}
        {{ $produit->enStock ? '(en stock)' : '(épuisé)' }}
        @if ($loop->first) - le premier @endif
        @if ($loop->last) - le dernier, vu par {{ $modele->nom }} @endif
      </li>
    @endforeach
  </ul>
  {{-- 5. la liste vide : @forelse ... @empty --}}
  <p>5. Votre panier :
    @forelse ($modele->panier as $p)<span>{{ $p->nom }}</span>@empty il est vide. @endforelse
  </p>
  {{-- 6. des expressions calculées, les variables de @php, et number_format --}}
  <p>6. {{ $nombre }} produits, pour un total de {{ $total }} {{ $modele->devise }} ;
    prix moyen : {{ number_format($total / $nombre, 2, ',', ' ') }} {{ $modele->devise }}</p>
  {{-- 7. un objet dans un objet, et une fonction PHP (mb_strtoupper) --}}
  <p>7. Adresse : {{ $modele->adresse->rue }}, {{ mb_strtoupper($modele->adresse->ville) }}</p>
  {{-- 8. @ n'est une instruction Blade qu'en début de mot ; @@ écrit un @ --}}
  <p>8. Une adresse électronique : contact@exemple.fr ; une instruction affichée : @@if</p>
</body>
</html>
  • Lines 9–12: The directives [@php] and [@endphp] delimit a block of code [PHP], which is executed at this point in the page. Two view variables are created there: the total price, calculated by the [sum] method of a collection (example 03), which sums a property of each element, and the number of products. The [@php] block should be reserved for this type of preparation: the calculation normally belongs to the action;
  • line 17: a [null] value is displayed as an empty string. The [??] operator in [PHP] (Example 08) replaces a [null] value with a default value;
  • Lines 19–20: [{{ }}] escapes HTML (2a); [{!! !!}], on the other hand, inserts the value as-is, without escaping it (2b). [{!! !!}] is reserved for HTML generated by the application itself, never for user input;
  • lines 22–26: a condition: [@if], [@elseif], [@else], [@endif], with a [PHP] condition in parentheses. Each block is closed by a [@end...] directive;
  • lines 30–36: a loop [@foreach] ... [@endforeach], which is written as the loop [foreach] of [PHP]. Within it, the special variable [$loop] describes the state of the loop: [$loop->index] (the iteration number, starting at 0), [$loop->iteration] (starting at 1), [$loop->first], [$loop->last] (true on the first and last iterations), [$loop->count] (the number of elements). Variables outside the loop ([$modele->nom]) remain accessible;
  • Line 32: the ternary operator for [PHP], [condition ? a : b] (Example 11);
  • line 40: the directive [@forelse] ... [@empty] ... [@endforelse] is a loop in which the block [@empty] is executed if the list is empty. This is simpler than a [@if] that would test the length of the list;
  • lines 43–44: calculated expressions ([$total / $nombre]) and the variables from the [@php] block. The function [number_format] from [PHP] formats a number: two decimal places, a comma as the decimal separator, and a space as the thousands separator. In Example 16, we’ll see a much better way to format numbers and amounts;
  • Line 46: The [->] operator iterates through the objects ([$modele->adresse->ville]), and any [PHP] function can be called: [mb_strtoupper] capitalizes a string (the [mb_...] functions, for *multi-byte*, correctly handle accented characters encoded in UTF-8);
  • line 48: the character [@] is interpreted by [Blade] only at the beginning of a word; in an email address, it is copied as-is. To write a [@] followed by a directive name, it is doubled: [@@if] produces [@if]. Similarly, [@{{ ... }}] produces [{{ ... }}], which is useful when a page contains curly braces intended for a framework [JavaScript].

A note on comments: [Blade] processes [@php] blocks before comments. A comment containing the word [@php] would therefore be interpreted as the start of a code block, with unexpected results: this is why the comment on line 8 does not include it.

docs.title: 4.3. Example 15: Templates, Fragments, Static Files
docs.text:
The pages of a website usually share the same structure: a header, a navigation bar, a footer, and the same style sheets. Rather than repeating this structure in every view, it is written once in a template (*layout*), which the pages extend. This example also uses [Bootstrap], the most widely used CSS framework, for the layout.

15-gabarit/
├── app/
│   ├── Http/
│   │   └── Controllers/
│   │       └── PagesController.php
│   └── Models/
│       └── Membre.php
├── bootstrap/
│   └── app.php
├── public/
│   └── css/
│       └── styles.css
├── resources/
│   └── views/
│       ├── components/
│       │   └── carte.blade.php
│       ├── fragments/
│       │   └── navbar.blade.php
│       ├── layout.blade.php
│       └── pages/
│           ├── accueil.blade.php
│           ├── brute.blade.php
│           └── equipe.blade.php
├── routes/
│   └── web.php
└── ...

docs.title: 4.3.1. Static Files
docs.text:
A HTML page references other files: style sheets, [JavaScript] scripts, and images. These files, which the server sends as-is, are called static files. With [Laravel], they are stored in the [public] folder, which the web server serves as-is (example 01): The file [public/css/styles.css] is available at URL [/css/styles.css], without [Laravel] being involved.

/* a few additional Bootstrap settings */
body {
  background-color: #f5f7fa;
}

/* the template's footer */
.pied {
  margin-top: 2rem;
  font-size: 0.85rem;
  color: #6c757d;
}

/* error messages at the bottom of the page on a light pink background */
.zone-erreur {
  margin-top: 1.5rem;
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
  background-color: #fdecef;
  border: 1px solid #f5c2c7;
  border-radius: 0.375rem;
  color: #842029;
}

A few additional CSS rules in addition to [Bootstrap]: a light gray background, the footer style, and the style for an error area that will be used in the following examples.

[Bootstrap] is used in examples 15 through 28. Rather than placing a copy in each user’s [public] folder, the examples share it: it is located in the [exemples/commun/bootstrap] folder. This folder is not served by the web server: a route, common to all these examples, serves its files. It is described by the file [exemples/commun/bootstrap.php]:

<?php
// common/bootstrap.php: a path that serves Bootstrap files, shared by
// examples 15 through 28 (the examples/common/bootstrap folder), under URL /bootstrap/...

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::get('bootstrap/{fichier}', function (string $fichier) {
    $dossier = realpath(__DIR__.'/bootstrap');
     // realpath: the absolute path of the requested file, without the . and ..; false
     // if the file does not exist
    $chemin = realpath($dossier.'/'.$fichier);
     // a file that exists, and whose directory is DANS (no ../ to exit it)
    abort_unless($chemin && str_starts_with($chemin, $dossier.DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR)
        && is_file($chemin), 404);
     // the file type, based on its extension
    $types = ['css' => 'text/css', 'js' => 'text/javascript', 'map' => 'application/json'];
    $type = $types[pathinfo($chemin, PATHINFO_EXTENSION)] ?? 'application/octet-stream';
    return response()->file($chemin, ['Content-Type' => $type]);
})->where('fichier', '.*')->name('bootstrap');
  • line 7: a route whose action is an anonymous function (example 01). The route parameter [{fichier}] accepts any path ending, including slashes (constraint [.*], line 19, see example 02): the URL [/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css] refers to the file [css/bootstrap.min.css] in the folder. The path is named [bootstrap];
  • lines 8–14: Serving files designated by URL requires a precaution: a URL such as [/bootstrap/../../15-gabarit/.env] must not grant access to a file located outside the folder. The [realpath] function of [PHP] calculates the absolute path of a file, stripped of its [.] and [..] components, or returns [false] if the file does not exist. We verify that the resulting path does indeed start with the folder path ([str_starts_with]) and that it refers to a file ([is_file]); otherwise, [abort_unless] terminates the request with a 404 error. [abort_unless(condition, code)] is equivalent to [if (! condition) abort(code)]; similarly, [abort_if] also exists. [DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR] is the system path separator: [\] under [Windows], [/] elsewhere;
  • lines 16–18: [response()->file] generates a response that sends the contents of a file. The content type is chosen based on the file extension (provided by [pathinfo]), so that a stylesheet is correctly declared as [text/css]: a browser will reject a stylesheet declared as something else.

The route is declared by the [bootstrap/app.php] file in each example:

<?php
// bootstrap/app.php: the application from Example 15

use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\View;

(require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php')->addPsr4('App\\', __DIR__.'/../app/');

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(
        web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php',
         // then: routes declared outside the web group (without sessions or cookies):
         // the one serving Bootstrap, common to Examples 15 through 28
        then: fn () => require __DIR__.'/../../commun/bootstrap.php')
    ->withMiddleware()
    ->withExceptions()
     // booted: code executed once the application has started
    ->booted(function () {
         // a "view composer": executed before the view is rendered (*),
         // it adds its variables to all views
        View::composer('*', function ($vue) {
            $vue->with(['chemin' => request()->path(), 'annee' => date('Y')]);
        });
    })
    ->create();
  • lines 11–14: the [then] parameter of [withRouting] is a function, called after the routes in [routes/web.php] have been declared, to declare additional routes. These are not part of the [web] group: they have neither a session nor cookies, which is suitable for static files. The arrowed function executes the file [commun/bootstrap.php];
  • lines 18–24: the [booted] method registers a function that is executed once the application starts;
  • lines 21–23: the [View] facade registers a view composer: a function that [Laravel] executes before rendering each view whose name matches the given pattern, in this case [*] (all of them). It receives the view and can add variables to it ([with]). Here, [$chemin] (the path to the requested URL, provided by [request()], the current request) and [$annee] (the current year) are thus available in all views, without the actions having to provide them. The template uses them for its footer. The method [View::share('nom', valeur)] would similarly share a fixed value with all views.

docs.title: 4.3.2. The template: resources/views/layout.blade.php
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
{{-- le gabarit des pages : les pages l'ÉTENDENT, et remplissent ses sections --}}
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  {{-- @yield : un emplacement que la page peut remplir ; ici avec un contenu par défaut --}}
  <title>@yield('titre', 'Accueil') - Mon site</title>
  {{-- route() : l'URL de la route nommée [bootstrap] ; asset() : l'URL d'un fichier de public/ --}}
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ route('bootstrap', 'css/bootstrap.min.css') }}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ asset('css/styles.css') }}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3">
    {{-- insertion du fichier fragments/navbar.blade.php --}}
    @include('fragments.navbar')
    <main>
      {{-- le contenu de la page demandée par l'action est inséré ici --}}
      @yield('contenu')
    </main>
    {{-- $chemin, $annee : ajoutés à toutes les vues (cf. bootstrap/app.php) --}}
    <footer class="pied">Page [{{ $chemin }}] - © {{ $annee }}</footer>
  </div>
</body>
</html>
  • line 6: the [viewport] tag instructs mobile browsers to display the page at the screen’s width, which is what [Bootstrap] expects;
  • Line 8: The directive [@yield] marks a named slot—which pages that extend the template can fill—with a section of the same name. The second parameter is the default content for the slot, used by a page that does not provide the section;
  • Lines 10–11: [route('bootstrap', 'css/bootstrap.min.css')] generates the URL for the named route [bootstrap] (Example 04), using the value of its parameter [{fichier}]. The function [asset] creates URL from a file in the [public] folder. Writing the URL file manually ([/css/styles.css]) would also work, but [asset] works if the application is installed under a URL prefix;
  • line 16: [@include] inserts the content of another view, in this case the navigation bar. The included view has access to the variables of the view that includes it;
  • line 19: the area that each page fills with its own content;
  • line 22: the footer uses the two variables from the view composer.

The class [container] of [Bootstrap] centers the content and limits its width; [py-3] adds vertical padding: [Bootstrap] provides hundreds of classes like this, which are combined in the [class] attribute.

docs.title: 4.3.3. The navigation bar: resources/views/fragments/navbar.blade.php
docs.text:
{{-- un fragment : un morceau de page, inséré par @include --}}
<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <span class="navbar-brand">Mon site</span>
  <div class="navbar-nav">
    <a class="nav-link" href="/">Accueil</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="/equipe">Équipe</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="/brute">Page sans gabarit</a>
  </div>
</nav>

A fragment: a piece of a page that has no meaning on its own. The classes [navbar], [navbar-brand], and [nav-link] are those of the navigation bar in [Bootstrap].

docs.title: 4.3.4. A component: resources/views/components/carte.blade.php
docs.text:
{{-- un COMPOSANT : un morceau de page qui a des paramètres, comme une fonction --}}
@props(['nom', 'fonction'])
<div class="card">
  <div class="card-body">
    <h5 class="card-title">{{ $nom }}</h5>
    <p class="card-text">{{ $fonction }}</p>
  </div>
</div>
  • Line 2: A component is a section of a page that has parameters; this is the function of [Blade]. An anonymous component is a simple view from the [resources/views/components] folder; the [@props] directive declares its parameters, which become variables of the view. It is used as a HTML tag whose name begins with [x-]: [<x-carte nom="..." fonction="..." />] inserts the page fragment generated with these values. Parameters can have a default value: [@props(['nom', 'fonction' => ''])]. The map ([card]) is a component of [Bootstrap].

docs.title: 4.3.5. The pages
docs.text:
{{-- cette page ÉTEND le gabarit : elle ne fournit que le contenu de ses sections --}}
@extends('layout')

@section('contenu')
  <h1>Bienvenue</h1>
  <p>Cette page ne contient que son propre contenu : l'entête, la barre de
    navigation et le pied de page viennent du gabarit <code>layout.blade.php</code>.</p>
  {{-- le composant [carte], avec deux paramètres écrits sur place --}}
  <x-carte nom="Un composant" fonction="appelé avec des paramètres écrits sur place" />
@endsection
  • line 2: the page extends the template: [Blade] generates the template page, replacing its [@yield] placeholders with the sections defined by the page. In a view that extends a template, text written outside the sections does not appear in the generated page;
  • Lines 4–10: The section [contenu], which fills the placeholder of the same name. The page does not define the section [titre]: the placeholder retains its default content, “Home”;
  • line 9: the use of the [carte] component. The parameters are written as HTML attributes; their values are strings.
@extends('layout')

@section('titre', 'Notre équipe')

@section('contenu')
  <h1>Notre équipe</h1>
  <div class="row g-3">
    @foreach ($membres as $membre)
      <div class="col-md-4">
        {{-- :nom="..." : la valeur du paramètre est une EXPRESSION PHP --}}
        <x-carte :nom="$membre->nom" :fonction="$membre->fonction" />
      </div>
    @endforeach
  </div>
@endsection
  • line 3: a short section, whose content is provided as the second parameter;
  • lines 8–13: one card per team member, in a grid of [Bootstrap] ([row], [col-md-4]: three columns on a medium or large screen, one column on a narrow screen);
  • line 11: a parameter whose name is preceded by [:] is assigned the value of an expression [PHP], not a string: [:nom="$membre->nom"].

The controller does not introduce any new features:

<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/PagesController.php: three pages

The path to the home page is [/]; the paths to other pages are written without a leading slash ([equipe]): this is the convention for [request()->path()]. You can verify that the style sheets are being applied correctly (the [-I] option of [curl] displays only the response headers):

curl -I http://localhost:8000/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css

docs.title: 4.4. Example 16: Helpers
docs.text:
A view often needs to format values: an amount with its currency, a date written out in full, or text in uppercase. This code doesn’t belong in the action (which doesn’t handle presentation), and would be cumbersome to write in the view. Instead, it is written in [PHP], in functions that the views call: these are the view’s helpers. [Blade] offers several ways to make them available: calling a function or a static method, writing your own directives ([@monnaie($prix)]), and using components, which we’ve already encountered.

16-helpers/
├── app/
│   ├── Aides/
│   │   └── Formats.php
│   ├── Http/
│   │   ├── Controllers/
│   │   │   └── PagesController.php
│   │   └── Middleware/
│   │       └── FixerLangue.php
│   └── Models/
│       └── Produit.php
├── resources/
│   └── views/
│       ├── components/
│       │   ├── badge.blade.php
│       │   └── lien.blade.php
│       ├── fragments/
│       │   └── navbar.blade.php
│       ├── layout.blade.php
│       └── pages/
│           ├── accueil.blade.php
│           └── produits.blade.php
└── ...

docs.title: 4.4.1. Functions: app/Helpers/Formats.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Helpers/Formats.php: Functions called by views

namespace App\Aides;

use Brick\Math\BigDecimal;
use Carbon\CarbonInterface;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\App;
use Illuminate\Support\Number;

class Formats
{
     // "keyboard" -> "CLAVIER"
    public static function majuscules(?string $texte): string
    {
        return $texte === null ? '' : mb_strtoupper($texte);
    }

     // an amount in a currency, formatted according to the request language (see the
     // FixerLangue middleware): 1149.9 -> "1 149,90 €" in French, "€1,149.90" in
     // English. The intl extension of PHP recognizes the conventions for each country
    public static function monnaie(BigDecimal $montant, string $devise = 'EUR'): string
    {
        return Number::currency($montant->toFloat(), in: $devise, locale: App::getLocale());
    }

     // a date written out in full, in the language of the request: "Saturday, September 26, 2026"
    public static function dateLongue(CarbonInterface $jour): string
    {
        return $jour->locale(App::getLocale())->isoFormat('dddd D MMMM YYYY');
    }
}
  • Lines 14–17: a static method ([static]): it is called on the class, without an object ([Formats::majuscules('clavier')]). It accepts [null];
  • lines 22–24: formatting an amount. This depends on the language: in French, [1 149,90 €] (space to separate thousands, decimal comma, symbol after the amount); in English, [€1,149.90]. The class [Number] of [Laravel] is based on the extension [intl] of [PHP], which supports the conventions of all countries (it uses data from the Unicode project *CLDR*): [Number::currency] formats an amount, with the currency designated by its international code ([EUR], [USD]). [intl] can only format numbers [float]: the decimal is converted ([toFloat()]), which is safe here since the number is no longer used for calculations. The language ([fr], [en]) is that of the application for the current query, returned by [App::getLocale()]; we’ll see who sets it;
  • Lines 28–30: Formatting a date [Carbon] (Example 12). [locale(...)] returns a copy of the date set for a specific language; [isoFormat] formats it as follows: [dddd] spells out the day of the week, [D] the day of the month, [MMMM] spells out the month, and [YYYY] the year. [Carbon] comes with translations of these names in over two hundred languages. The [CarbonInterface] type accepts all [Carbon] dates.

docs.title: 4.4.2. The language of each request: app/Http/Middleware/FixerLangue.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Middleware/FixerLangue.php: the formatting language for each request

namespace App\Http\Middleware;

use Closure;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\App;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;

class FixerLangue
{
     // the ?lang=en parameter from URL; otherwise, French
    public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next): Response
    {
        App::setLocale($request->query('lang') === 'en' ? 'en' : 'fr');
        return $next($request);
    }
}

The formatting language depends on the request: the [?lang=en] parameter of URL selects English; French is the default language. A middleware component (example 03) sets it before each action, via [App::setLocale]: the facade [App] refers to the application itself. The language set in this way applies only to the current request: the next request will revert to the language of [.env] ([APP_LOCALE], with English as the default). The chapter on internationalization will use this same language to translate the texts.

docs.title: 4.4.3. Configuration: bootstrap/app.php
docs.text:
<?php
// bootstrap/app.php: the application from Example 16

use App\Http\Middleware\FixerLangue;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Application;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Middleware;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Blade;

(require __DIR__.'/../../vendor/autoload.php')->addPsr4('App\\', __DIR__.'/../app/');

return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    ->withRouting(
        web: __DIR__.'/../routes/web.php',
         // then: routes declared outside the web group (without sessions or cookies):
         // the one serving Bootstrap, common to Examples 15 through 28
        then: fn () => require __DIR__.'/../../commun/bootstrap.php')
    ->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
         // the language of each request (see app/Http/Middleware/FixerLangue.php)
        $middleware->web(append: FixerLangue::class);
    })
    ->withExceptions()
    ->booted(function () {
         // from the "internal" DIRECTIVES: @monnaie($prix), @dateLongue($jour). A directive
         // receives TEXTE as its parameter and returns the code PHP, which will replace it
        Blade::directive('monnaie', fn (string $expression) =>
            "<?php echo e(\\App\\Aides\\Formats::monnaie($expression)); ?>");
        Blade::directive('dateLongue', fn (string $expression) =>
            "<?php echo e(\\App\\Aides\\Formats::dateLongue($expression)); ?>");
    })
    ->create();
  • Line 19: The middleware is added to the end of the [web] group: it runs for all routes in [routes/web.php], after the middleware in the group (session, cookies, etc.). Example 03 used [append], which adds a global middleware that runs for all requests, including those from routes outside the [web] group;
  • Lines 25–28: The [Blade] facade registers two “custom” directives: [@monnaie(...)] and [@dateLongue(...)]. A directive is processed when the view is compiled (Example 13): its function receives the text written between the parentheses (for example, [$produit->prix, 'USD']) and returns the code [PHP], which will replace the directive in the compiled view. Here, a call is made to the corresponding method of ***[Formats]***, whose result is escaped ([e]***) and written ([echo]***). In a string enclosed in quotes, [\\] refers to a single [\];
  • the directives are stored in a function [booted] (Example 15) once the application has started: the facade [Blade] is only usable at that point.

Because they generate compiled code, directives require a precaution: after modifying a directive, you must clear the compiled views (command [php artisan view:clear]) so that the views are recompiled with the new version.

docs.title: 4.4.4. The controller: app/Http/Controllers/PagesController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/PagesController.php: two pages

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Models\Produit;
use Brick\Math\BigDecimal;
use Carbon\CarbonImmutable;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class PagesController
{
    public function accueil(): View
    {
        return view('pages.accueil', ['aujourdhui' => CarbonImmutable::today()]);
    }

    public function produits(): View
    {
        return view('pages.produits', ['produits' => [
            new Produit('clavier', BigDecimal::of('25'), 12),
            new Produit('souris', BigDecimal::of('12.5'), 0),
            new Produit('écran', BigDecimal::of('1149.9'), 3),
        ]]);
    }
}

Actions pass raw values to the views: a date ([CarbonImmutable::today()], today’s date at midnight) and decimal numbers. Formatting is handled by the views. The [Produit] class combines a name, a price (a [BigDecimal], see Example 06), and a stock level. The routes are named [accueil] and [produits].

docs.title: 4.4.5. The views
docs.text:
{{-- un composant : un lien de la barre de navigation, qui reçoit la classe
     [active] si la page courante est sous le chemin [chemin]. request() : la
     requête en cours, disponible dans toutes les vues ; $slot : le contenu placé
     entre les balises du composant --}}
@props(['href', 'chemin'])
<a @class(['nav-link', 'active' => request()->is($chemin)]) href="{{ $href }}">{{ $slot }}</a>
  • line 5: a component that creates a link in the navigation bar. The link for the current page is assigned the class [active] from [Bootstrap], which highlights it;
  • Line 6: The directive [@class] generates the attribute [class] for a tag from an array: a class written on its own (['nav-link']) is always present; a class written as a key (['active' => condition]) is present only if the condition is true. The function [request()] returns the current query; its method [is] compares the path of URL to a pattern, where [*] matches any sequence of characters. The variable [$slot] contains the content between the component’s opening and closing tags ([<x-lien ...>Produits</x-lien>]).
<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <span class="navbar-brand">Helpers</span>
  <div class="navbar-nav">
    {{-- 1. une condition écrite dans la vue --}}
    <a class="nav-link{{ request()->is('/') ? ' active' : '' }}" href="/">Accueil</a>
    {{-- 2. le composant [lien] --}}
    <x-lien href="/produits" chemin="produits*">Produits</x-lien>
    {{-- 3. route() fabrique l'URL d'une route nommée ; un paramètre qui n'est pas un
         paramètre de la route s'ajoute à la fin de l'URL : /produits?lang=en --}}
    <a class="nav-link" href="{{ route('produits', ['lang' => 'en']) }}">Products (en)</a>
  </div>
</nav>
  • line 5: the same thing, written directly in the view, without a component, using the ternary operator. [request()->is('/')] only recognizes the home page. The component avoids repeating the condition for each link;
  • line 7: using the component;
  • line 10: a parameter from [route] that is not a route parameter is added to URL as a parameter: [/produits?lang=en].
{{-- un badge Bootstrap : vert si le produit est en stock, rouge sinon --}}
@props(['stock'])
<span @class(['badge', 'text-bg-success' => $stock > 0, 'text-bg-danger' => $stock <= 0])>{{ $stock > 0 ? "$stock en stock" : 'épuisé' }}</span>
  • Line 3: A badge from [Bootstrap], green ([text-bg-success]) or red ([text-bg-danger]) depending on inventory, using [@class]. The text on the badge is selected by the ternary operator; ["$stock en stock"] is an interpolated string.
@extends('layout')
@section('titre', 'Accueil')

@section('contenu')
  <h1>Accueil</h1>
  {{-- la directive "maison" @dateLongue --}}
  <p>Nous sommes le @dateLongue($aujourdhui).</p>
  {{-- app()->getLocale() : la langue de la requête, fixée par le middleware FixerLangue --}}
  <p>Langue de formatage : {{ app()->getLocale() }}
    (<a href="/?lang=en">en anglais</a>, <a href="/">en français</a>)</p>
@endsection
  • line 7: the call to the “home” directive;
  • line 9: the function [app()] returns the application, and [getLocale()] sets its language for the current request.
@extends('layout')
{{-- @use : l'équivalent, dans une vue, de l'instruction use de PHP --}}
@use('App\Aides\Formats')
@section('titre', 'Produits')

@section('contenu')
  <h1>Produits</h1>
  <table class="table table-sm w-auto">
    <thead><tr><th>Produit</th><th>Prix</th><th>Prix en dollars</th><th>Stock</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      @foreach ($produits as $produit)
        <tr>
          {{-- une méthode statique, puis une directive, sans puis avec paramètre --}}
          <td>{{ Formats::majuscules($produit->nom) }}</td>
          <td>@monnaie($produit->prix)</td>
          <td>@monnaie($produit->prix, 'USD')</td>
          {{-- le composant [badge] fabrique le HTML du badge --}}
          <td><x-badge :stock="$produit->stock" /></td>
        </tr>
      @endforeach
    </tbody>
  </table>
@endsection
  • line 3: the [@use] directive imports a class into the view, just like the [use] statement from a [PHP] file;
  • line 14: a call to a static method, which acts as a function;
  • Lines 15–16: the [@monnaie] directive, first with its default currency, then with a parameter;
  • line 18: the use of the [badge] component.

The [layout.blade.php] template is a simplified version of the one in Example 15.

docs.title: 4.5. Example 17: A GET form
docs.text:
A HTML form sends its fields to the server in one of two ways, depending on its [method] attribute:

  • [method="get"]: The fields are added to the URL as parameters ([/recherche?motCle=le&genre=roman]). This is the method used by a form that performs a query: a search or a filter. The URL containing the results can be bookmarked, shared, or reloaded safely;
  • [method="post"]: The fields are included in the request body (see Example 11). This is the method used by a form that modifies data: a registration, an addition, or a deletion.

This first form is a book search.

docs.title: 4.5.1. The model: app/Models/Livre.php and RechercheModele.php
docs.text:

readonly class RechercheModele
{
    /**
     * @param list<string> $genres
     * @param list<Livre> $resultats

docs.title: 4.5.2. The controller: app/Http/Controllers/LivresController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/LivresController.php: a search form, submitted by GET

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Models\Livre;
use App\Models\RechercheModele;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class LivresController
{
     // from the CONSTANTES class: the data, written in the code for the example
    private const GENRES = ['roman', 'poésie', 'théâtre'];

     /** @return list<Book> */
    private static function livres(): array
    {
        return [
            new Livre('Le Rouge et le Noir', 'Stendhal', 'roman'),
            new Livre('Les Fleurs du mal', 'Baudelaire', 'poésie'),
            new Livre('Madame Bovary', 'Flaubert', 'roman'),
            new Livre('Alcools', 'Apollinaire', 'poésie'),
            new Livre('Le Cid', 'Corneille', 'théâtre'),
        ];
    }

     // GET / and GET /search?motCle=...&genre=... : the ET form and its results
    public function recherche(Request $request): View
    {
         // string: the parameter, as a string ('' if absent)
        $motCle = $request->string('motCle')->value();
        $genre = $request->string('genre')->value();
        $mot = mb_strtolower($motCle);
        $resultats = array_values(array_filter(self::livres(), fn (Livre $livre) =>
            ($mot === '' || str_contains(mb_strtolower($livre->titre), $mot)
                || str_contains(mb_strtolower($livre->auteur), $mot))
            && ($genre === '' || $livre->genre === $genre)));
        return view('livres.recherche', [
            'modele' => new RechercheModele($motCle, $genre, self::GENRES, $resultats),
        ]);
    }
}
  • Line 14: a private class constant named [self::GENRES] ([self] refers to the current class). A constant cannot contain objects: therefore, the books are provided by a static method (lines 17–25). In a real-world application, they would come from a database;
  • lines 32–33: the form fields are read as parameters of URL (example 07). The [string] method returns the parameter as a [Stringable] object of type [Laravel] (a string enriched with methods), which is empty if the parameter is missing; [value()] extracts the string [PHP] from it;
  • Lines 35–38: filtering. The function [array_filter] retains the elements of an array for which the given function returns [true]: a book is retained if the keyword is empty or appears in its title or author (in lowercase on both sides), and if the genre is empty or matches its own. [array_filter] retains the keys of the selected elements (0, 2...): [array_values] renumbers them starting from 0;
  • lines 39–41: the view template.

The routing table associates two URL entries with the same action: on the first visit ([/]), there are no parameters, and all books are displayed.

<?php
// routes/web.php: the routes from Example 17

use App\Http\Controllers\LivresController;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

// two routes for the same action
Route::get('/', [LivresController::class, 'recherche']);
Route::get('recherche', [LivresController::class, 'recherche']);

docs.text:
@extends('layout')

@section('contenu')

  {{-- method="get" : les champs sont envoyés dans l'URL (?motCle=...&genre=...) --}}
  <form method="get" action="/recherche" class="row g-2 align-items-end mb-3">
    <div class="col-auto">
      <label class="form-label" for="motCle">Titre ou auteur</label>
      {{-- value : le champ réaffiche ce qui a été saisi (échappé par {{ }}) --}}
      <input class="form-control" id="motCle" name="motCle" value="{{ $modele->motCle }}">
    </div>
    <div class="col-auto">
      <label class="form-label" for="genre">Genre</label>
      <select class="form-select" id="genre" name="genre">
        <option value="">(tous)</option>
        @foreach ($modele->genres as $genre)
          {{-- @selected : l'attribut booléen selected, écrit si la condition est vraie, omis sinon --}}
          <option value="{{ $genre }}" @selected($genre === $modele->genre)>{{ $genre }}</option>
        @endforeach
      </select>
    </div>
    <div class="col-auto">
      <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Rechercher</button>
    </div>
  </form>
  <p>{{ count($modele->resultats) }} livre(s) trouvé(s).</p>
  <ul>
    @foreach ($modele->resultats as $livre)
      <li><i>{{ $livre->titre }}</i>, {{ $livre->auteur }} ({{ $livre->genre }})</li>
    @endforeach
  </ul>
@endsection
  • Line 6: the [<form>] tag. The [action] attribute is the URL to which the form is submitted; [method="get"] places the fields within the URL. The classes of [Bootstrap] arrange the fields on a single line;
  • Line 8: a label. Its [for] attribute specifies the identifier ([id]) of the field it describes: clicking the label places the cursor in the field, and screen readers read the label along with the field;
  • line 10: an input field. Its attribute [name] is the name of the parameter sent to the server: this is the link between the form and the action ([$request->string('motCle')]). The attribute [value] is the displayed value: the previous entry, redisplayed (and escaped by [{{ }}], which is essential in an attribute: an entry containing a quotation mark ["] would otherwise close the attribute);
  • lines 14–20: a drop-down list. Each [<option>] has a value ([value]), sent to the server, and text, displayed. The first option, with an empty value, means “all genres”;
  • line 18: the option selected in the previous request is assigned the attribute [selected]. This is a Boolean attribute: its presence alone is sufficient; it has no value. The directive [@selected(condition)] sets it if the condition is true, and sets nothing otherwise. Similarly, there are [@checked], [@disabled], [@readonly], and [@required];
  • line 23: the submit button;
  • line 26: the number of results.

      </ul>
...

“Madame Bovary” is not selected: “le” does not appear in either the title or the author’s name.

docs.title: 4.6. Example 18: Form fields
docs.text: This example presents all the field types in a HTML form, which is sent in this instance by POST. It demonstrates how to redisplay each field type along with its current value, how the browser sends the values for each field, and how the server verifies that a received value is indeed one of the available options. [Laravel] does not have a library that defines forms using classes (as in [WTForms] and [Python]): the fields are written in HTML within the view, and the directives in [Blade] ([@checked], [@selected]...) help to render them.

docs.title: 4.6.1. The lists service: app/Services/ListesService.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Services/ListesService.php: the lists provided by the form. In a
// real-world application, they would come from a database.

namespace App\Services;

class ListesService
{
     // Each list: an associative array where the sent value maps to the displayed text
    public function titres(): array
    {
        return ['Mr' => 'Mr', 'Mme' => 'Mme', 'Melle' => 'Melle'];
    }

    public function pays(): array
    {
        return ['fr' => 'France', 'be' => 'Belgique', 'ch' => 'Suisse', 'ca' => 'Canada'];
    }

    public function loisirs(): array
    {
        return ['lecture' => 'lecture', 'musique' => 'musique', 'sport' => 'sport',
            'cinéma' => 'cinéma'];
    }

    public function langues(): array
    {
        return ['français' => 'français', 'anglais' => 'anglais', 'espagnol' => 'espagnol',
            'allemand' => 'allemand'];
    }
}

The form’s dropdown lists (titles, countries, hobbies, languages) are provided by a service, following the model in Example 06: in a real application, they would come from a database. Each list is an associative array: the key is the value sent to the server, and the value is the text displayed. The service is a concrete class: the container for [Laravel] knows how to create it without a declaration (Example 06).

docs.title: 4.6.2. The controller: app/Http/Controllers/FormulaireController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/FormulaireController.php: a form that uses all types of fields

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Services\ListesService;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Validator;
use Illuminate\Validation\Rule;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class FormulaireController
{
     // the list service is injected by the container (see Example 06)
    public function __construct(private ListesService $listes)
    {
    }

     // GET: the form, with initial values (one per field)
    public function afficher(): View
    {
        $saisie = ['titre' => 'Mme', 'pays' => 'fr', 'langues' => ['français'], 'jeton' => 'A7X2'];
        return view('formulaire.formulaire', ['listes' => $this->listes, 'saisie' => $saisie]);
    }

     // POST: the submitted fields are validated and then redisplayed by the form
    public function traiter(Request $request): View
    {
        $l = $this->listes;
         // array_keys: the valid VALEURS values for each list (the array keys)
        $validateur = Validator::make($request->post(), [
            'titre' => ['required', Rule::in(array_keys($l->titres()))],
            'naissance' => 'nullable|date_format:Y-m-d',
            'loisirs' => 'array',
            'loisirs.*' => Rule::in(array_keys($l->loisirs())),
            'pays' => ['required', Rule::in(array_keys($l->pays()))],
            'langues' => 'array',
            'langues.*' => Rule::in(array_keys($l->langues())),
        ]);
         // what the browser actually sent, parameter by parameter
        $recu = [];
        foreach ($request->post() as $nom => $valeur) {
            $recu[] = "$nom = [".implode(', ', (array) $valeur).']';
        }
        return view('formulaire.formulaire', [
            'listes' => $l,
            'saisie' => $request->post(),
            'recu' => implode("\n", $recu),
            'valide' => $validateur->passes(),
            'erreurs' => $validateur->errors(),
        ]);
    }
}
  • line 15: the service is injected by the constructor;
  • lines 20–23: the initial form values, an associative array: one value per field (an array for a multi-value field). The view receives these values in the variable [$saisie], along with the list service;
  • lines 31–39: The received fields are validated. Dropdown fields must contain one of the suggested values: a malicious user could send anything, not just what the page suggested. [Rule::in(...)] generates the rule [in] (example 08) from an array of values—in this case, the list keys ([array_keys]). Multiple fields are checked element by element ([loisirs.*], example 10). [date_format:Y-m-d]: A [<input type="date">] field exchanges its values with the server in the [aaaa-mm-jj] format, regardless of the format in which the browser displays it;
  • lines 41–44: for the example, the list of what the browser actually sent. [(array) $valeur] converts a single value into a one-element array (an array remains an array); [implode] combines the elements of an array into a string, separated by the first parameter;
  • lines 45–51: the form is redisplayed with the received values ([$saisie]), what the server received, the validation result ([passes()], the opposite of [fails()]), and any errors.

The routing table associates URL and [/formulaire] with action [afficher] for method GET, and to action [traiter] for method POST.

@extends('layout')

  <h1 class="h3">Un formulaire complet</h1>

        <input class="form-control" type="text" id="nom" name="nom" value="{{ $saisie['nom'] ?? '' }}">
      </div>
      <div class="col">
        {{-- un mot de passe n'est JAMAIS renvoyé dans la page : pas d'attribut value --}}
        <label class="form-label" for="mot_de_passe">Mot de passe</label>
        <input class="form-control" type="password" id="mot_de_passe" name="mot_de_passe">

      @foreach ($listes->loisirs() as $valeur => $texte)

          @endforeach

      </div>

  {{-- isset : vrai si la variable $recu a été passée à la vue (par l'action POST) --}}
  @isset($recu)

    <pre class="bg-light p-2 border">{{ $recu }}</pre>
    <p>Formulaire valide : {{ $valide ? 'oui' : 'non' }}</p>
    {{-- $erreurs->messages() : champ -> liste de ses messages d'erreur --}}

      @foreach ($erreurs->messages() as $champ => $messages)
