      @endforeach
    </ul>
  @endisset
@endsection
  • line 5: a form named POST;
  • line 7: the [@csrf] directive writes a hidden field named [_token], which contains the anti-CSRF token. A CSRF attack (*Cross-Site Request Forgery*) involves a malicious site tricking the victim’s browser into sending a form to our application. The browser includes our application’s cookies in the request—and thus the logged-in user’s session—making the request appear legitimate. The defense: every form in our application contains a random token linked to the user’s session, which the malicious site cannot know. The [PreventRequestForgery] middleware in the [web] group (Example 01) rejects any POST request (as well as PUT, PATCH, and DELETE) whose token is missing or invalid, even before the action is called: no action can omit it. This is the one that Examples 02 and 11 excluded for their [curl] requests;
  • line 8: our own hidden field;
  • lines 13–19: a group of radio buttons, one per title. All have the same attribute [name]: only one is selected at a time, and only one value is sent. Each button has its own identifier ([titre-0], [titre-1]...), generated using [$loop->index], to which its label refers. The [@checked] directive checks the button whose value matches the current title;
  • line 25: the name input field; [?? ''] handles the case where a name is not in the table;
  • Line 30: A password should never be sent back and forth within a page HTML: The field has no attribute [value]; it is always empty when displayed;
  • Lines 41–47: Checkboxes, styled like radio buttons. They also share the same name; however, multiple checkboxes can be selected, and the browser then sends multiple values: the name [loisirs[]] instructs [PHP] to organize them into an array (Example 10). The function [in_array] checks whether a value is present in an array;
  • lines 53–57: a drop-down list, whose current option is marked by [@selected];
  • line 62: a multi-select list (attribute [multiple]), displayed over four lines ([size]), whose name also ends with [[]];
  • line 73: a text field spanning two lines. Its value is entered between its tags, not in an attribute;
  • Lines 80–90: The directive [@isset] checks for the existence of a variable: [$recu] was passed to the view only by the action POST. [$erreurs->messages()] returns, for each invalid field, a list of its error messages (example 09).

docs.title: 4.6.4. Execution
docs.text:
The default values are visible: the “Mrs.” radio button, the country “France,” and the language “French.” HTML produces (excerpts):

<input type="hidden" name="_token" value="S9LZGqXi2UDriLcGxWPJl4llnyqA8IDHySIbjtPW" autocomplete="off">
<input type="hidden" name="jeton" value="A7X2">
...
<input class="form-check-input" type="radio" id="titre-1" name="titre"
       value="Mme" checked>
<label class="form-check-label" for="titre-1">Mme</label>
...
<input class="form-control" type="date" id="naissance" name="naissance" value="">
...
<input class="form-check-input" type="checkbox" id="loisirs-0" name="loisirs[]"
       value="lecture" >
<label class="form-check-label" for="loisirs-0">lecture</label>
...
<select class="form-select" id="pays" name="pays">
  <option value="fr" selected>France</option>
  <option value="be" >Belgique</option>
...
<select class="form-select" id="langues" name="langues[]" multiple size="4">
  <option value="français" selected>français</option>
...
<textarea class="form-control" id="commentaire" name="commentaire" rows="2"></textarea>

The anti-CSRF token is a random 40-character string, stored in the user’s session (example 20). Let’s fill out the form and submit it:

The page shows what the server received: one parameter per field, with multiple values for the checkboxes and the dropdown list; the password was sent but is not displayed again in its field. The hidden field [jeton] was returned exactly as it was: this is how to send and receive information that the user cannot see (the case study uses this for a record’s version number). However, a hidden field is not a protected field: the user can modify it using their browser’s developer tools, and the server must validate it just like any other field. We also note that the anti-CSRF token ([_token]) is among the received fields.

Now let’s submit a form without a token, using [curl]:

curl -i -d "nom=Martin&pays=xx" http://localhost:8000/form

HTTP/1.1 419 unknown status
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
...
        <title>Page Expired</title>
...

The request is rejected by the [PreventRequestForgery] middleware with status code 419, specific to [Laravel] (*Page Expired*: this is the message seen by a user whose session expired between the time the form was displayed and the time it was submitted). To resolve this, [curl] must behave like a browser: first request the form, while retaining the session cookie (option [-c], which saves received cookies to a file), then resend the cookie (option [-b]) and the token read from the page:

curl -c cookies.txt http://localhost:8000/form
curl -b cookies.txt -d "_token=h1huM8SWBJjWSgB4TTZz5jc8SnUDQtbrg4u0fHbf&nom=Martin&pays=xx" http://localhost:8000/form

...
    <h2 class="h5 mt-3">Ce que le serveur a reçu</h2>
    <pre class="bg-light p-2 border">_token = [h1huM8SWBJjWSgB4TTZz5jc8SnUDQtbrg4u0fHbf]
nom = [Martin]
pays = [xx]</pre>
    <p>Formulaire valide : non</p>
    <ul>
              <li>titre : The titre field is required.</li>
              <li>pays : The selected pays is invalid.</li>
          </ul>
...

(the token is the one from the page received by the first command). Two errors: the country [xx] is not among the options; no title was sent. The messages are in English: the following example translates them into French.

docs.title: 4.7. Example 19: Form Validation
docs.text: A registration form, where each field has its own validation rules. If an error occurs, the form is redisplayed with the user’s input and a message below each invalid field. This example uses the standard approach of [Laravel]: a form request (Example 08) validates the fields before the action; if an error occurs, [Laravel] redirects to the form page, preserving the user’s input and the errors for the next request.

docs.title: 4.7.1. The form: app/Http/Requests/InscriptionRequest.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Requests/InscriptionRequest.php: the form fields and their constraints

namespace App\Http\Requests;

use Illuminate\Foundation\Http\FormRequest;

class InscriptionRequest extends FormRequest
{
     // the rules for each field. The spaces surrounding the input have already been
     // removed by the TrimStrings middleware, and an empty entry replaced with null
    public function rules(): array
    {
        return [
            'nom' => 'required|max:20',
             // email:filter: validation of the filter_var function from PHP, which
             // requires a fully qualified domain name (exemple.fr, not "example")
            'email' => 'required|email:filter',
            'age' => 'required|integer|between:18,120',
            'mot_de_passe' => 'required|min:6',
             // a rule that applies to DEUX fields: "same" compares this field to another
            'confirmation' => 'required|same:mot_de_passe',
        ];
    }

     // error messages, champ.règle => message
    public function messages(): array
    {
        return [
            'nom.required' => 'Le nom est obligatoire.',
            'nom.max' => 'Le nom ne doit pas dépasser 20 caractères.',
            'email.required' => "L'adresse électronique est obligatoire.",
            'email.email' => 'Adresse électronique invalide.',
            'age.required' => "L'âge est obligatoire.",
            'age.between' => "L'âge doit être compris entre 18 et 120 ans.",
            'mot_de_passe.required' => 'Le mot de passe est obligatoire.',
            'mot_de_passe.min' => 'Le mot de passe doit comporter au moins 6 caractères.',
            'confirmation.required' => 'La confirmation est obligatoire.',
            'confirmation.same' => 'La confirmation ne correspond pas au mot de passe.',
        ];
    }
}
  • Lines 12–23: the validation rules for each field (Example 08). The spaces surrounding the input have already been removed by the [TrimStrings] middleware (example 08): a name consisting of spaces becomes an empty string, then [null], and will be rejected by [required];
  • Line 18: The [email] rule accepts variants, which determine which validation is applied. By default, it follows the email address standard, which accepts [martin@exemple] (a hostname without a domain). [email:filter] uses the [filter_var] function from [PHP] (example 07), which requires a fully qualified domain name ([exemple.fr]);
  • line 19: [integer] followed by [between:18,120];
  • Line 22: A rule that applies to two fields: [same:mot_de_passe] compares the value of one field to that of another field. [Laravel] also provides the rule [confirmed], which, when applied to the field [mot_de_passe], would require a field named [mot_de_passe_confirmation];
  • Lines 27–40: The method [messages] provides messages specific to this form. Each key designates a field and a rule ([nom.required]); a single key such as [required] would apply to all fields. These messages take precedence over those in the language files (example 09).

Messages not provided by the class come from the file [lang/fr/validation.php] (the file [.env] sets the language to [fr]; see example 09):

<?php
// lang/fr/validation.php: messages that the class InscriptionRequest
// does not provide itself
return [
    'integer' => 'Un nombre entier est attendu.',
];

This is the case for the message from rule [integer], which is displayed only if something other than a number is entered in the age field—something a browser does not do (we’ll see this with [curl]).

docs.title: 4.7.2. The controller: app/Http/Controllers/InscriptionController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/InscriptionController.php: a form validated by the server

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Http\Requests\InscriptionRequest;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class InscriptionController
{
     // GET /registration: the form; ?html5=true: we let the browser
     // validate it before submission
    public function afficher(Request $request): View
    {
        return view('inscription.inscription', ['html5' => $request->query('html5') === 'true']);
    }

     // POST /registration: the action is called only if the form is VALIDE.
     // Otherwise, Laravel REDIRIGE redirects to the form page, preserving the input and
     // the errors for the next request (see `old` and `@error` in the views)
    public function inscrire(InscriptionRequest $request): View
    {
        return view('inscription.bienvenue', ['inscription' => $request->validated()]);
    }
}
  • lines 14–17: the form display. The parameter [?html5=true] enables browser validation (see below);
  • lines 22–25: the action only accepts valid forms: the form request [InscriptionRequest] was validated before it was called (example 08). It displays the welcome page with the validated data. (The following example will show that it is better to redirect after a successful POST.)

What about an invalid form? It never reaches the action. The form request triggers a [ValidationException] (example 08), which [Laravel] handles as follows for a request coming from a browser: it stores the errors and the entered values (except passwords) in the user’s session, then responds with a redirect to the previous page—the form page. The browser immediately requests this page again (via a GET), and the form view retrieves the errors and user input, which the session provides only once (we will see this “flash” data mechanism in the next example). The form is thus redisplayed via its GET action, rather than via the POST action: this is already the Post/Redirect/Get pattern from the following example, applied to errors.

docs.title: 4.7.3. A reusable field: resources/views/components/champ.blade.php
docs.text:
Each field is displayed in the same way: a label, the input field, and, in the event of an error, the area outlined in red and the message below it. A component prevents you from having to write this five times:

{{-- un champ de saisie, avec son libellé et son PREMIER message d'erreur.
     old($nom) : la saisie précédente, conservée par Laravel après un formulaire
     invalide ; $attributes : les autres attributs donnés au composant (required,
     min, max...), recopiés sur la balise input --}}
@props(['nom', 'libelle', 'type' => 'text'])
<div class="mb-2">
  <label class="form-label" for="{{ $nom }}">{{ $libelle }}</label>
  <input {{ $attributes->class(['form-control', 'is-invalid' => $errors->has($nom)]) }}
         type="{{ $type }}" id="{{ $nom }}" name="{{ $nom }}"
         @if ($type !== 'password') value="{{ old($nom) }}" @endif>
  {{-- @error : le bloc n'est affiché que si le champ a une erreur, dont le
       premier message est dans la variable $message --}}
  @error($nom)
    <div class="invalid-feedback">{{ $message }}</div>
  @enderror
</div>
  • line 5: the component’s parameters: the field name, its label, and its type, [text] by default;
  • line 8: the variable [$attributes] contains the attributes assigned to the component that are not parameters declared by [@props] (here, [required], [min], [max]...): when written in the tag, it copies them over. Its method [class] adds the attribute [class] to it, similar to the directive [@class] (Example 16): The [is-invalid] class of [Bootstrap] outlines the field in red if the field contains an error. The variable [$errors] is available in all views: it is a “bag” of messages (Example 09)—containing errors from the previous form stored in the session—or an empty bag; [has] checks for errors in a field;
  • Line 10: The function [old] returns the value entered in the previous form, stored in the session, or [null]. A field of type [password] does not have the [value] attribute (example 18);
  • Lines 13–15: The block [@error] ... [@enderror] is displayed only if the field contains an error; in that case, its first message is stored in the variable [$message]. The element [invalid-feedback] is displayed in red by [Bootstrap], below a zone labeled [is-invalid].

docs.title: 4.7.4. The views
docs.text:
@extends('layout')

       envoie le formulaire tel quel ; seul le serveur valide --}}

  • line 12: the [novalidate] attribute disables browser validation: the form is submitted as-is, and only the server validates it. This is what we want to observe first;
  • lines 14–18: one component per field. The attributes HTML5 ([required], [maxlength], [min], [max], [minlength], [type="email"]) allow the browser to verify the input even before it is submitted (we’ll cover this later). [Laravel] does not derive these from the validation rules: they are written in the view and must remain consistent with the rules.

    @endif

</body>
</html>
  • lines 16–18: a general message at the bottom of the page if the previous form contained errors ([any()] checks whether the bag contains at least one message), in an area whose style is defined by [public/css/styles.css] (example 15). The [role="alert"] attribute flags this for screen readers.
@extends('layout')

@section('contenu')
  {{-- $inscription : les données validées --}}
  <h1 class="h3">Bienvenue {{ $inscription['nom'] }}</h1>
  <p>Votre inscription est enregistrée : adresse <b>{{ $inscription['email'] }}</b>,
    âge <b>{{ $inscription['age'] }}</b> ans.</p>
@endsection

[$inscription] contains the validated data: the name with spaces removed, the age (a string; see Example 08).

docs.title: 4.7.5. Execution
docs.text:
Let’s submit a form full of errors: a name consisting of spaces, an email address without a full domain, an age of 12, a password that’s too short, and a different confirmation:

The input was preserved (except for the passwords), and each error is flagged below its corresponding field. URL is the form’s token, and [/inscription] indicates that the page was displayed by the action GET after the redirect. With [curl], by providing the anti-CSRF token as in Example 18, we see this redirection:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -d "_token=...&nom=Martin&email=martin@exemple.fr&age=abc&mot_de_passe=abcdef&confirmation=abcdef" http://localhost:8000/registration

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: http://localhost:8000/registration
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
...

You can also send something a browser wouldn’t send, such as a non-numeric age. The following page ([curl -b cookies.txt http://localhost:8000/inscription]) shows the age field, with its input and the message from rule [integer], taken from the language file:

  <input class="form-control is-invalid" required="required" min="18" max="120"
         type="number" id="age" name="age"
          value="abc" >
      <div class="invalid-feedback">Un nombre entier est attendu.</div>

We also see the attributes HTML5 copied by [$attributes]: [required] (written as [required="required"], an equivalent form), [min], [max].

docs.title: 4.7.6. Browser validation
docs.text:
Let’s remove the [novalidate] attribute by following the “Enable” link ([?html5=true] setting). The browser then checks the attributes [required], [type="email"], [min], [maxlength]... before submitting the form, and displays its own messages in a tooltip below the first invalid field (“Please fill in this field,” “The value must be greater than or equal to 18,” etc.): the form is not submitted as long as there is an error.

This validation is convenient for the user: it’s immediate, with no back-and-forth with the server. But it does not replace server-side validation: a user can disable it, and a program like [curl] ignores it completely. The rule is absolute: the server always validates; browser-side validation is merely an added convenience.

A correct entry, at last. The name, entered with spaces on either side, was cleaned up by the [TrimStrings] middleware:

docs.title: 4.8. Example 20: The Post/Redirect/Get pattern
docs.text:
When a POST action returns a page, that page is the result of a POST. If the user refreshes the page (by pressing [F5]), the browser sends the POST request, following a warning that few people read: the command is sent twice, and the message is posted twice. The Post/Redirect/Get pattern (PRG) avoids this problem: a successful POST action does not return a page; it responds with a redirect (example 04) to a page GET, which the browser requests immediately. Reloading this page simply re-executes the GET action.

One problem remains: the GET page would like to display a message (“the task has been added”), but it is the POST action that knows this message, and it cannot pass a variable to a request that has not yet occurred. The solution: the flash message, stored in the session by the action POST, is retained until the next request, displayed, and then discarded. This is the mechanism that [Laravel] was already using, in Example 19, for form errors.

docs.title: 4.8.1. The service: app/Services/TachesService.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Services/TachesService.php: the task list, shared by all
// users. In PHP, objects are not retained after the request: the list is
// stored in Laravel’s CACHE (here, a file in the storage/framework/cache directory)

namespace App\Services;

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Cache;

class TachesService
{
    private const CLE = 'taches';

     /** @return list<string> */
    public function liste(): array
    {
         // the value stored under the key [taches], or the initial list
        return Cache::get(self::CLE, ['Lire le chapitre 3']);
    }

    public function ajouter(string $libelle): void
    {
         // multiple requests may be executed (EN, MÊME, TEMPS—the server
         // processes them in multiple processes): a lock ensures that only once at a
         // time reads, modifies, and rewrites the list. block(5, ...) waits for lock 5
         // seconds at most, executes the function, and then releases the lock
        Cache::lock('taches-verrou', 10)->block(5, function () use ($libelle) {
            $taches = $this->liste();
            $taches[] = $libelle;
             // forever: the value is retained indefinitely
            Cache::forever(self::CLE, $taches);
        });
    }
}

The task list is shared by all users and must persist from one request to the next. In [Java], [C#], or [Python], it would be kept in memory within a single service. In [PHP], this is impossible: as we saw in examples 01 and 06, nothing survives the query. The list must therefore be stored outside of [PHP]: in a database, a file... or in the cache of [Laravel], which we are using here.

  • Line 18: The [Cache] interface provides access to the application’s cache: a store of key→value pairs. The [.env] file in the examples stores this data in files within the [storage/framework/cache] folder ([CACHE_STORE=file], Example 01); in production, a dedicated server, such as [Redis], is preferred. [get] returns the value stored under a key, or the default value provided as the second parameter. Any value (in this case, an array of strings) can be stored: [Laravel] serializes it—that is, it converts it to text—using the [serialize] function from [PHP];
  • Lines 27–32: The development server, like a production server, can process multiple requests at the same time, in multiple processes (the environment variable [PHP_CLI_SERVER_WORKERS] sets the number of processes for [php artisan serve]). Two simultaneous inserts could read the same list, each add its own task to it, and then write it back: the second write would overwrite the first task. A lock ensures that only one request at a time executes the code it protects: [Cache::lock('taches-verrou', 10)] creates a named lock—which is also stored in the cache—that expires after no more than 10 seconds (if the request holding it were to abruptly terminate); [block(5, fonction)] waits up to 5 seconds for the lock to become available, acquires it, executes the function, and then releases it. The keyword [use] in an anonymous function gives it access to a variable in the containing function (here, [$libelle]); an arrow function, on the other hand, automatically sees these variables;
  • Line 31: [forever] stores a value indefinitely; [put(clé, valeur, secondes)] would store it for a specified duration.

docs.title: 4.8.2. The controller: app/Http/Controllers/TachesController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/TachesController.php: the Post/Redirect/Get pattern

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Services\TachesService;
use Illuminate\Http\RedirectResponse;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class TachesController
{
    public function __construct(private TachesService $taches)
    {
    }

     // GET /tasks: the list and the add form
    public function afficher(): View
    {
        return view('taches.taches', ['taches' => $this->taches->liste()]);
    }

     // POST /tasks: the Post/Redirect/Get pattern
    public function ajouter(Request $request): View|RedirectResponse
    {
        $libelle = $request->string('libelle')->value();
        if ($libelle === '' || mb_strlen($libelle) > 40) {
             // Invalid input: the page is reloaded without redirection
            return view('taches.taches', ['taches' => $this->taches->liste(),
                'libelle' => $libelle,
                'erreur' => 'Le libellé doit comporter de 1 à 40 caractères.']);
        }
        $this->taches->ajouter($libelle);
         // No page: redirect to the GET page; `with` displays a message
         // "flash" in the session: it will survive the redirection for the request SUIVANTE
        return redirect()->route('taches')->with('message', "La tâche [$libelle] a été ajoutée.");
    }

     // POST /tasks/no-program: the counterexample (a page in response to POST)
    public function ajouterSansPrg(Request $request): View
    {
        $this->taches->ajouter($request->string('libelle')->value() ?: '(sans titre)');
        return view('taches.taches', ['taches' => $this->taches->liste(), 'sansPrg' => true]);
    }
}
  • lines 26–31: The input is validated manually to keep the example simple. An invalid entry is displayed again, without redirection: there is nothing to protect against a duplicate submission, since nothing has been modified. [mb_strlen] counts the characters in a string UTF-8;
  • line 36: the redirect to the page GET, named [taches]. The [with] method of a redirect places a flash message in the session: data retained only for the next request;
  • lines 40–43: the counterexample: a page in response to POST. The operator [?:] returns its left operand if it is “true” (here, a non-empty string), and the right operand otherwise.

The routing table:

<?php
// routes/web.php: the routes from Example 20

use App\Http\Controllers\TachesController;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::controller(TachesController::class)->group(function () {
    Route::get('taches', 'afficher')->name('taches');
    Route::post('taches', 'ajouter');
    Route::post('taches/sans-prg', 'ajouterSansPrg');
});

docs.title: 4.8.4. Where are flash messages stored?
docs.text:
Between the POST request and the subsequent GET request, the message must be stored somewhere: in the user’s session. The [Laravel] session is stored on the server: the [.env] file in the examples stores it in a file within the [storage/framework/sessions] folder ([SESSION_DRIVER=file]), with one file per user. The browser, on the other hand, receives only a session ID in the [exemple20_session] cookie (the name is derived from [APP_NAME]), which it sends back with every request. Let’s examine this using [curl], while storing the cookies in a file (options [-c] and [-b], Example 18), and providing the anti-CSRF token:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -d "_token=...&libelle=Faire%20les%20exercices" http://localhost:8000/tasks

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: http://localhost:8000/tasks
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Set-Cookie: XSRF-TOKEN=eyJpdiI6ImQ3ZVRaWXY5cUpLckxXdUhnbjNyNUE9PSIsInZhbHVlIjoiZWFsOVg3...; expires=...; Max-Age=7200; path=/; samesite=lax
Set-Cookie: exemple20_session=eyJpdiI6IjhOME1IWUZ3Q3J3bHpoWXVhZHYvdkE9PSIsInZhbHVlIjoiQUtz...; expires=...; Max-Age=7200; path=/; httponly; samesite=lax
...

The response to POST is a redirect (status code 302, header [Location]), accompanied by the session cookie. Its value is encrypted with the key [APP_KEY] (this is the role of the [EncryptCookies] middleware in the [web] group): the user cannot read or modify it. When decrypted, it contains only the session ID—40 random characters—which is also the name of the session file on the server: [storage/framework/sessions/HNuWctWJ0HcPvmsAhFN5v3iCiw1SFFDMXv46F6og]. Here is that file, following the request POST (displayed across multiple lines):

a:4:{s:6:"_token";s:40:"tCPYomkewzcCqTihVq2VZEdjpNl00hNm5oimGb4r";
     s:9:"_previous";a:2:{s:3:"url";s:28:"http://localhost:8000/taches";s:5:"route";s:6:"taches";}
     s:6:"_flash";a:2:{s:3:"old";a:1:{i:0;s:7:"message";}s:3:"new";a:0:{}}
     s:7:"message";s:49:"La tâche [Faire les exercices] a été ajoutée.";}

This is a serialized [PHP] array: [a:4] indicates an array of 4 elements, [s:6:"_token"] a 6-byte string... It contains the session’s anti-CSRF token, the URL from the previous page ([_previous], which is used by the redirect to the previous page in Example 19), our message, and the [_flash] list of flash data. At the end of each request, the flash data set during the request (list [new]) is moved to the list [old], and the data that was already in [old] is removed: thus, a piece of flash data survives for exactly one request. Let’s follow the redirection by sending the cookie back:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt http://localhost:8000/tasks

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
...
          <div class="alert alert-success" role="status">La tâche [Faire les exercices] a été ajoutée.</div>
...
          <li>Lire le chapitre 3</li>
          <li>Faire les exercices</li>
...

The message is displayed, and after this request, the session file no longer contains it:

a:3:{s:6:"_token";s:40:"tCPYomkewzcCqTihVq2VZEdjpNl00hNm5oimGb4r";
     s:9:"_previous";a:2:{s:3:"url";s:28:"http://localhost:8000/taches";s:5:"route";s:6:"taches";}
     s:6:"_flash";a:2:{s:3:"old";a:0:{}s:3:"new";a:0:{}}}

A new request, GET, would no longer display the message. The task list, however, is stored in a cache file whose name is calculated based on the key ([storage/framework/cache/data/02/a1/02a1657007815300c992ef16d5ee9ce22f6ef096]):

9999999999a:2:{i:0;s:18:"Lire le chapitre 3";i:1;s:19:"Faire les exercices";}

The first ten digits represent the value’s expiration date (in this case, never); the rest is the serialized list.

docs.title: 4.8.5. Execution
docs.text:
Adding a task: the browser followed the redirect; URL corresponds to the page GET, which can be safely reloaded.

An invalid entry, redisplayed with its error message:

The counterexample: the page is the response to POST, and its URL is [/taches/sans-prg]. If you click on [F5], the browser asks if you want to resubmit the form; if you agree, the task is added a second time.

docs.title: 4.9. Example 21: Links, Buttons, and Confirmation
docs.text:
A principle of the HTTP protocol: a GET request does not change anything. Browsers, search engines, and tools that preload pages freely follow links without asking the user for permission. A “delete” link ([<a href="/contacts/2/supprimer">]) would therefore be dangerous: a bot crawling the site would delete everything. In a web application:

  • viewing is done via a link ([<a href>]), which sends a GET request;
  • editing (save, duplicate, delete) is done via a button placed in a form, protected by an anti-CSRF token.

This example manages a contact list and displays a confirmation window before each deletion.

docs.title: 4.9.1. The service: app/Services/ContactsService.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Services/ContactsService.php: contacts, shared by everyone, stored in
// the Laravel cache (see Example 20)

namespace App\Services;

use App\Models\Contact;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Cache;

class ContactsService
{
    private const CLE = 'contacts';

     /** @return array{contacts: list<Contact>, dernierId: int} */
    private function donnees(): array
    {
        return Cache::get(self::CLE, [
            'contacts' => [
                new Contact(1, 'Marie Durand', '01 23 45 67 89'),
                new Contact(2, 'Paul Martin', '06 12 34 56 78'),
                new Contact(3, 'Philippe Jandot', '02 98 76 54 32'),
            ],
            'dernierId' => 3,
        ]);
    }

     // a data modification, under a lock: the function receives the data,
     // modifies it (&), and returns the result of the operation
    private function modifierDonnees(callable $operation): mixed
    {
        return Cache::lock('contacts-verrou', 10)->block(5, function () use ($operation) {
            $donnees = $this->donnees();
            $resultat = $operation($donnees);
            Cache::forever(self::CLE, $donnees);
            return $resultat;
        });
    }

     /** @return list<Contact> */
    public function liste(): array
    {
        return $this->donnees()['contacts'];
    }

     // the contact, or null if it does not exist
    public function lire(int $id): ?Contact
    {
        return array_find($this->liste(), fn (Contact $c) => $c->id === $id);
    }

    public function modifier(int $id, string $nom, string $telephone): ?Contact
    {
        return $this->modifierDonnees(function (array &$donnees) use ($id, $nom, $telephone) {
            foreach ($donnees['contacts'] as $i => $contact) {
                if ($contact->id === $id) {
                     // A contact is immutable (read-only): a new one is created,
                     // which replaces the old one in the array
                    return $donnees['contacts'][$i] = new Contact($id, $nom, $telephone);
                }
            }
            return null;
        });
    }

    public function ajouter(string $nom, string $telephone): Contact
    {
        return $this->modifierDonnees(function (array &$donnees) use ($nom, $telephone) {
            $contact = new Contact(++$donnees['dernierId'], $nom, $telephone);
            $donnees['contacts'][] = $contact;
            return $contact;
        });
    }

    public function supprimer(int $id): ?Contact
    {
        return $this->modifierDonnees(function (array &$donnees) use ($id) {
            foreach ($donnees['contacts'] as $i => $contact) {
                if ($contact->id === $id) {
                     // array_splice removes element i from the array and renumbers the subsequent elements
                    array_splice($donnees['contacts'], $i, 1);
                    return $contact;
                }
            }
            return null;
        });
    }
}

Contacts are stored in the cache, just like the tasks in Example 20. Each contact is an immutable [Contact] object (an ID, a name, a phone number), stored in an array with the most recently assigned ID. A few points about [PHP]:

  • Lines 29–37: All modifications follow the same pattern: acquire the lock, read the data, modify it, write it back, and release the lock. This method writes to the array once; each modification passes a function (of type [callable], “callable”) to it, which receives the data and modifies it. The function must modify the array itself, not a copy: its parameter is declared as [array &$donnees], where [&] specifies a pass-by-reference (without [&], an array is copied; see Example 06);
  • lines 51–63: A contact is immutable: a new one is created, which replaces the old one in the array. An assignment is an expression whose value is the assigned value: [return $donnees['contacts'][$i] = new Contact(...)] replaces the contact and returns it;
  • line 68: [++] placed before a variable increments it by 1 and returns the new value;
  • line 80: [array_splice] removes an element from the array and renumbers the subsequent elements;
  • The methods return [null] for a nonexistent contact: it is up to the controller to decide on the response.

docs.title: 4.9.2. The controller: app/Http/Controllers/ContactsController.php
docs.text:
<?php
// app/Http/Controllers/ContactsController.php: links (GET) and buttons (POST, DELETE)

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Models\Contact;
use App\Services\ContactsService;
use Illuminate\Http\RedirectResponse;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\View\View;

class ContactsController
{
    public function __construct(private ContactsService $contacts)
    {
    }

     // the contact, or a 404 response if it does not exist
    private static function contactOu404(?Contact $contact): Contact
    {
        abort_if($contact === null, 404, 'contact inconnu');
        return $contact;
    }

     // a LIEN (<a href>): a GET request, which does not change anything
    public function liste(): View
    {
        return view('contacts.liste', ['contacts' => $this->contacts->liste()]);
    }

    public function fiche(int $id): View
    {
        return view('contacts.fiche', ['contact' => self::contactOu404($this->contacts->lire($id))]);
    }

     // a BOUTON in a POST form: a request that modifies data
    public function enregistrer(Request $request, int $id): RedirectResponse
    {
        $contact = self::contactOu404($this->contacts->modifier($id,
            $request->string('nom')->value(), $request->string('telephone')->value()));
        return redirect()->route('contacts')->with('message', "Le contact [$contact->nom] a été modifié.");
    }

     // same form, different button (formaction attribute): different action
    public function dupliquer(Request $request, int $id): RedirectResponse
    {
        $copie = $this->contacts->ajouter($request->string('nom')->value().' (copie)',
            $request->string('telephone')->value());
        return redirect()->route('contacts')->with('message', "Le contact [$copie->nom] a été créé.");
    }

     // a DELETE request, simulated by a POST form (see @method in the view)
    public function supprimer(int $id): RedirectResponse
    {
        $contact = self::contactOu404($this->contacts->supprimer($id));
        return redirect()->route('contacts')->with('message', "Le contact [$contact->nom] a été supprimé.");
    }
}
  • lines 19–23: a utility function: a nonexistent contact terminates the action with a 404 response ([abort_if], see Example 15);
  • lines 26–34: the two actions GET, which do not modify anything: the list and a contact’s record;
  • lines 37–42: saving the record: an action POST, which follows the schema PRG. The same URL and [/contacts/2] are handled by two different actions, depending on the method: GET displays, POST saves;
  • Lines 45–50: duplication—another action, POST, triggered by a second button on the same form;
  • Lines 53–57: Deletion, handled by a query DELETE.

The routing table:

<?php
// routes/web.php: the routes from Example 21

use App\Http\Controllers\ContactsController;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Route;

Route::prefix('contacts')->controller(ContactsController::class)->group(function () {
    Route::get('/', 'liste')->name('contacts');
    Route::get('{id}', 'fiche')->whereNumber('id')->name('contacts.fiche');
    Route::post('{id}', 'enregistrer')->whereNumber('id')->name('contacts.enregistrer');
    Route::post('{id}/dupliquer', 'dupliquer')->whereNumber('id')->name('contacts.dupliquer');
    Route::delete('{id}', 'supprimer')->whereNumber('id')->name('contacts.supprimer');
});
  • Line 12: Deletion is declared for the HTTP method DELETE, which the HTTP protocol specifies for deleting a resource. However, a HTML form can only send GET and POST requests. [Laravel] circumvents this limitation: a POST form containing a hidden field [_method], with a value of [DELETE] (or [PUT], [PATCH]), is treated as a request for that method. This is method spoofing, which is implemented by the [@method] directive in views.

docs.title: 4.9.4. The confirmation window
docs.text:
The browser can display a confirmation box (function [JavaScript] [confirm]), but it is not very attractive, and its appearance depends on the browser. Here we use a modal window from [Bootstrap], displayed by a few lines of [JavaScript]. The window is a fragment included in the template and is therefore present—though hidden—on all pages:

{{-- une seule fenêtre pour toute la page, cachée (d-none) au départ --}}
<div id="modale-confirmation" class="d-none">
  <div class="modal-backdrop fade show"></div>
  <div class="modal fade show d-block" tabindex="-1" role="alertdialog" aria-modal="true">
    <div class="modal-dialog modal-dialog-centered">
      <div class="modal-content">
        <div class="modal-header">
          <h5 class="modal-title">Confirmation</h5>
        </div>
        <div class="modal-body">
          <p class="mb-0" id="modale-confirmation-message"></p>
        </div>
        <div class="modal-footer">
          <button type="button" class="btn btn-secondary" data-action="non">Non, revenir</button>
          <button type="button" class="btn btn-danger" data-action="oui">Oui, confirmer</button>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
  • line 2: the [d-none] class from [Bootstrap] hides the element;
  • lines 3–4: the gray background, followed by the window, are rendered by the classes of [Bootstrap];
  • line 11: the message's position;
  • lines 14–15: the two buttons, of type [button] (not [submit]: they do not submit any form), distinguished by their [data-action] attribute.

  • line 19: the window, included on all pages;
  • line 21: the script, placed at the end of the page: when it runs, the elements it searches for already exist. It is stored in the [public/js] folder.

The script [public/js/app.js]:

// Confirmation of forms with the attribute `data-confirmation="..."`
// Without JavaScript, these forms are simply submitted without confirmation.
(() => {
  const modale = document.getElementById('modale-confirmation');
  const message = document.getElementById('modale-confirmation-message');
  let enAttente = null; // The form to submit if confirmation is given

   // 1. We intercept the submission of forms that require confirmation
  document.querySelectorAll('form[data-confirmation]').forEach((formulaire) => {
    formulaire.addEventListener('submit', (evenement) => {
      evenement.preventDefault(); // Sending is suspended
      enAttente = formulaire;
      message.textContent = formulaire.dataset.confirmation;
      modale.classList.remove('d-none'); // The window appears
    });
  });

   // 2. The two buttons in the window
  modale.addEventListener('click', (evenement) => {
    const action = evenement.target.dataset.action;
    if (action === 'oui') {
      enAttente.submit(); // Submit, SANS trigger the 'submit' event again
    } else if (action === 'non') {
      modale.classList.add('d-none');
      enAttente = null;
    }
  });
})();
  • line 3: the code is enclosed in an anonymous function, which is executed immediately; its variables do not interfere with those of the other scripts on the page;
  • lines 4–6: the window, the message location, and the form awaiting confirmation;
  • lines 9–14: for each form that has a [data-confirmation] attribute, the [submit] event—triggered when the form is submitted—is intercepted. [preventDefault()] suspends submission; the form is put on hold, and its message ([dataset.confirmation], the value of the [data-confirmation] attribute) is displayed in the window, which appears;
  • lines 19–25: a single handler for clicks in the window: [evenement.target] is the element clicked; its attribute [data-action] specifies which button it is. “Yes” submits the pending form using the [submit()] method, which—unlike clicking a button—does not trigger the [submit] event (otherwise, the window would reappear); “No” hides the window.

Without [JavaScript], the form is simply submitted without confirmation: the page remains usable. This is progressive enhancement: [JavaScript] adds convenience, but the application does not depend on it.
